About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
Sigmund Freud (say FROYD) was a doctor in Vienna, Austria, more than a hundred years ago. He listened to people talk about their worries, and he noticed that they often talked about their dreams.

Freud asked a big question: do dreams mean anything? Many people in his time said dreams were just nonsense from a tired brain. Freud thought every dream has a hidden meaning, like a puzzle or a secret code.

Scientists today do not agree with all of Freud's answers. But they agree on one thing you can test yourself: dreams often borrow pieces of your own day, such as a place you visited, a person you talked to, or something you were looking forward to.

blocks.name: gb-freud-sleep
blocks.cap: Slide through one night of sleep. Your brain goes through cycles, and the most story-like dreams come in the stage called REM. (A typical pattern, not one person's night.)

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

A dream journal. Keep a notebook by your bed for a week. As soon as you wake up, write or draw anything you remember, even one picture. Later in the day, look for links: did anything in the dream come from the day before? Many dreams fade within minutes of waking, so be quick!

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Sigmund Freud (1856–1939) grew up in Vienna, trained as a physician, and did research on the nervous system before he turned to treating patients with nervous complaints. In Paris in 1885–86 he watched the neurologist Jean-Martin Charcot at work, and with his Viennese colleague Josef Breuer he published Studies on Hysteria (1895). Out of that work came his "talking cure," which he named psychoanalysis.

The Interpretation of Dreams appeared in November 1899, though the title page says 1900. It sold slowly at first, but Freud always counted it his most important book. A. A. Brill, a New York psychiatrist, made the first English translation in 1913.

Freud begins with a long survey of what earlier writers had said about dreams. Then, in Chapter II, he gives his method and tries it on a dream of his own from July 1895, about a patient he calls Irma. He takes the dream apart piece by piece and writes down whatever comes to mind about each piece. This is free association.
Freud's reading of his Irma dream (our summary): the dream let him off the hook. It showed that a patient's continuing illness was someone else's fault, not his, which was what he wished.

blocks.text: Two layers: what you remember and what lies beneath

blocks.html: Freud separates the dream as you remember it, the manifest content, from the hidden thoughts he looks for beneath it, the latent content. Why the disguise? Freud's answer is a kind of inner censorship: thoughts the dreamer would not accept are allowed through only in disguise.

head: Freud's name
What it does (our summary)
rows: Many dream thoughts are squeezed into one image or one mixed-up person.
The feeling moves from what matters onto some small, unimportant detail.
Ideas are turned into pictures that a dream can show.
The dream is patched into a story that seems to hang together.
blocks.cap: The "dream-work" in Chapter VI.

blocks.name: gb-freud-dreamwork
blocks.cap: An invented, everyday dream, read step by step: first as Freud would, then as many researchers would today.

blocks.html: In the last chapter Freud builds a model of the mind with conscious, preconscious and unconscious parts. He ends with the sentence the book is most remembered for:
Via regia is Latin for "royal road," the main highway.

Freud's dream book changed how people talked about the mind, in medicine, literature and everyday speech. Its scientific claims have fared unevenly. In 1953 Eugene Aserinsky and Nathaniel Kleitman discovered REM sleep, the stage of sleep most linked with vivid dreams, and dream research moved into sleep laboratories. In 1977 J. Allan Hobson and Robert McCarley proposed that dreams arise as the brain makes a story out of its own signals during REM, a direct challenge to Freud. Large studies of dream reports find that dreams often carry the dreamer's waking concerns, which fits part of Freud's picture, but they do not support the claim that every dream fulfils a wish; many dreams are anxious or plain. The philosopher Karl Popper argued that psychoanalysis could explain any outcome and so could not be tested. Defenders reply that some of Freud's broader ideas, such as mental processes outside awareness, are now widely accepted in other forms. Most researchers today treat the book as a landmark in the history of ideas rather than as current science.

Thinking Freud used a dream dictionary ("a snake always means X"). He mostly worked from the dreamer's own associations, and warned that the same image could mean different things for different people, though he did also discuss some common symbols.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Aristotle wrote short works on sleep and dreams, explaining them from the body; Freud quotes him in his opening survey.

Sophocles' Oedipus the King, earlier on this ladder: in this book Freud first sketched what he later called the Oedipus complex, his claim that young children have strong, mixed feelings toward their parents that are later forgotten. It became one of his most disputed ideas, with little support from later research.
William James (the rung before this one in the 19th century) also wrote about parts of the mind outside awareness, but he doubted Freud's methods when they met in 1909.
Freud's later works, the next rung, build the ideas of this book into a full theory of the mind.
Can a method that always finds a meaning ever show that it is wrong?
Why do we forget most dreams within minutes?
How much of what we do happens without our noticing why?
Is a dream a message, a memory, a story the brain tells itself, or something else?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. What is the strangest dream you remember? Did any piece of it come from real life?
  2. Why might it be hard to remember dreams once you are fully awake?
  3. Freud thought dreams hide their meaning. Many scientists think they do not. What would help you decide?
  4. Why do you think so many words from Freud ("unconscious," "Freudian slip") are used in everyday talk?
  5. Is it fair to judge an old scientific book by what we know today? What else could we judge it by?

Have you ever said the wrong word by mistake, like calling your teacher "Mom"? Sigmund Freud, a doctor in Vienna, thought little mistakes like that were interesting. He wondered whether they showed something we were thinking about without noticing.

Later in his life Freud drew a picture of the mind as three parts that often argue. One part just wants things right now. One part is like a strict rule-keeper inside us. And one part, the "I", has to find a sensible way between them and the real world.

blocks.name: gb-freud-mind
blocks.cap: Choose a situation and hear the three "voices" of Freud's picture (our own examples). It is a picture, not something scientists have found in the brain.

blocks.html: Many people today find this picture a useful way to talk about feelings. Scientists also point out that it is hard to test, and they study the mind in other ways too.

🧩 Try this

Three voices. Think of a small choice you made today, like whether to do chores before play. Write what the "I want it now" voice said, what the "rules" voice said, and what you actually decided. Was it a good middle way?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

blocks.text: From dreams to a theory of the mind

blocks.html: After The Interpretation of Dreams Freud wrote for almost forty more years. Volume 54 of the set gathers many of these works, among them his lectures at Clark University in Massachusetts (1909), papers on repression and the unconscious (1915), the General Introduction to Psychoanalysis (lectures given in Vienna in 1915–17), Beyond the Pleasure Principle (1920), The Ego and the Id (1923), Civilization and Its Discontents (1930) and the New Introductory Lectures (1933).
In 1938, after Nazi Germany took over Austria, Freud and his family fled to London, where he died the next year. His daughter Anna Freud carried on his work with children.
The General Introduction starts with ordinary mistakes: slips of the tongue, forgetting a name, losing things. Freud argues that many of them are not chance.
From slips and dreams he moves to his central claim, which he knew many listeners would resist:

Later in the lectures he names three blows to human pride: Copernicus showed the earth is not the center of the universe; Darwin showed our descent from other animals; and psychology, he says, now shows the mind is not in charge of itself.

In The Ego and the Id (1923) Freud gave his best-known model. In German he used plain words: das Es ("the It"), das Ich ("the I") and das Über-Ich ("the Over-I"). His English translators made them Latin: id, ego and superego.

head: Part
Freud's idea (our summary)
rows: Inborn drives that want satisfaction now, without regard to reality or rules.
The organizing self that deals with the real world and must find a way between the id's demands and the superego's.
The inner judge, formed from the rules and ideals of parents and society; the source of guilt.

blocks.name: gb-freud-mind
blocks.cap: Freud's three parts of the mind, in everyday situations (our examples).

blocks.html: Freud also described defenses, ways the ego protects itself from painful thoughts, such as repression (pushing a thought out of awareness). His daughter Anna Freud listed and described many more in 1936.

In Civilization and Its Discontents Freud asks why people are often unhappy in the very civilization that protects them. His answer: living together requires us to hold back strong drives, including aggression, and the superego turns that held-back force inward as guilt. Civilization, he thought, is worth its price, but the price is real.

blocks.text: How later research and critics judged him

blocks.html: Freud is one of the most influential thinkers of the 20th century, and one of the most argued about. His talking cure is the ancestor of many kinds of psychotherapy, and ideas such as defenses, the unconscious and the importance of childhood entered medicine, literature and daily speech. Critics raise serious objections: Freud built his theory mostly from his own patients and self-analysis, without controlled studies; the philosopher Karl Popper argued the theory could explain any outcome and so could not be tested; the philosopher Adolf Grünbaum (1984) and others questioned whether his case evidence showed what he claimed; and historians have found that some case reports were less successful than he said. On the other side, experimental psychology has confirmed in its own terms that much mental work happens outside awareness, and controlled trials of modern psychodynamic therapy, which grew from Freud's, have found benefits for some problems. Most psychologists today regard the id, ego and superego as a historical model rather than a scientific finding.
Thinking "unconscious" in Freud just means "asleep" or "knocked out." He meant thoughts and wishes active in the mind that a person is not aware of.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Plato's Republic divides the soul into three parts too: reason, spirit and appetite, with reason meant to rule. Compare Freud's ego, superego and id, and notice the differences.
Hobbes and Rousseau, earlier on this ladder, also asked what people give up to live in society; Freud's answer is psychological rather than political.
Nietzsche wrote before Freud about drives and the bad conscience; Freud said he avoided reading Nietzsche closely so as to keep his own ideas independent.
Writers on the 20th-century literature rungs, such as Woolf and Joyce, explored inner life and memory in a world that was reading Freud.
How much of what we do is decided by thoughts we do not notice?
Is guilt a useful guide, a burden, or both?
Can an idea be valuable for thinking even if it fails as science?
What does a person give up to live with others, and what do they gain?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Have you ever made a slip of the tongue? Do you think it meant anything?
  2. When you face a choice, do you ever feel two "voices" inside? What do they say?
  3. Where do our ideas of right and wrong come from: family, friends, faith, books, or our own thinking?
  4. Why do you think Freud called his three ideas "blows" to human pride?
  5. What kind of evidence would you want before believing a theory about the mind?

William James was a Harvard professor who loved to settle arguments. One summer, on a camping trip, he found his friends in a hot dispute about a squirrel.

A squirrel clings to one side of a tree trunk. A man walks all the way around the tree to see it, but the squirrel keeps moving too, always staying on the far side. Did the man go "round" the squirrel? Half the campers said yes, half said no.

blocks.name: gb-james-squirrel
blocks.cap: Walk the man around the tree. Then switch between the two meanings of "going round" and see the answer change.

blocks.html: James said both sides were right: it depends on what you mean by "going round." If you mean north, east, south and west of the squirrel, yes. If you mean in front of it, then to its side, then behind it, no, because the squirrel always faced him. Once you ask "what difference does it make?", the quarrel goes away. That way of thinking is called pragmatism.

🧩 Try this

The difference test. Next time your family argues about a word ("Is a hot dog a sandwich?"), ask James's question: what would be different if one side were right? Is the argument about the world, or only about the word?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

William James (1842–1910) was already famous for The Principles of Psychology (1890), on the 19th-century part of this ladder. In late 1906 and early 1907 he gave lectures in Boston and New York on a way of thinking his friend Charles Sanders Peirce had named pragmatism years before. They came out in 1907 as Pragmatism: A New Name for Some Old Ways of Thinking, dedicated to the memory of John Stuart Mill.

James begins with temperament. Some thinkers are "tender-minded": they trust principles, hope for a unified and good world, and lean toward religion and free will. Others are "tough-minded": they trust facts, see many separate things, and lean toward materialism and doubt. James offers pragmatism as a way to keep the facts and still leave room for hope.
After the squirrel story James draws the lesson:

The method, in our words: ask what practical difference it would make if one idea were true rather than the other. If there is no difference at all, the dispute is idle. If there is a difference, now you know what you are really arguing about.

blocks.name: gb-james-squirrel
blocks.cap: James's camping-trip puzzle, Lecture II.

blocks.html: The most controversial lectures turn the method on truth itself. For James, an idea is not true by simply copying reality like a photograph. It becomes true as it guides us well through experience and holds up when we check it.

Pragmatism was a sensation and a target. Bertrand Russell and G. E. Moore objected that if "true" meant "useful to believe," a false belief that made someone happy would count as true; James replied that he meant what works in the long run and against all the evidence, not comfort of the moment. Peirce, uneasy with James's version, renamed his own view "pragmaticism," a word he said was "ugly enough to be safe from kidnappers." John Dewey carried pragmatism into education and public life, and it is often called America's most distinctive philosophy. Philosophers still debate theories of truth; many who reject James's account keep his method of asking what difference a claim makes.
Reading "truth is what works" as "believe whatever is convenient." James insisted that a true idea must fit with facts, with our other beliefs, and with what later experience shows.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Mill's Utilitarianism judges actions by their results; James, who dedicated the book to Mill, judges ideas by theirs.
Hume and Berkeley asked what we mean by our words in terms of experience; James counts them as forerunners.
Dewey's Experience and Education, a later rung, applies pragmatist ideas to schooling.
Russell's Problems of Philosophy, the next rung, appeared five years later and took a very different view of truth.
Is a belief true because it works, or does it work because it is true?
Are some arguments only about words? How can you tell?
Can it be reasonable to believe something before all the evidence is in?
What is the difference between "useful" and "true"?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. So: did the man go round the squirrel? Explain both answers.
  2. Think of a family argument that turned out to be about the meaning of a word.
  3. Are you more tough-minded or tender-minded? Can a person be both?
  4. James asked, "What difference would it make?" Try it on a question you have wondered about.
  5. Can a belief make you happy and still be false? What would James say?

Henri Bergson (say BERG-son) was a French thinker who asked: how many ways are there to know something?

Imagine your hometown. You could look at a hundred photographs of it, taken from every corner. Or you could walk its streets on a summer evening. Bergson said the photographs, however many, never add up to the walk. Knowing from outside, piece by piece, is one way. Knowing from inside, all at once, is another.

blocks.name: gb-bergson-views
blocks.cap: Add more and more snapshots from outside, then step inside. Switch to the melody to see the same idea with music.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Outside and inside. Pick a song you love. First describe it in a list: how fast, how loud, which instruments. Then sing or hum it. Which tells you more about the song? Talk about what the list leaves out.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Henri Bergson (1859–1941) taught at the Collège de France in Paris, where his lectures drew crowds. His books on time, memory and life made him one of the most famous thinkers of his day, and he won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1927. An Introduction to Metaphysics is a long essay of 1903. The English poet and critic T. E. Hulme translated it in 1912, with Bergson checking the proofs.

The first way Bergson calls analysis. It looks from a point of view and uses symbols: words, numbers, diagrams. It is the way of science, and it is very useful. But, he says, it always stays "relative," tied to where we stand.

blocks.name: gb-bergson-views
blocks.cap: Bergson's own example of the town, and a melody: analysis gathers more and more views or points; intuition enters the whole.

blocks.html: The first thing we can know from inside, Bergson says, is ourselves: our own flowing life in time, which he calls duration (durée). Clock time cuts time into equal moments, like beads on a string. Lived time is more like a melody, where each note is colored by the ones before. Analysis breaks it into pieces; intuition follows it as it flows.

Bergson was a celebrity before the First World War. William James admired him warmly and praised his work in print; writers and artists drew on his ideas of time and memory. Critics were sharp too. Bertrand Russell, in 1912, attacked Bergson's trust in intuition over intellect as a step away from careful reasoning. In 1922 Bergson debated Albert Einstein in Paris about whether physics had said all there is to say about time; most physicists sided with Einstein. Bergson's fame faded after the 1920s, but philosophers of process, such as Whitehead, and later French thinkers took up his questions again.
Thinking Bergson was against science. He respected it; he argued that its method of analysis, though powerful, is not the only way to know.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Plato and Plotinus, earlier on this ladder, also spoke of a knowing beyond step-by-step reasoning, though Bergson's "absolute" is the flow of change, not unchanging forms.
Augustine asked in the Confessions what time is, and found it in the stretching of the mind; compare Bergson's duration.
Kant argued we know things only through the forms of our own mind; Bergson thought intuition could reach further.
Whitehead, two rungs on, built a philosophy of process; Proust and Woolf, in the literature rungs, wrote novels of memory and lived time.
Is there knowledge that cannot be put into words or numbers?
Is lived time the same as clock time?
Can science explain what it is like to be you?
When is intuition a good guide, and when is it not?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. What is something you know "from inside" that is hard to explain to someone else?
  2. Does an hour always feel the same length? When does time feel fast or slow?
  3. Are photographs of a place as good as being there? What is missing?
  4. Russell worried that trusting intuition could lead people astray. When should we check our hunches?
  5. Can you describe a friend completely in a list of facts?

Bertrand Russell was an English thinker who liked to start with very ordinary things, like the kitchen table, and ask very hard questions about them.

Look at a table. What color is it? It looks brown, but where the light shines it looks almost white, and in the shadows nearly black. Walk around it and its shape seems to change too: a rectangle from above, a slanted shape from the side. So which is the real table? The one you see, or something behind what you see?

blocks.name: gb-russell-table
blocks.cap: Move around the table and move the lamp. Watch how its shape and shine seem to change, while the table itself stays the same.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

A changing coin. Hold a coin flat in front of you and look straight down: it is a circle. Now tilt it slowly. What shape do you see? Draw three shapes the coin made. Is the coin still round?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Bertrand Russell (1872–1970) was a mathematician and philosopher at Cambridge. With Alfred North Whitehead he wrote Principia Mathematica (1910–13), which tried to build mathematics from logic. The Problems of Philosophy (1912) was a small book for a popular series, the Home University Library. It is still one of the most widely read introductions to philosophy. Russell won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1950.
Russell's first example is his table. Its color, shape and feel change with the light, the angle and the person. He concludes:

What we directly know, Russell says, are sense-data: the colors, shapes and sounds we are aware of. The table itself, if it exists, is something we infer. He admits we cannot prove there is a world beyond our sense-data, but our "instinctive belief" in it is the simplest way to explain what we experience, so it is reasonable to accept it.

blocks.name: gb-russell-table
blocks.cap: The same table from different places and in different light.

blocks.html: Russell separates knowledge by acquaintance, direct awareness of something (this patch of color, this feeling), from knowledge by description, knowing something as "the so-and-so" (the first emperor of Rome, the center of the earth). Most of what we know about the world, and all we know of other times and places, is by description.

Why do we expect the sun to rise tomorrow? Because it always has. But a past pattern does not prove a future one. Russell's example is the chicken that is fed every day, and so expects food each morning, until one day the farmer comes for it instead. Inductive reasoning makes conclusions probable, never certain; and, Russell argues, the principle of induction itself cannot be proved from experience without arguing in a circle.

blocks.title: An inductive argument, tested
blocks.q: Every swan I have ever seen is white. So all swans are white. Is this argument deductive or inductive, and could the conclusion be false even if the premise is true?
steps: The premise reports past observations; the conclusion reaches beyond them to all swans.
That is inductive reasoning: it can make a conclusion more probable, but not certain.
Black swans were in fact found in Australia by European explorers in 1697.
blocks.a: Inductive; yes, the conclusion can be false (and was).

blocks.text: Truth, and the value of philosophy

blocks.html: A belief is true, Russell says, when it corresponds to a fact, and false when it does not. Truth depends on the world, not on whether a belief is useful, a direct reply to William James's pragmatism. The book ends with the value of philosophy itself:

Russell later changed many of his views, and philosophers have challenged the idea of sense-data as the things we directly see; many now say we see tables, not data about tables. But the book's questions, about appearance and reality, induction, and truth, remain the standard starting points of the subject.
Thinking Russell said the table is not real. He said our belief in it is reasonable but cannot be proved, and that we know it through its appearances.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Descartes' Meditations, on the 17th-century part of this ladder, also began with doubt; Russell discusses him in Chapter II.
Berkeley argued that there is nothing behind the appearances; Russell's Chapter IV answers him.
Hume first raised the problem of induction; Russell's Chapter VI restates it.
James's Pragmatism, the rung before Bergson, defined truth by what works; Russell defined it by correspondence with fact.
Wittgenstein, Russell's student, later questioned how words connect to the world at all.
How do you know the world exists when you are not looking?
Can we ever be certain the future will be like the past?
Is a belief true because it matches the facts, or because it works?
What is the use of a question that has no final answer?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Pick an object in the room. How does it look different from where each of you sits?
  2. Why does the sun rising every day make you expect it tomorrow? Is that a good reason?
  3. Name something you know by acquaintance and something you know only by description.
  4. Russell said philosophy is worth it for the questions, not the answers. Do you agree?
  5. Have you ever been sure of something and found you were wrong? What did you learn?

Alfred North Whitehead was a mathematician who became a philosopher. He asked: why did modern science start when and where it did? And does science tell us everything about the world?

Think of a sunset at the beach. A scientist can describe it with numbers: the angle of the sun, the length of the light waves, the temperature of the air. All true! But the warm colors, the sound of the waves and the feeling of the evening are left out of the numbers. Whitehead said we should not forget that the numbers come from the real evening, not the other way round.

blocks.name: gb-whitehead-abstraction
blocks.cap: Climb the ladder of abstraction: each step up keeps less of the real evening, and becomes more useful for calculating.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

What the numbers leave out. Choose something you love: a dog, a pie, a song. Write three facts about it a scientist could measure. Then write three things about it that no measurement catches. Are both lists true?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Alfred North Whitehead (1861–1947) taught mathematics in Cambridge and London for decades and wrote Principia Mathematica with his former student Bertrand Russell. In 1924, aged 63, he moved to Harvard to teach philosophy. Science and the Modern World grew from his Lowell Lectures in Boston in 1925. It is a history of how science shaped modern thought, and a philosopher's criticism of the picture of nature that science seemed to leave behind.

blocks.text: Where the faith in science came from

blocks.html: Why did modern science arise in Europe in the 1500s and 1600s? Whitehead points to an attitude older than any theory: the confident belief that nature is orderly and can be understood.
Where did that belief come from? His answer, which historians still discuss:

He means the medieval teaching that the world was made by a rational God, so its order could be trusted and searched out. Whitehead adds that Greek thought and the new habit of careful observation were needed too.

The scientists of the 1600s pictured nature as bits of matter moving in space and time. Colors, sounds and smells were put "in the mind" rather than in nature. Whitehead sums up, with irony, what that picture implies:

That picture, he argues, mistakes a useful abstraction for the full concrete reality, an error he names the fallacy of misplaced concreteness. Bits of matter at points are what we get when we leave most of experience out; they are not more real than the experience they came from.

blocks.name: gb-whitehead-abstraction
blocks.cap: What each level of description keeps and leaves out.

blocks.html: Whitehead looks to the Romantic poets, Wordsworth and Shelley, as witnesses that nature as we meet it is full of value and life. His own alternative, the "philosophy of organism," treats the world as made of interconnected events and processes rather than lumps of stuff, a view he worked out fully in Process and Reality (1929).

He means the research laboratory and the habit of turning science into technology on purpose. The last chapters ask how religion and science can each learn from the other, and what a society needs to make progress without losing its balance.

The book was widely read and helped make the history of science a serious subject. Historians still debate Whitehead's claim about medieval theology: some have built on it, while others stress the role of Greek and Islamic science, the rise of crafts and trade, or argue that science and religious authority were sometimes in conflict. His "process" philosophy remains influential among some philosophers and theologians, though less so in mainstream academic philosophy, which followed Russell and Wittgenstein.
Thinking Whitehead was against science. He was a mathematician who loved it; he objected to a particular philosophy that treated science's abstractions as the whole of reality.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Galileo and Descartes sorted qualities into those "in" things (shape, motion) and those in the mind (color, taste); Whitehead's Chapter III examines the result.
Plato's Timaeus pictures a world ordered by a divine craftsman; Whitehead admired it.
Aquinas and the medieval thinkers held that faith and reason do not conflict; Whitehead traces the scientific attitude back to that confidence.
Bergson, the earlier rung, also attacked the habit of mistaking our cuts in reality for reality itself.
Is a description in numbers more real than how something looks and feels?
Why did modern science begin where and when it did?
Can science and religion learn from each other?
Is the world made of things, or of events?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Describe your kitchen as a scientist would, then as a poet would. Which is truer?
  2. Why might believing that the world is orderly help someone become a scientist?
  3. What is something important that cannot be measured?
  4. Whitehead said the 19th century invented the "method of invention." What inventions came from laboratories?
  5. Is a map of a place more real than the place? What is the map good for?

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
Karl Barth (say BART) was a pastor in a small village in Switzerland. Every Sunday he had to preach, and every week he asked himself a hard question: what does the Bible really say?

Many teachers in his time read the Bible as a book about people searching for God. Barth, opening it again and again, came to believe it was the other way round: that the Bible is about God searching for people. He said reading it was like stepping through a door into a "strange new world."

blocks.name: gb-barth-direction
blocks.cap: Two ways of reading, as Barth described them. Tap to switch the arrow.

blocks.html: Christians, Jews and others read the Bible in many ways, and families talk about it in their own way. This rung explains what Barth believed and why his ideas mattered so much in the 20th century.

🧩 Try this

A door into a book. Barth compared the Bible to a door into a house. Think of a book that felt like a door into another world for you. What did you find when you went through it? Draw the door and what lay behind it.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Karl Barth (1886–1968) was a Swiss Reformed pastor and theologian. He trained under the leading liberal theologians of Germany, who taught that Christianity was best understood through history, human religious experience and culture. In 1914, as the First World War began, many of those teachers signed a public statement supporting Germany's war policy. Barth was shaken: if theology could bend so easily to the mood of the age, something had gone wrong at its root.

As pastor of Safenwil (1911–21) he went back to the Bible, above all Paul's Letter to the Romans. His commentary on Romans (1919, rewritten in 1922) caused a sensation. The Word of God and the Word of Man collects addresses he gave from 1916 to 1923, published in German in 1924 and in English, translated by the American minister Douglas Horton, in 1928.

blocks.text: The strange new world within the Bible

blocks.html: His answer surprised his hearers:

blocks.name: gb-barth-direction
blocks.cap: The turn Barth made, in our own summary.

blocks.html: In a 1922 address to ministers Barth put the whole difficulty of his work in three sentences:

This style of thinking, which holds a "yes" and a "no" together, was called dialectical theology. Barth insisted God is "wholly other," not a higher version of human ideals, and can be known only as God speaks.

blocks.name: gb-barth-life
blocks.cap: Barth's life and work: step through the timeline.

blocks.html: Barth became one of the most influential Protestant theologians of the century. In 1934 he was the main author of the Barmen Declaration, in which a group of German Protestants rejected the Nazi state's claim to control the church; he was soon forced out of his post at Bonn and returned to Switzerland. His Church Dogmatics, written from 1932 until his death and left unfinished, runs to more than 9,000 pages. Critics came from several sides. The liberal historian Adolf von Harnack, his former teacher, worried that Barth cut faith off from reason, history and culture. His ally Emil Brunner argued, against Barth, that people can know something of God through nature and conscience. Others, including Roman Catholic thinkers, admired his seriousness while disagreeing on key points. Readers of other faiths and of none have studied him as a major voice in 20th-century thought.
Thinking Barth simply rejected learning. He was a deeply learned scholar; his objection was to letting culture, rather than the Bible, set the terms of theology.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Augustine and Calvin, earlier on this ladder, are the theologians Barth read most closely; like them he put God's grace first.
Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling stressed the gulf between God and human reason; Barth drew on him in his early work and later moved away.
Schleiermacher and the liberal tradition grounded religion in human feeling; Barth's whole program answered them.
Pascal contrasted the God of the philosophers with the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; compare Barth's God who speaks.
When is it right for a religious group to say no to its own government?
Can people find out about God by reasoning, or only if God makes himself known?
Should faith change with the culture of its time, or stand apart from it?
How do we tell the difference between what we hope is true and what a text actually says?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Barth was shocked when people he admired supported a war. Has someone you admired ever disappointed you? What did you do?
  2. What is the difference between reading a book to find what you already think, and reading it to be surprised?
  3. Barth said a preacher both must and cannot speak of God. Can something be a duty and also impossible to do perfectly?
  4. In 1934 Barth helped write a statement refusing the government control of the church. Why might that have been dangerous?
  5. How does your family talk about big questions of faith?

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
Martin Heidegger (say HY-deg-er) was a German philosopher who asked one of the biggest questions there is: why is there something, rather than nothing at all?

Scientists study things: rocks, plants, stars, people. Heidegger noticed that every science studies some kind of thing, and nothing else. But what about that "nothing"? Can we even think about it? He thought certain moments, like a strange quiet feeling when everything seems far away, make us wonder at the fact that anything exists at all.

blocks.name: gb-heidegger-rings
blocks.cap: Tap the rings: each science studies one region of what exists; Heidegger asks about all of it at once, and about the nothing around it.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Wonder walk. Go outside for five minutes without talking. Look at a tree, a cloud, a stone. Instead of asking "what is it?", ask "isn't it strange that it is there at all?" Talk afterward about how that felt.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Martin Heidegger (1889–1976) studied with Edmund Husserl, the founder of phenomenology, and made his name with Being and Time (1927). What Is Metaphysics? is the lecture he gave on July 24, 1929, when he took over Husserl's chair at the University of Freiburg. He later added a Postscript (1943) and an Introduction (1949).

No excerpts here. The lecture was first translated into English in 1949, so no English version is in the public domain in the U.S. This lesson describes it in our own words. Several translations are in libraries.

Heidegger starts with the university itself. Its many sciences, physics, biology, history and the rest, each study some region of beings (things that are), and nothing beyond it. Science says: we study beings, and nothing else. Then Heidegger asks: what about this nothing that science sets aside?

Logic cannot answer, he argues, because to think of "the nothing" seems to turn it into a something. But we do not meet the nothing first by thinking. We meet it in certain moods. In deep boredom, beings as a whole fall into a strange sameness. In what he calls anxiety (Angst), a mood with no particular object, everything seems to slip away from us, and we are left facing the bare fact that there is something at all.

blocks.name: gb-heidegger-rings
blocks.cap: Heidegger's picture (our summary), and the reply of his critics.

blocks.html: From that experience Heidegger draws his conclusion: human existence is always "held out into the nothing," and that is why we can ask about beings as a whole, which is what metaphysics does. The lecture ends with the old question the philosopher Leibniz had asked two centuries before: why are there beings at all, rather than nothing?

The lecture became a classic of 20th-century "continental" philosophy, and its themes of mood, anxiety and the question of being shaped existentialism, theology and literary theory. It also became the most famous target of the logical positivists. In 1932 Rudolf Carnap took sentences from it, such as one that turns the word "nothing" into a verb, as his prime examples of statements that look meaningful but, he argued, say nothing that could be true or false. Heidegger's defenders reply that he was pointing to something language struggles to say, not making a claim of logic. Any account of Heidegger must also note that he joined the Nazi Party in 1933 and served for a year as rector of Freiburg under the regime; private notebooks published in 2014 contain antisemitic passages. Scholars still debate how far his politics affected his philosophy.
Thinking Heidegger meant that nothing is a kind of thing, or that he wanted people to feel anxious. He used moods as clues to what it means to exist at all.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Aristotle's Metaphysics called first philosophy the study of being as being; Heidegger thought the tradition since then had forgotten to ask what "being" means.
Leibniz asked "why is there something rather than nothing?"; Heidegger called it the fundamental question.
Kierkegaard, in the 19th-century rungs, wrote about anxiety as a mood that reveals freedom; Heidegger knew his work.
Wittgenstein, two rungs on, thought many such questions arise when language "goes on holiday"; compare Carnap's reply.
Beckett's Waiting for Godot, in the literature rungs, stages people facing emptiness with jokes and waiting.
Why is there anything at all?
Can a feeling teach us something true about the world?
Are there questions science cannot ask, or are they not real questions?
How should we read a great thinker who did wrong things?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Why is there something rather than nothing? Does the question have an answer?
  2. Have you ever had a quiet moment when the world seemed strange? What was it like?
  3. Is it possible to think about "nothing"? Try, and say what happens.
  4. Carnap said some philosophical sentences are meaningless. How would you decide whether a sentence means anything?
  5. Heidegger joined the Nazi Party. Should that change how we read his books? Why or why not?

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
John Dewey was an American teacher of teachers. He spent his long life asking: what makes a lesson really teach you something?

Dewey said every experience teaches you something, but not always something good. If you are bored stiff in class, you might learn that learning is boring! A good experience is one that makes you want to know more and helps you do more next time. He called that growth.

blocks.name: gb-dewey-grid
blocks.cap: Tap an example to place it on Dewey's two tests. The best experiences are high on both. (Our examples, not Dewey's.)

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

A growing project. Pick something to make together: a pancake breakfast, a bird feeder, a family newspaper. Along the way, notice what new questions come up (How much flour for twice as many people? Which birds came?). Write them down. Those questions are what Dewey meant by growth.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

John Dewey (1859–1952) was a philosopher, a founder of pragmatism with Peirce and James, and the most famous American writer on education. In 1896 he opened a Laboratory School at the University of Chicago to test his ideas, and in 1916 he published Democracy and Education. By the 1930s a "progressive education" movement claimed him as its leader. Experience and Education (1938), a short book from a lecture series, is partly his warning to that movement.
No excerpts here. The book was published in 1938 and is still under copyright, so this lesson describes it in our own words. Library editions are easy to find.

Dewey describes two camps. Traditional education passes down a fixed body of knowledge and rules from above: textbooks, drills, silent rows of desks. Progressive education begins from the child's interests and activity. Dewey criticizes the first for imposing material that has little to do with students' lives. But he criticizes many progressives just as sharply: rejecting the old ways, he says, is not a philosophy. Freedom without direction, and activity without thought, can be as empty as drill.

blocks.text: Two tests of a good experience

blocks.html: The heart of the book is a theory of experience with two principles:

head: Principle
Dewey's idea (our summary)
rows: Every experience takes something from those before it and changes those that come after. A good one opens the way to further growth; a bad one closes it, for example by making a student bored, careless or afraid.
Every experience is a meeting between the learner (needs, abilities, past experience) and the outer situation (materials, people, setting). The teacher's job is to arrange situations that fit both.

blocks.name: gb-dewey-grid
blocks.cap: Placing experiences on Dewey's two principles (our own examples).

blocks.html: An experience can be lively and still be mis-educative if it leads nowhere or builds bad habits. Dewey also points to collateral learning: the attitudes students pick up alongside the lesson, such as a love of reading or a dislike of it, which may last far longer than the facts.

Dewey compares a good classroom to a game. In a game, the rules are not felt as a boss's orders; they are part of the activity, and the group keeps them. So in a good school, order comes mainly from shared work, not from the teacher's will alone. The freedom that matters most is freedom of intelligence: the power to form purposes and judge how to reach them, not merely to move about. The teacher is not a bystander: because he or she has more experience, the teacher must plan, select materials and guide, and organized subject matter, science, history, mathematics, should grow out of experience into ordered knowledge.

Dewey's ideas shaped American schooling for much of the century, from project work and hands-on science to the idea that schools should prepare citizens for democracy. They have always been argued over. Critics on one side blamed "progressive" schools for weak teaching of basic skills and knowledge; Dewey's defenders reply that this book already criticizes exactly that. Others, such as the educator E. D. Hirsch, have argued that children need a large shared core of knowledge to think well, and that progressive methods can widen gaps between students. Research on learning today supports some of Dewey's points, for example the value of active practice and of building on what students already know, while also finding that beginners often learn best from clear, guided instruction.
Thinking Dewey said children should do whatever they like. This book argues the opposite: experience must be chosen and guided, and the teacher carries real responsibility.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Plato's Republic and Rousseau's Emile both made education the key to a good society; Dewey ties it to democracy.
James's Pragmatism, an earlier rung, judged ideas by their working; Dewey judges experiences by where they lead.
Locke wrote that the mind is shaped by experience; Dewey added that experience is an active meeting of person and world.
The site's Memory Ladder looks at what research says about practice and review, a modern conversation about how learning lasts.
What makes an experience educational rather than just fun, or just hard?
How much should children choose what they learn?
What is the teacher for, if students learn by doing?
Why might a school matter for a democracy?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Think of the best lesson you ever had. Did it pass Dewey's two tests?
  2. What is something you learned "on the side" (an attitude or habit) without anyone teaching it?
  3. Are rules in a game different from rules made by a boss? How?
  4. Dewey criticized both old-style and new-style schools. What would you keep from each?
  5. What new questions did your last project lead you to?

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
Ludwig Wittgenstein (say VIT-gen-shtine) was an Austrian thinker who taught at Cambridge in England. He wondered about something we do every day: how do words mean things?

You might think every word is a name for a thing, like "apple" for an apple. But what thing does "hello" name? Or "maybe"? Or "ouch"? Wittgenstein said words are more like tools in a toolbox: a hammer, a saw, a ruler, glue. Each does a different job. To know what a word means, watch how people use it.

blocks.name: gb-witt-builders
blocks.cap: Wittgenstein imagined two builders with a language of just four words. Call out a word and see what the helper does.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

The word game. Choose a word like "game," "chair" or "fun." Try to write a definition that fits every example and nothing else. Then have someone try to find an example that breaks your definition. Is it harder than you thought?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Ludwig Wittgenstein (1889–1951) came from one of the richest families in Vienna. He studied with Bertrand Russell at Cambridge, served in the Austrian army in the First World War, and in 1921 published the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus, a short, severe book that pictured language as a mirror of facts. He then left philosophy for years, working as a village schoolteacher and a gardener. Back at Cambridge from 1929, he came to think his first book was badly mistaken. Philosophical Investigations, his answer to it, was published in 1953, two years after his death.
No excerpts here. The Investigations was first published in 1953, in German with an English translation, and is under copyright. This lesson describes it in our own words. It is in most libraries.
The book opens with a passage from Augustine's Confessions (earlier on this ladder), in which Augustine remembers how he learned to speak as a child:
Here, Wittgenstein says, is a picture of language: words name objects, and sentences combine names. He grants it fits some words. But it leaves out most of what language does.

He imagines two builders. One calls out "block," "pillar," "slab" or "beam," and the other brings that stone. That is a complete language for them, a language game. Our own language is a crowd of such games: giving orders, describing, telling stories, guessing riddles, thanking, greeting, praying, making jokes. The meaning of a word, in many cases, is its use in the language.

blocks.name: gb-witt-builders
blocks.cap: The builders' language game (our drawing of Wittgenstein's example).

blocks.html: What do all games have in common? Board games, card games, ball games, a child throwing a ball at a wall? Instead of assuming there must be something in common, Wittgenstein says, go and look. You find many overlapping similarities but no single feature they all share, the way members of a family share a chin here, eyes there. He calls this family resemblance. Many useful words work this way and have no neat definition.

blocks.name: gb-witt-games
blocks.cap: Tap a game to see its features. Look for one feature every game shares. (Our own list, in the spirit of Wittgenstein's example.)

blocks.html: How do we know what it means to follow a rule, like "add 2"? No rule can contain instructions for its own use; in the end, Wittgenstein argues, following a rule is a practice, something we do together, trained into us. That leads to his famous private language argument: a language whose words referred only to one person's private sensations, understood by no one else, could not work, because there would be no difference between using a word correctly and merely seeming to.

Many philosophical puzzles, Wittgenstein thought, arise when we take words out of the everyday games where they work and make them do something strange. Philosophy's task is to describe how language is really used, so that the puzzle dissolves. His image is a fly trapped in a glass bottle, buzzing against the sides: the philosopher's job is to show it the way out.

The Investigations is often ranked among the most important philosophy books of the 20th century. It shaped "ordinary language" philosophy at Oxford, and later work in linguistics, the philosophy of mind and the social sciences. Critics have argued that it dismisses real philosophical problems as confusions too quickly, that its loose, numbered remarks leave its arguments open to many readings, and, in Saul Kripke's famous 1982 interpretation, that the rule-following argument leads to a startling skepticism Wittgenstein may not have intended. Scholars still disagree about what exactly the book claims.
Thinking "meaning is use" means a word can mean anything anyone likes. Use is shared and governed by the practices of a community; that is the point of the private language argument.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Augustine, whose picture of language opens the book.
Plato's dialogues often ask "what is courage?" or "what is justice?" and look for one definition; family resemblance questions whether there always is one.
Russell, his teacher, analysed language with logic; the Investigations turns away from that method.
Heidegger and Wittgenstein were born the same year and both thought philosophy had been misled by language, though in very different ways.
The site's Logic Ladder topics on definitions and verbal disputes take up practical versions of his questions.
Can every word be defined?
Could you have a language only you understood?
Are philosophical puzzles about the world, or about our words?
How do children learn to follow rules?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. What does "game" mean? Try to find something all games share.
  2. Make up a tiny language game with four words for your family. What can you do with it?
  3. Name a word that is not the name of anything. What does it do?
  4. Wittgenstein changed his mind about his first book. Why is it hard, and good, to change your mind?
  5. Have you ever argued with someone and found you meant different things by the same word?

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Henri Poincaré was a French mathematician who lived from 1854 to 1912. He was famous for being able to solve hard problems in his head, and for asking big questions about science itself. One of them was: which of the things scientists say are discovered, and which are choices we make?

Here is a puzzle he liked. On a flat sheet of paper, the three angles of any triangle add up to 180 degrees. But draw a big triangle on a ball, and the angles add up to more than 180. Draw one on a saddle shape, or on a curly lettuce leaf, and they add up to less. Which world are we living in? If you only ever measure small triangles, you can’t tell!

blocks.name: gb-geometries
blocks.cap: Pick a world and grow the triangle. Small triangles add up to about 180° everywhere. Big ones show the difference.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Triangles on a ball. Take a ball or an orange. With a marker, draw a line from the top straight down to the middle (the equator), then a quarter of the way around the middle, then straight back up to the top. Look at the three corners. Each one is a square corner, 90 degrees. Three of them make 270 degrees, not 180! Now try a tiny triangle on the same ball. Does it look almost flat?

Poincaré said scientists use rules a little like the rules of a game, or like choosing to measure in inches or in centimeters. Neither one is “true”; one is just handier. But he also said real science needs experiments, because most of what science says can be checked against nature.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Henri Poincaré (1854–1912) was one of the great mathematicians of his age. He worked in nearly every part of mathematics and physics: the motion of planets (his prize-winning study of the three-body problem in 1889 opened the way to what we now call chaos theory), the shape of spaces (topology), light and electricity, and the new physics of moving electrons, where in 1905 he reached some of the same results as Einstein’s relativity. He also wrote clear books for general readers about what science is.

La Science et l’hypothèse appeared in Paris in 1902. W. J. Greenstreet’s English translation came out in 1905, with an introduction by the physicist Joseph Larmor. Two more books followed, The Value of Science (1905) and Science and Method (1908).

Some people think science gives us certain truth. Others think it is all guesswork. Poincaré rejects both. In his preface he says that the skeptic has the lazy answer, and that we should look carefully at what role each kind of hypothesis plays.
The book moves through four parts: number and magnitude, space, force and nature. In each, Poincaré sorts the statements of science into kinds.

head: Part
What Poincaré argues
rows: Proof by mathematical induction (if a rule holds for 1, and holding for n makes it hold for n + 1, it holds for every whole number) is the true engine of mathematics. It is not mere logic, and not learned from experience: it rests on the mind’s power to imagine a step repeated without end.
The axioms of geometry are neither forced on us by reason nor discovered by measuring. They are conventions: free choices, guided by experience, which we keep because they are convenient.
Several principles of mechanics, such as the law of inertia, began in experiment but have been raised to the rank of definitions that no single experiment can overturn.
Physics also needs real hypotheses, which experiment can confirm or refute. A good theory may be replaced and still leave behind true relations between things.

blocks.html: In the 1800s Lobachevsky, Bolyai and Riemann had built geometries in which Euclid’s parallel postulate fails. In one, the angles of a triangle add to less than 180°; in another, to more. Each is as consistent as Euclid’s. So which is the geometry of real space?

Poincaré imagined beings living in a great sphere where it grows colder toward the edge, and every ruler shrinks as it moves outward. Such beings, measuring carefully, would find that the geometry of their world is not Euclid’s. Yet we could just as well describe their world with Euclid’s geometry plus a law about temperature. Measurement always involves both geometry and physics, so experiment alone can’t pick the geometry.

blocks.name: gb-geometries
blocks.cap: The same equilateral triangle in a flat, a spherical and a saddle-shaped world. On a sphere the extra angle (the spherical excess) grows with the area.

blocks.title: The angles of a big triangle
blocks.q: On a sphere, a triangle’s angles add to 180° plus an extra amount called the spherical excess E, and its area is (E ÷ 180°) × π R². A triangle on the Earth (R ≈ 6,371 km) runs from the North Pole down to the equator, a quarter of the way around, and back up. Find its angles, its excess and its area.
steps: Each corner is a right angle: 90° + 90° + 90° = 270°.
Check: that is one eighth of the whole surface, 4π R² ≈ 510 million km².
blocks.a: Three 90° angles; excess 90°; about 64 million km², one eighth of the globe.

blocks.title: Reasoning by recurrence
blocks.q: Show that 1 + 3 + 5 + … + (2n − 1) = n² for every n.
steps: Suppose it holds for n. The next odd number is 2n + 1, so the new sum is n² + 2n + 1 = (n + 1)².
So if it holds for n, it holds for n + 1. Starting from 1, it holds for 2, then 3, and so on forever.
blocks.a: True for every n. This kind of step, Poincaré said, is where mathematics leaves pure logic behind and makes something new.

blocks.html: Poincaré’s conventionalism: some basic statements of science, especially the axioms of geometry and certain principles of mechanics, are neither self-evident truths nor experimental facts but agreed definitions, chosen because they are simple and useful. Most other scientific statements remain open to testing.

Thinking Poincaré meant that science is just made up. He said the opposite: conventions are few, and they are guided by experience; the rest of science is answerable to experiment, and its lasting gains are real relations between things.

The book was widely read. In Bern, around 1902–1904, the young Albert Einstein and his friends in their small reading circle, the “Olympia Academy,” studied it closely. But Einstein’s general relativity (1915) described gravity as the curving of space and time, and astronomers came to treat the geometry of space as something measured, not chosen. Poincaré had expected Euclid to remain the most convenient choice. Philosophers still debate how much of his conventionalism survives; many agree he was right that a theory meets experiment as a whole, geometry and physics together.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Euclid, earlier on this ladder, built geometry on a few postulates. The fifth, about parallels, troubled readers for two thousand years. Poincaré explains why other choices are possible.
Kant held that Euclid’s geometry is known a priori, before any experience. Poincaré agreed that the mind brings something of its own (in mathematical induction) but denied that it imposes Euclid.
Einstein’s Relativity, the next rungs on, makes geometry part of physics.
Whitehead and Russell tried to build mathematics from logic. Poincaré was a sharp critic of that program.
Which parts of what you were taught in science are facts you could check, and which are choices of words or units?
If two descriptions of the world fit every possible measurement equally well, is there any sense in which one is true?
Can an experiment ever test one statement on its own, or only a whole web of them?

blocks.html: See the Math Ladder’s topics on proof by induction and the Physics Ladder’s relativity topics.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Inches or centimeters: is one of them more true? What makes one more convenient for a job?
  2. Why can’t a person measuring small triangles in a garden tell whether the Earth is round?
  3. Poincaré says doubting everything is as lazy as believing everything. Do you agree? Why?
  4. Think of a rule in a game you play. Could the game work with a different rule? Would it be a worse game, or just a different one?
  5. Einstein read this book as a young man. What questions in it might have set him thinking?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Alfred North Whitehead was an English mathematician who later became a philosopher in America. In 1911 he wrote a small book for anyone curious about what mathematics is for. His answer: mathematics is the study of patterns that fit many things at once.

When you learn that 2 apples and 3 apples make 5 apples, you have learned something about cats, stars and pennies too. Two of anything and three of anything make five. That jump, from these things to any things, is where mathematics begins, Whitehead said.

He also loved things that repeat: day and night, the seasons, a swing going back and forth, the note of a guitar string. Mathematics has a special wave shape, the sine wave, for all of them. Even sharp, jagged shapes can be built by adding smooth waves together.

blocks.name: gb-waves
blocks.cap: Add more and more smooth waves. Watch them build a square wave with sharp corners.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Find the repeats. With a grown-up, make a list of things in your day that repeat: the ticking of a clock, your heartbeat (count it for 15 seconds and multiply by 4), the lights at a crossing. For each one, how long does it take to come back around? That time is called the period.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Alfred North Whitehead (1861–1947) taught mathematics at Trinity College, Cambridge, where one of his students was Bertrand Russell. Together they wrote Principia Mathematica (1910–1913), a vast attempt to build mathematics from logic. In the middle of that labor Whitehead wrote An Introduction to Mathematics (1911) for the Home University Library, a series of short, cheap books by experts for general readers. Later he moved to Harvard (1924) and became a philosopher; his Science and the Modern World (1925) is another rung on this ladder.
His aim is not to teach techniques but to show the main ideas, so that a reader understands why mathematics matters in science and in thinking. He knew how school mathematics often feels:

Mathematics, Whitehead says, is about any things, not particular ones. A statement like “two and three make five” is true of anything you can count. The tool that captures “any” is the variable: a letter such as $x$ that stands for any number of a certain kind.

Whitehead praises mathematical notation, from the decimal place system to the signs of algebra, because it lets us do routine steps without thinking about them, and saves our attention for the hard part.

The later chapters tour imaginary numbers, coordinate geometry and the conic sections, functions (a rule linking each value of one variable to a value of another), periodicity in nature, trigonometry, series and the calculus. The sine and cosine functions are the natural language of anything that repeats, because they repeat themselves: $\sin(x + 360°) = \sin x$.

A great result of the century before Whitehead, due to Joseph Fourier, carries the idea further: almost any repeating shape, even one with corners, is a sum of sine waves. This is the mathematics behind sound, tides, radio and much more.

blocks.name: gb-waves
blocks.cap: A Fourier series: each added wave is a sine with a higher frequency and smaller size. The more you add, the closer the total comes to the square wave or the sawtooth.

blocks.title: The period of a wave
blocks.q: The function $y = \sin(3x)$, with $x$ in degrees, repeats after how many degrees? How many full waves fit between 0° and 360°?
steps: $\sin$ repeats when its input grows by 360°.
So the period is 120°, and 360 ÷ 120 = 3 waves fit in one turn.
blocks.a: Period 120°; three waves.

blocks.title: Multiplying imaginary numbers
blocks.q: Whitehead explains that numbers like $i$, with $i^2 = -1$, obey the ordinary rules. Work out $(2 + 3i)(1 - i)$.

blocks.html: Whitehead’s picture of mathematics: it begins with abstraction (statements about any things), works through variables and functions, and is useful exactly because it is general. A pattern found once applies wherever the same form appears.

Thinking that abstract means useless. Whitehead argues the reverse: the more general an idea, the more places it applies. Imaginary numbers, once a puzzle, became everyday tools of electrical engineering.

The little book stayed in print for decades and is still recommended as one of the best short explanations of what mathematics is about. Readers note its clarity and its humor. Its wider hope, that mathematics rests on logic, was dealt a blow in 1931 by Kurt Gödel, who showed that no such system can prove every true statement of arithmetic. That did not touch the book’s main lesson about patterns and their uses.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Euclid and Nicomachus, earlier on this ladder, are the Greeks whose “propositions about any things” Whitehead has in mind.
Descartes joined algebra to geometry with coordinates, a chapter Whitehead retells.
Poincaré, the rung before, doubted that mathematics could be reduced to logic. Whitehead and Russell tried; the argument went on for decades.
Hardy’s A Mathematician’s Apology, a few rungs on, defends mathematics for its beauty rather than its uses. Compare the two.
Why should a pattern found by thinking also fit the physical world?
Is mathematics discovered, like a continent, or invented, like a game?
Which things in your daily life do you now do “without thinking about them,” and what did that free you to do?

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Whitehead says mathematics often begins in disappointment. Has that been true for you? What would make it less so?
  2. Two and three make five for apples and for stars. Why is that surprising when you think about it?
  3. What operations can you now do without thinking (tying shoes, adding small numbers)? How does that help?
  4. Name three things in nature that repeat. What is the period of each?
  5. Is it better to learn many techniques or a few big ideas? Why might you need both?

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Albert Einstein was a scientist who asked questions a child might ask, and then kept asking. One was: what would I see if I could ride along with a beam of light? His answers changed how we think about space and time.

He wrote a short book to explain his ideas to ordinary readers, using trains, lightning and clocks. Here is the surprising part. Light always travels at the same speed, about 300,000 kilometers every second, for everyone, however fast they are moving. To make that work, time itself must run differently for people moving past each other.

Picture a clock made of light: a flash bounces up and down between two mirrors, and each bounce is one tick. Now put the clock on a speeding train. To you, standing beside the track, the flash has to travel on a slanted zigzag, a longer path. Light can’t go faster, so each tick takes longer. The moving clock runs slow!

blocks.name: gb-light-clock
blocks.cap: Press Play. The moving clock’s flash runs a longer, slanted path, so it ticks fewer times. Slide the speed up close to the speed of light.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Walking on a moving walkway. If you walk at 1 meter per second on an airport walkway that moves at 1 meter per second, a person standing still sees you going 2 meters per second. That is how speeds add for slow things. Einstein found that the rule breaks down near the speed of light: nothing, not even a beam of light from a moving train, goes faster than light. With a grown-up, look up how long light takes to reach us from the Sun (about 8 minutes).

These effects are far too small to notice at the speed of a car or a plane. But they are real. The satellites of the GPS system have to correct their clocks for them, or your map would drift by kilometers a day.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Albert Einstein (1879–1955) published his special theory of relativity in 1905, while working as a patent examiner in Bern, Switzerland. Ten years later, in November 1915, he completed the general theory, a new account of gravity. In 1916 he wrote a short popular book, Relativity: The Special and the General Theory, for readers interested in the ideas but not trained in the mathematics, as his preface explains. Robert W. Lawson’s English translation appeared in 1920, just after a British eclipse expedition, led by Arthur Eddington and Frank Dyson, had confirmed one of the theory’s predictions and made Einstein world-famous.
The book has three parts: the special theory, the general theory, and some thoughts on the universe as a whole. It uses almost no mathematics beyond simple algebra, and a great many trains.

blocks.text: Two principles that seem to clash

items: The principle of relativity: the laws of nature are the same for every observer moving steadily, without turning or speeding up. A passenger in a smooth train cannot tell by any experiment inside it whether it is moving.
The constancy of the speed of light: light in empty space travels at the same speed $c$ (about 300,000 km/s) for every such observer, whatever the motion of its source.

blocks.html: Ordinary experience says speeds add: a man walking forward in a train moves faster relative to the ground than the train does. Apply that to light and the two principles contradict each other. Einstein’s way out was to look again at what we mean by time.

blocks.text: What does “at the same time” mean?

blocks.html: Einstein asks the reader to imagine lightning striking the railway embankment at two distant places, A and B, and to say what it means that the two strokes were simultaneous. His answer is a definition you could test: put an observer at the midpoint M, with mirrors so that he can see A and B at once.

Now let a long train run along the track. An observer M′ in the middle of the train is beside M at the moment of the strokes, but she is moving toward B. She meets the light from B before the light from A arrives. Since light moves at the same speed for her too, she must conclude that B struck first.

blocks.name: gb-light-clock
blocks.cap: Einstein’s train and embankment. Press Play: M sees both flashes together; M′, riding toward B, sees B’s flash first.

blocks.text: Slow clocks, short rods, and E = mc²

blocks.html: Out of these two principles come the Lorentz transformation and its surprises. A clock moving at speed $v$ runs slow by the factor $\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}$, and a rod moving lengthwise is shortened by the same factor. No body can be pushed up to the speed of light. And mass and energy turn out to be two forms of one thing, $E = mc^2$.

blocks.title: Time dilation
blocks.q: A spaceship passes the Earth at 0.8 c. Its clock records 30 minutes for a trip. How long does the trip take by Earth’s clocks?
blocks.a: 50 minutes.

blocks.title: Adding speeds near the speed of light
blocks.q: On a train moving at 0.6 c, a lamp at the back sends a rocket forward at 0.6 c relative to the train. Galileo’s rule would give 1.2 c. What does Einstein’s rule $w = (u + v)/(1 + uv/c^2)$ give?
blocks.a: About 0.88 c.

blocks.title: Mass into energy
blocks.q: How much energy is in 1 gram of mass, by $E = mc^2$?
steps: That is about what a large power station makes in a day.
blocks.a: $9 \times 10^{13}$ joules.

blocks.text: The general theory: gravity as geometry

blocks.html: In Part II Einstein imagines a man inside a closed chest far out in space, pulled steadily upward by a rope. Objects he lets go fall to the floor, exactly as on Earth. No experiment inside can tell whether he is being pulled or resting in a gravitational field. This is the principle of equivalence. It leads to the idea that gravity is not a force in the old sense but the curving of space and time by matter, so that the geometry of space becomes a question for measurement (compare Poincaré, two rungs back).

The theory made three famous predictions: the extra turning of Mercury’s orbit (43 seconds of arc per century, which Newton’s theory could not explain), the bending of starlight passing the Sun (confirmed in the 1919 eclipse), and the reddening of light climbing out of a strong gravitational field (confirmed later). Gravitational waves, another prediction, were first detected directly in 2015.

Relativity does not say “everything is relative.” Its starting point is something absolute: the laws of physics and the speed of light are the same for everyone. What becomes relative is the measure of time and length between events.

Thinking the slow clock is an illusion or a fault in the clock. Every kind of clock, from atoms to heartbeats, is affected the same way. Fast particles called muons, made high in the atmosphere, live long enough to reach the ground only because their time runs slow as seen from Earth.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Galileo, earlier on this ladder, first stated that a steady motion can’t be felt from inside a ship’s cabin. Einstein extended Galileo’s principle to light.
Newton assumed an absolute time flowing the same for all. Einstein gave that up, and showed that Newton’s laws are an excellent approximation at low speeds.
Faraday and Maxwell’s electromagnetism, with its fixed speed of light, set the puzzle that relativity solved.
Poincaré had reached parts of the special theory at about the same time.
Eddington, the next rung, tested general relativity in 1919 and wrote about the expanding universe it allowed.
If two observers disagree about which event came first, is there any fact of the matter?
How can a theory overturn our everyday ideas of time and still agree with everyday experience?
Einstein begins with thought experiments, not laboratories. When can thinking alone tell us about the world?

blocks.html: See the Physics Ladder’s topics on the postulates of relativity, simultaneity, time dilation and the Lorentz transformation.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Have you ever sat in a train or car and thought you were moving when it was the one next to you? What does that show?
  2. Why do you think Einstein used trains and lightning to explain his ideas?
  3. If clocks on a fast spaceship run slow, who is “really” older at the end of a trip? Talk it through.
  4. Einstein said the laws of nature are the same for everyone. Why is that a kind of fairness in physics?
  5. Which seems stranger to you: that time can stretch, or that gravity is the shape of space?
