Arthur Eddington was an English astronomer who could make the hardest ideas sound like an adventure story. In 1933 he wrote a little book about a big surprise: the galaxies are rushing away from us, and from each other. The whole universe is getting bigger.

How can that be? Picture a balloon with dots drawn on it. Blow it up. Every dot moves away from every other dot, and no dot is the center. A dot twice as far away moves away twice as fast. The galaxies behave the same way.

blocks.name: gb-balloon
blocks.cap: Press Inflate. Tap any dot to stand on it: all the others move away, and the farther ones move faster. The same is true from every dot.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Balloon universe. Draw 8 or 10 dots on a balloon with a marker, with a grown-up’s help. Blow it up a little and measure, with a string, the distance from one dot to its neighbors. Blow it up more and measure again. Which distances grew the most? Now pick a different dot. Does the universe look different from there?

Astronomers learned this by looking at the light of far-off galaxies. Their light is stretched toward the red end of the rainbow, the way the sound of a passing car’s engine drops in pitch as it drives away. The farther the galaxy, the more its light is stretched.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Sir Arthur Eddington (1882–1944) was Plumian Professor of Astronomy at Cambridge and the leading English-speaking interpreter of Einstein. In 1919 he led the eclipse expedition to the island of Príncipe, off West Africa, whose photographs of stars near the darkened Sun helped confirm general relativity. He worked out much of how stars shine (The Internal Constitution of the Stars, 1926) and wrote popular books that sold widely.

The Expanding Universe (Cambridge University Press, 1933) grew from a public lecture he gave at the meeting of the International Astronomical Union in Cambridge, Massachusetts, in September 1932. It is a short, witty account of a discovery only a few years old.
This book was first published in 1933, so it is still under copyright, and this rung quotes none of it. Everything here is our own summary. Look for it in a library (it was reprinted many times).

items: From 1912 on, Vesto Slipher measured the spectra of faint spiral nebulae and found that most of them were moving away from us, fast.
In the 1920s Edwin Hubble showed these nebulae are galaxies far outside our own Milky Way.
In 1929 Hubble found that the farther a galaxy is, the faster it recedes: speed is proportional to distance. This is Hubble’s law, $v = H_0 d$.

Meanwhile the theorists had found that Einstein’s equations allow a universe that expands. Alexander Friedmann (1922) and Georges Lemaître (1927) had worked it out. Eddington helped bring Lemaître’s paper to English readers in 1931.

blocks.name: gb-balloon
blocks.cap: A two-dimensional model: the galaxies sit on the surface of the balloon. Speed divided by distance is the same for every pair, which is Hubble’s law.

blocks.html: Eddington explains the expansion as a property of space itself, not galaxies flying through a fixed space. In Einstein’s theory the universe can be finite but without an edge, like the surface of a sphere, and that surface can grow. He describes the cosmical constant, a term Einstein had added to his equations, as a kind of cosmic repulsion that pushes the galaxies apart, and he hopes to calculate it from the theory of the atom. He did not like the idea of a sudden beginning; he favored a universe that had rested in balance for ages before it began, slowly, to expand.
The book also faces a puzzle. Using Hubble’s measurements, the expansion seemed to have started only about 2 billion years earlier, less than the age geologists were finding for the Earth.

blocks.title: Hubble’s law
blocks.q: A galaxy is 100 megaparsecs away (one megaparsec is about 3.26 million light-years). Today’s value of the Hubble constant is about 70 km/s per megaparsec. How fast is it receding?
blocks.a: About 7,000 km/s.

blocks.title: How old is the universe?
blocks.q: If the galaxies have always receded at their present speeds, they were all together a time $1/H_0$ ago. With $H_0$ in km/s per megaparsec, that time in billions of years is about $978 \div H_0$. Compare Hubble’s 1929 value, about 500, with today’s, about 70.
steps: The careful modern figure, allowing for changes in the rate, is 13.8 billion years.
blocks.a: About 2 billion years then; about 14 billion now.

blocks.html: In an expanding universe, every observer sees the same thing: everything else moving away, with speed proportional to distance. There is no center of the expansion, just as no dot is the center of a balloon’s surface.

Picturing the galaxies as fragments flying out from one spot in space, like a bomb. The expansion is of space itself, everywhere at once. That is also why far galaxies can recede faster than light without breaking relativity’s speed limit, which applies to motion through space.

The age puzzle was solved in the 1950s, when Walter Baade and others found that the distances to galaxies had been badly underestimated. The Hubble constant dropped, and the age of the universe grew past the age of the Earth. Eddington’s preferred slow start lost out: the evidence of the 1960s, above all the faint microwave glow left over from a hot, dense early universe (discovered in 1965), supported a big bang beginning of the kind Lemaître had proposed. Eddington’s attempt to calculate the cosmical constant from atomic numbers was not accepted by other physicists. But the book’s picture of a universe of galaxies in an expanding space is the one astronomers still use, and in 1998 they found that the expansion is speeding up, which brought back something like Einstein’s and Eddington’s cosmical constant.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Ptolemy and Copernicus, earlier on this ladder, argued about what is at the center. Eddington’s universe has no center at all.
Einstein’s Relativity, the rung before, ends with thoughts on whether the universe is finite. Eddington shows what the equations made of that question.
Planck and Bohr, the next rungs, built the quantum physics that Eddington tried, without success, to join to cosmology.
If everything is moving away from us, why aren’t we at the center?
Eddington disliked the idea of a beginning. Should a scientist’s taste in ideas count for anything?
What would it mean for the universe to be finite but have no edge?

blocks.html: See the Physics Ladder’s astronomy topics on Hubble’s law, redshift and the age of the universe.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. What is something you once thought was standing still but turned out to be moving?
  2. On a balloon, every dot sees the others moving away. Why does that mean there’s no center?
  3. Astronomers learned the universe is expanding from the color of starlight. What else can light tell us?
  4. Eddington’s numbers made the universe younger than the Earth. What would you do if your measurements gave an impossible answer?
  5. Why do you think Eddington spent so much time writing for ordinary readers?

Niels Bohr was a Danish scientist who loved to argue, kindly and for hours, about the deepest puzzles in physics. In 1913 he drew a new picture of the atom, the tiny building block of everything.

In Bohr’s picture, an atom of hydrogen has a tiny heavy center with one even tinier electron around it. The electron can’t be just anywhere. It can only sit on certain “steps,” like the rungs of a ladder, and never between them. When it hops down from a higher step to a lower one, the atom gives out a little flash of light. Each kind of hop makes one exact color.

blocks.name: gb-bohr-levels
blocks.cap: Choose a step to start on and one to fall to, then press Jump. Falls to step 2 give the colors you can see; falls to step 1 give ultraviolet.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Rainbow fingerprints. Look at a lit streetlight or a neon sign through a cheap “diffraction grating” card or the shiny side of a CD (never look at the Sun). Instead of a smooth rainbow you may see separate bright lines of color. Every kind of atom has its own set of lines, like a fingerprint, because its electrons have their own ladders of steps.

Bohr also had a long, friendly argument with Albert Einstein about what atoms are really doing when nobody is looking. They never fully agreed, but they stayed friends, and their argument taught everyone a great deal.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Niels Bohr (1885–1962) studied in Copenhagen and then worked with Ernest Rutherford in Manchester, who had just found that an atom has a small, heavy nucleus. In 1913 Bohr published a theory of the hydrogen atom that explained its spectrum for the first time. He founded the Institute for Theoretical Physics in Copenhagen (1921), which became the meeting place of quantum physics, and won the Nobel Prize in 1922.

The volume collects two kinds of writing. Atomic Theory and the Description of Nature (English, 1934) gathers essays from 1925 to 1929, including the 1927 lecture at Como in which Bohr first set out his idea of complementarity. “Discussion with Einstein on Epistemological Problems in Atomic Physics” (1949) is Bohr’s own account of his decades of debate with Einstein, written for a book in Einstein’s honor.
These essays were first published in English in 1934 and 1949, so they are still under copyright, and this rung quotes none of them. Everything here is our own summary.

By the old physics, an electron circling a nucleus should give off light all the time, lose energy and spiral inward in a tiny fraction of a second. Atoms would not last. Bohr proposed instead that the electron has only certain allowed stationary states, each with a fixed energy, in which it does not radiate. Light comes out only when the electron jumps from one state to a lower one, as a single photon carrying the difference, $hf = E_{\text{upper}} - E_{\text{lower}}$ (Planck’s rule, two rungs on).

For hydrogen the allowed energies are $E_n = -\dfrac{13.6\ \text{eV}}{n^2}$, for $n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$ A photon’s wavelength in nanometers is about $1240 \div \Delta E$ (with $\Delta E$ in electron-volts).

blocks.name: gb-bohr-levels
blocks.cap: Hydrogen’s energy levels. Jumps down to n = 2 make the visible Balmer lines, red, blue-green and violet.

blocks.title: Hydrogen’s red line
blocks.q: Find the energy and wavelength of the photon given off when hydrogen’s electron falls from n = 3 to n = 2.
steps: $\lambda \approx 1240 / 1.889 \approx 656$ nm: red light, the brightest visible line in hydrogen’s spectrum.
blocks.a: 1.89 eV; about 656 nm.

blocks.title: Pulling the electron free
blocks.q: How much energy does it take to remove the electron entirely from the n = 2 level?

blocks.html: Bohr’s model worked beautifully for hydrogen and badly for anything more complex. In 1925–1926 Heisenberg, Schrödinger and others replaced it with quantum mechanics, which kept Bohr’s energy levels and jumps but gave up the idea of definite orbits.

Light and electrons behave in some experiments like waves and in others like particles. Bohr argued that these two pictures are complementary: each is needed, neither is complete, and the experimental arrangement decides which one shows. The setup that measures exactly where something is rules out measuring exactly how it moves (Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle). Bohr insisted that we must still describe every experiment in ordinary language, the language of the laboratory, even when what we describe is not ordinary.

Einstein admired quantum mechanics but could not accept that nature at bottom runs on chance, or that it is incomplete to say what a particle is doing between measurements. At the Solvay conferences in Brussels in 1927 and 1930 he brought Bohr one clever thought experiment after another, each meant to beat the uncertainty principle. In 1930 he proposed a box of light that would release one photon at a timed moment while being weighed. Bohr, after a sleepless night, found the flaw, using Einstein’s own general relativity: weighing the box moves it in the Earth’s gravity, and that changes the rate of its clock. In 1935 Einstein, with Podolsky and Rosen, argued that quantum mechanics must be incomplete; Bohr replied the same year. Bohr’s 1949 essay retells all of this with great respect for his friend.
Bohr’s lessons: atoms have discrete energy levels; wave and particle pictures are complementary; and in atomic physics the conditions of observation are part of the description of what is observed.
Thinking the Bohr atom is the final picture. Electrons don’t move on tiny planetary orbits. Bohr’s energy levels survive in quantum mechanics, but the orbits were replaced by clouds of probability.

Bohr’s 1913 model is still taught as the first step into quantum physics, and his energy-level formula is exact for hydrogen’s main lines. His view of complementarity became the core of the “Copenhagen interpretation,” for decades the standard way of talking about quantum mechanics. It has also had steady critics. Experiments since the 1980s, testing ideas that grew out of the Einstein–Podolsky–Rosen argument, have agreed with quantum mechanics and against the kind of hidden, definite reality Einstein hoped for; physicists still debate what that means. Bohr himself spent his later years urging open international cooperation on atomic energy.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Lucretius and the Greek atomists, earlier on this ladder, imagined atoms as tiny solid bits. Bohr’s atom is mostly empty space with rules that sound like music: only certain notes allowed.
Newton’s Optics spread sunlight into a smooth spectrum; atoms make sharp lines, and Bohr explained why.
Planck found the quantum of energy; Heisenberg found the uncertainty that limits what can be known together. Both are rungs here.
Einstein’s Relativity is the other great physics of the century. The Bohr–Einstein debate is about whether the two views of nature can be joined.
Can two descriptions that seem to contradict each other both be true, each in its place?
Does it make sense to ask what something is doing when no one is measuring it?
What made the Bohr–Einstein argument a model of how to disagree?

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Bohr and Einstein disagreed for thirty years and stayed friends. How did they manage it?
  2. Why might the way you look at something change what you see? Think of an example from everyday life.
  3. Every kind of atom has its own set of colors. How might astronomers use that to learn what stars are made of?
  4. Bohr’s model was wrong in some ways but very useful. Can a wrong idea be a good step?
  5. Is it ever good to say “both pictures are needed”? When is it a way of avoiding a hard question?

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Theodosius Dobzhansky grew up in Ukraine, collecting ladybugs, and became one of the great scientists of evolution in America. He studied tiny fruit flies by the millions, in the lab and in the wild mountains of the American West.

Charles Darwin had shown that living things change over many generations. But Darwin didn’t know how traits pass from parents to children. By Dobzhansky’s time scientists knew about genes, the instructions passed down in every living thing. Dobzhansky’s 1937 book put the two ideas together.

His big idea: evolution is a change in how common different versions of genes are in a group. Some versions get more common because they help their owners survive (natural selection). Some get more common or rarer just by luck, especially in small groups. That luck is called genetic drift.

blocks.name: gb-drift
blocks.cap: Eight separate groups of animals, each starting with half the A version of a gene. Small groups wander by luck. Make the groups bigger and see what changes.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Bean-bag drift. Put 5 red and 5 white beans in a cup. Without looking, pull one out, note its color, put it back, and do this 10 times. Make a new cup of 10 beans with the colors you drew. Repeat for a few “generations.” Does one color sometimes take over just by luck? Try again with 50 beans in the cup. Is it harder for luck to win?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Theodosius Dobzhansky (1900–1975) was born in Nemyriv, in what is now Ukraine, and studied and taught biology in Kyiv and Leningrad. In 1927 he came to the United States to work in Thomas Hunt Morgan’s famous fruit-fly laboratory at Columbia University, followed Morgan to Caltech, and stayed. He returned to Columbia as a professor in 1940.

Genetics and the Origin of Species (Columbia University Press, 1937) grew out of lectures he gave at Columbia in 1936. It went through three editions (1937, 1941, 1951) and is counted as the founding book of the modern synthesis, the joining of Darwin’s natural selection with Mendel’s genetics.
This book was first published in 1937, so it is still under copyright, and this rung quotes none of it. Everything here is our own summary.

In 1900 Mendel’s laws of inheritance were rediscovered. For a while many geneticists thought they competed with Darwin: genes seemed to come in sudden jumps, while Darwin had described slow change. In the 1920s and early 1930s the mathematicians R. A. Fisher, J. B. S. Haldane and Sewall Wright showed on paper that Mendelian genes and selection fit together. But their work was hard for most biologists to follow, and it needed evidence from real, wild populations. Dobzhansky supplied both: clear explanations and field data.

items: Mutation supplies new versions of genes (alleles) and changes in chromosomes. It is the raw material.

Wild populations are full of hidden variation. Dobzhansky’s studies of the fruit fly Drosophila pseudoobscura found different arrangements of its chromosomes (inversions) in different mountain ranges, and even changing with the seasons.
Selection, migration and drift change how common each variant is. In small populations chance alone can carry a variant to 0% or 100% (Wright’s genetic drift).
Evolution is a change in the genetic make-up of populations.

Species form when populations become reproductively isolated, so they no longer interbreed. Dobzhansky named and sorted the isolating mechanisms: living in different places or seasons, different courtship, failure of mating, and hybrids that die or are sterile (like the mule).

blocks.name: gb-drift
blocks.cap: A simulation of the Wright–Fisher model: each generation is a random draw from the last. Compare a population of 20 with one of 500, then add a small selective advantage.

blocks.html: If a gene has two versions, A with frequency $p$ and a with frequency $q = 1 - p$, and mating is random, the three kinds of individuals appear in the proportions $p^2$ (AA), $2pq$ (Aa) and $q^2$ (aa). This is the Hardy–Weinberg rule (1908), named for the mathematician G. H. Hardy, a few rungs on, and the physician Wilhelm Weinberg. Without selection, drift, migration or mutation, the proportions stay the same forever. Evolution is any departure from it.

blocks.title: Hardy–Weinberg
blocks.q: In a population, 16% of the flies show a recessive trait (genotype aa). Assuming Hardy–Weinberg proportions, what share of flies carry one hidden copy (Aa)?
blocks.a: 48% are carriers: three times as many as show the trait. This is the hidden variation Dobzhansky found.

blocks.title: Drift by chance
blocks.q: A tiny population has 4 gene copies, 2 of them A. The next generation’s 4 copies are drawn at random, each with chance 1/2 of being A. What is the chance that A is lost at once?
steps: Each copy must be a: chance 1/2 each.
blocks.a: 1 in 16. In a population of 100 copies, the chance would be far too small to notice.

blocks.html: The modern synthesis in one line: mutation makes variation, selection and drift sort it, and isolation splits one species into two.
Thinking genes and Darwin were rivals. Before the synthesis many scientists thought so. Dobzhansky’s book showed that Mendel’s genes are the very variation that natural selection acts on.

The book was an immediate success and shaped evolutionary biology for decades. Ernst Mayr (1942), Julian Huxley (1942), George Gaylord Simpson (1944) and G. Ledyard Stebbins (1950) extended the synthesis to classification, fossils and plants. Since Dobzhansky’s time, the discovery of DNA, molecular genetics, and the study of development have added a great deal, and biologists debate how much the synthesis must be widened. But its core, evolution as genetic change in populations, remains the framework of modern biology. Dobzhansky later wrote a famous 1973 essay whose title says that nothing in biology makes sense except in the light of evolution. He was a religious believer himself and wrote that he saw no conflict between his faith and evolution; readers hold different views on that question, and this rung leaves it to them.

Aristotle classified animals into fixed kinds; for Dobzhansky a species is a group of populations that can interbreed.

How can chance (drift and mutation) and something like design (adaptation by selection) both be at work?
Where exactly is the line between two species, and does nature draw it sharply?

G. H. Hardy was an English mathematician who loved numbers the way some people love music, and who also loved cricket. Near the end of his life he wrote a short book explaining why he had spent his life on mathematics, even though, he said, his own discoveries had never been useful for anything practical.

His reason: some ideas are simply beautiful, and finding them is worth doing for its own sake, like painting a picture or writing a poem. To show what he meant, he chose a proof that is more than 2,000 years old: Euclid’s proof that the prime numbers never run out.

Prime numbers are numbers like 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11 that can only be divided evenly by 1 and themselves. Suppose someone says, “Here is a list of all the primes.” Multiply them all together and add 1. The new number can’t be divided evenly by any prime on the list (you always get a remainder of 1). So it must be made of primes that weren’t on the list. The list was never complete!

blocks.name: gb-euclid-primes
blocks.cap: Pick any list of primes. Multiply them and add 1. The result always has a prime factor that isn’t on your list.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Prime hunting. Write the numbers 1 to 50 on paper. Cross out 1. Circle 2, then cross out every second number after it. Circle 3, and cross out every third number. Keep going with the next number that isn’t crossed out. The circled ones are the primes. (This method is called the sieve of Eratosthenes, after a Greek who lived about 2,200 years ago.)

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Godfrey Harold Hardy (1877–1947) spent most of his life at Trinity College, Cambridge, with twelve years as a professor at Oxford (1919–1931). He was the leading English pure mathematician of his time, a master of number theory and analysis. For thirty-five years he worked in partnership with J. E. Littlewood. In 1913 he received a letter from an unknown clerk in Madras, Srinivasa Ramanujan, full of astonishing formulas; Hardy brought him to Cambridge, and their work together from 1914 to 1919 became one of the famous stories of mathematics.

A Mathematician’s Apology (Cambridge University Press, 1940) was written after a heart attack, when Hardy felt that his creative power was gone. An “apology” here means a defense, as in Plato’s Apology of Socrates. The book is short, proud, funny and sad. Since 1967 it has usually been printed with a long foreword by his friend C. P. Snow.
This book was first published in 1940, so it is still under copyright, and this rung quotes none of it. Everything here is our own summary.

items: Mathematics is a young person’s game. Hardy claims that the great discoveries are mostly made early in life, and he writes as one who believes his own best work is behind him.

A defense must be honest about uses. He separates the elementary mathematics that engineers and everyone need from “real” mathematics, the deep theories of the great mathematicians. Real mathematics, he says, is almost wholly useless in practice.
Its value is beauty. Like a painter’s or a poet’s, the mathematician’s work is to make patterns, and they must be beautiful. Ugly mathematics, he says, has no lasting place.
What makes a theorem beautiful: it is serious (connected to many other ideas), general and deep, and its proof has surprise, inevitability and economy.
Mathematical reality is out there. Hardy holds that the mathematician discovers truths that exist independently of us, rather than inventing them.
Useless means harmless. Writing as a lifelong opponent of war, he takes comfort that number theory had never served any warlike purpose.

blocks.html: Hardy chooses two Greek proofs to show what a beautiful theorem looks like, because they are short enough to give in full and as fresh as when they were found.

blocks.title: Euclid: the primes never run out
blocks.q: Show that no finite list of primes can contain them all.
steps: Take any list of primes, say $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_k$, and form $N = p_1 p_2 \cdots p_k + 1$.
Dividing $N$ by any prime on the list leaves remainder 1, so none of them divides $N$.
But every whole number above 1 has at least one prime factor. So $N$ has a prime factor that is not on the list.
Example: $2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 7 \cdot 11 \cdot 13 + 1 = 30{,}031 = 59 \times 509$. Neither 59 nor 509 was on the list.
blocks.a: The list is never complete: there are infinitely many primes.

blocks.name: gb-euclid-primes
blocks.cap: Try it with your own lists. Notice that the new number need not be prime itself; it only has to have a new prime factor.

blocks.title: Pythagoras: √2 is not a fraction
blocks.q: Show that no fraction $a/b$ squares to exactly 2.
steps: Suppose $\sqrt2 = a/b$ in lowest terms, so $a$ and $b$ are not both even.
Then $a^2 = 2b^2$, so $a^2$ is even, so $a$ is even: $a = 2c$.
Then $4c^2 = 2b^2$, so $b^2 = 2c^2$, and $b$ is even too.
Both even contradicts “lowest terms.” So the supposition was false.
blocks.a: √2 is irrational. This is a proof by contradiction, the kind of argument Hardy admired above almost any other.

blocks.html: Hardy’s test for a great theorem: serious, general, deep, with a proof that is surprising, inevitable and economical. Both Greek proofs pass after more than two thousand years.

Taking Hardy’s claim of uselessness as the last word. Within forty years the theory of prime numbers, his own field, became the basis of the public-key codes that protect online banking and messages (RSA, 1977). Hardy had also counted relativity and quantum theory among the harmless subjects; physics built on them produced the atomic bomb only five years after the book appeared.

Hardy’s best-known result outside mathematics is one he thought trivial. In 1908 he wrote a short letter to the journal Science showing that, with random mating, gene frequencies stay steady from generation to generation. The Hardy–Weinberg rule is now in every biology textbook (see the Dobzhansky rung).

The Apology is one of the most widely read books about mathematics, loved for its prose and its passion. Many mathematicians recognize their own experience of beauty in it. Critics have answered several of its claims: that pure and applied mathematics are separate (they keep crossing), that mathematicians always peak young (many have done great work late), and that beauty is the main reason mathematics matters. Snow’s foreword, and Hardy’s own pages, also leave readers with a portrait of a man who was kind, shy and devoted to his friends, including Ramanujan.

Erwin Schrödinger was a physicist, one of the people who worked out the strange rules of atoms. In 1943, in Dublin, he gave some talks for the public that asked a question from a different science: what is life? How can the rules of physics explain a growing, breathing, living thing?

One of his puzzles was about genes, the instructions passed from parents to children. Genes are tiny, far too small to see. Yet they are copied again and again, for hundreds of years, almost without mistakes. A family’s nose or chin can show up generation after generation. How can something so small stay so steady?

Schrödinger guessed that a gene is one big, carefully built molecule, a kind of code, like Morse code with its dots and dashes. Just a few kinds of symbols, put in a long row, can spell out a huge number of different messages. Ten years later, scientists found that genes are written in the DNA molecule, using a code of four chemical “letters.”

🧩 Try this

Code builder. Using only two signs, a dot and a dash, how many different codes can you make with 1 sign? (2: · and –.) With 2 signs? (4: ··, ·–, –·, ––.) With 3? With 4? Add them all up. Schrödinger used this very example: with groups of up to four signs you already have enough codes for the whole alphabet. DNA has four letters instead of two. How many codes of 3 letters could it make? (4 × 4 × 4 = 64.)

He also noticed that living things keep themselves in good order while the world around them tends to run down and get messy, the way a tidy room gets messy unless someone keeps tidying. Living things do their tidying by taking in food and sunlight.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Erwin Schrödinger (1887–1961), born in Vienna, created the wave equation of quantum mechanics in 1926 and shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1933. He left Germany that year, after the Nazis came to power, and in 1939 settled in Dublin at the new Institute for Advanced Studies. In February 1943 he gave three public lectures at Trinity College, Dublin; the book What Is Life? The Physical Aspect of the Living Cell (Cambridge University Press, 1944) came from them.
This book was first published in 1944, so it is still under copyright, and this rung quotes none of it. Everything here is our own summary.

blocks.text: Question 1: why are atoms so small?

blocks.html: Turn the question around, Schrödinger says: why are we so big compared with atoms? Because the exact laws of physics and chemistry are statistical: they describe the average behavior of enormous numbers of molecules. If you count $n$ molecules doing something at random, the count is typically off by about $\sqrt n$, so the error is a share of about $1/\sqrt n$. With a hundred molecules that is 10%; with a million, 0.1%. An organism must be built of vast numbers of atoms for its workings to be reliable. This is his “$\sqrt n$ law.”

blocks.name: gb-root-n
blocks.cap: Each dot is one trial: n molecules wander at random between the two halves of a box. With 100 molecules the share on the left varies a lot; with a million it barely moves from 50%.

blocks.title: The √n law
blocks.q: In a gas, you count the molecules in a small region where you expect 1,000,000. About how far off might the count be, and what percentage is that?
blocks.a: Off by about 1,000, or 0.1%.

blocks.text: Question 2: how can a tiny gene be so steady?

blocks.html: Here is the puzzle. Experiments with X-rays on fruit flies suggested a gene holds at most a million or so atoms, and perhaps far fewer. By the $\sqrt n$ law, anything that small should be shaky and unreliable. Yet genes are copied faithfully over many generations, and the famous lower lip of the Habsburg royal family appeared in portraits across centuries.

Schrödinger’s answer, built on the work of the young physicist Max Delbrück and his colleagues, was quantum mechanics. A gene must be a molecule, held together by the same quantum forces that make molecules stable. To change it you must lift it over an energy barrier, which at body temperature happens only rarely. Those rare jumps are mutations: sudden, lasting changes, just as the geneticists had found.

blocks.text: The code-script and the aperiodic crystal

blocks.html: What kind of molecule could hold the plan of a whole organism? Not an ordinary crystal, which repeats the same unit over and over and so says very little. Schrödinger proposed an aperiodic crystal: a solid, orderly structure in which the units do not simply repeat, so that their sequence can carry a message, a code-script. A small number of kinds of unit, in a long enough row, can spell an astronomical number of different plans.

blocks.title: How much can a code say?
blocks.q: Schrödinger illustrated the code idea with Morse code’s two signs. How many different groups of 1, 2, 3 or 4 signs can be made? And how many three-letter “words” can DNA’s four letters make?
steps: With two signs: groups of 1, 2, 3 and 4 give $2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 30$ codes.
With four letters, three at a time: $4 \times 4 \times 4 = 64$.
The genetic code found in the 1960s uses exactly such three-letter words (codons) for its 20 amino acids.
blocks.a: 30 Morse groups; 64 DNA triplets.

blocks.text: Question 3: how does life keep its order?

blocks.html: The second law of thermodynamics says that the disorder (entropy) of an isolated system tends to grow. A living thing keeps itself highly ordered. It does not break the law, Schrödinger says: it takes order in from outside, from the food it eats (and, in the end, from sunlight), and gives disorder back as heat and waste. He described this as feeding on “negative entropy”; in a later note he agreed that physicists would rather say “free energy.” Life, he concluded, works by producing order from order, guided by the gene’s code, rather than order from the random jostling of molecules.

Three of Schrödinger’s ideas: the laws of large bodies are statistical ($\sqrt n$); the gene must be a stable molecule carrying a code-script; and life keeps its order by taking order from its surroundings.
Thinking living things break the second law of thermodynamics. They are not isolated: the total disorder of a living thing plus its surroundings still grows.

The book’s influence was enormous. Francis Crick, James Watson and Maurice Wilkins, who shared the Nobel Prize for the double helix of DNA (1953), each said that reading it helped turn them toward the problem of the gene. Its main guess came true: genes are long molecules whose sequence of four bases is a code. Biologists have also pointed out what it missed or got wrong: Schrödinger thought the gene was probably a protein, knew nothing of DNA’s role (shown in 1944 by Avery, MacLeod and McCarty), and some of what he said had been said before by geneticists. Even so, it is remembered as the book that invited physicists into biology. In a short epilogue Schrödinger gave his own personal, philosophical view of free will and the self; this rung leaves that to readers.

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Lucretius, earlier on this ladder, explained life by the motions of atoms. Schrödinger asks why life needs so many of them.
Harvey and Aristotle asked how an egg becomes an animal; Schrödinger’s code-script is a modern answer to “where is the plan?” Waddington, the last science rung, takes the question further.
Dobzhansky described genes in populations; Schrödinger asked what a single gene is made of.
Planck, Bohr and Heisenberg made the quantum physics that Schrödinger used to explain why genes are stable.
Can life be explained entirely by physics and chemistry, or does it need new laws as well?
How can a guess that turns out partly wrong still lead to a great discovery?
What does it mean for a molecule to carry a message?

Max Planck was a German physicist, a careful, patient man who also played the piano beautifully. Near the end of his long life he wrote a short story of how he made the discovery that started quantum physics.

The puzzle he worked on was about glowing things. Heat a poker in a fire: first it glows dull red, then orange, then yellow-white. Stars glow too, and their colors tell how hot they are. In 1900 Planck found the exact rule for how much of each color a hot object gives off.

To make his rule work, he had to make a strange guess: that energy doesn’t flow out smoothly, like water from a tap, but in tiny packets, like coins. He called each packet a quantum. Blue light comes in bigger packets than red light. Planck himself was not sure at first that the packets were real. They were.

blocks.cap: Slide the temperature. Hotter bodies glow brighter and their peak color moves from red toward blue.

🧩 Try this

Color thermometer. With a grown-up, look at different lights: a candle flame, an old-style yellowish bulb, a bright white LED, a blue gas flame on a stove (from a safe distance). Line them up from “coolest” color to “hottest.” Astronomers do the same with stars: red stars are cooler, blue-white stars are hotter.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Max Planck (1858–1947) was born in Kiel and became professor of theoretical physics in Berlin in 1889. His first love in physics was the law of the conservation of energy, and his early work was on thermodynamics, the science of heat. In 1900 he found the law of blackbody radiation and, to explain it, introduced the quantum of action, $h$. He received the Nobel Prize in 1918 and was for decades the most respected figure in German science.

Scientific Autobiography and Other Papers appeared in English in 1949 (the autobiography itself was published in German in 1948), translated by Frank Gaynor. It gathers his short memoir of his scientific life with several lectures on what science can and can’t know, among them “Phantom Problems in Science” and “The Meaning and Limits of Exact Science.”
These essays were first published in English in 1949, so they are still under copyright, and this rung quotes none of them. Everything here is our own summary.

blocks.text: The problem: the color of heat

blocks.html: A blackbody is an ideal object that absorbs all light falling on it; heated, it glows with a spectrum that depends only on its temperature. Gustav Kirchhoff had shown in 1859 that this spectrum is a universal law of nature, which made it, for Planck, a search for something absolute. By the late 1890s, careful measurements in Berlin by Otto Lummer, Ernst Pringsheim, Heinrich Rubens and Ferdinand Kurlbaum showed that the best formula of the day (Wien’s) failed at long wavelengths. Another formula, from classical physics (later called the Rayleigh–Jeans law), worked at long wavelengths but predicted infinite brightness at short ones, an impossibility later called the ultraviolet catastrophe.

blocks.name: gb-blackbody
blocks.cap: Planck’s law (solid) and the older classical formula (dashed). They agree far to the right; at short wavelengths the old formula shoots upward without limit.

blocks.html: In October 1900 Planck found a formula that fit all the measurements: Rubens checked it against his data the next day. Then came weeks of what Planck describes as the hardest work of his life, to find out why it was true. He could derive it only by assuming that the energy of the vibrating sources of light comes in whole-number multiples of a small unit, $E = hf$, where $f$ is the frequency. He presented this on 14 December 1900, the date often called the birthday of quantum theory. For years he hoped the quanta could be fitted back into classical physics. It was Einstein (1905), and later Bohr, who took them to be real.

Planck’s two formulas. Each quantum of light carries energy $E = hf = hc/\lambda$, with $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}$ J·s. And the peak of a blackbody’s glow (Wien’s displacement law) is at $\lambda_{\text{peak}} \approx 2.898 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m·K} \div T$.

blocks.title: The Sun’s color
blocks.q: The Sun’s surface is about 5,800 K. At what wavelength does its light peak?
steps: $= 5.0 \times 10^{-7}$ m $= 500$ nm: blue-green, in the middle of visible light.
blocks.a: About 500 nm.

blocks.title: One quantum of green light
blocks.q: How much energy is in one quantum (photon) of green light with wavelength 500 nm?
blocks.a: About $4 \times 10^{-19}$ joules, which is why we never notice single quanta.

blocks.html: The autobiography also tells of Planck’s early disappointments. As a young man he could not get the leading physicists of the day to take his ideas on entropy seriously; they hardly read his work. From this he drew a sober lesson that is now called Planck’s principle: a new scientific truth usually wins not because its opponents are persuaded, but because they eventually pass away and a new generation grows up familiar with it. Historians and sociologists of science still debate how often that is so.

In the other papers Planck argues that some famous puzzles are “phantom problems,” questions that look deep only because they are badly posed, and that exact science reaches real knowledge of an outside world even though it can never be complete. He writes about religion and science as compatible; readers will judge that view for themselves.
Thinking Planck set out to start a revolution. He was a cautious, conservative physicist who reached the quantum reluctantly, because the measurements left no other way.

blocks.text: His life and how it was judged

blocks.html: Planck’s quantum is the foundation of modern physics, chemistry and electronics; the constant $h$ is now used to define the kilogram (since 2019). His personal life held great sorrows: his first wife and four of his five children died before him: his son Karl was killed in the First World War, his twin daughters died in childbirth, and his son Erwin was executed by the Nazi regime in 1945 for his ties to the plot against Hitler. Planck stayed in Germany through the Nazi years, trying to protect science and colleagues; historians have discussed how much such quiet efforts could do. After the war the Kaiser Wilhelm Society, which he had led, was renamed the Max Planck Society.

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Newton’s Optics and Huygens’s Treatise on Light, earlier on this ladder, argued over particles and waves. Planck’s quanta reopened the question.
Faraday and Maxwell made light an electromagnetic wave; Planck found that its energy still comes in packets.
Bohr used Planck’s $E = hf$ to explain the colors of hydrogen; Heisenberg, the next rung, built the new mechanics on $h$.
Kuhn’s later account of scientific revolutions made much of Planck’s principle about generations.
Why might a person who discovers something new be the slowest to accept it?
Is it true that new ideas win only when the old guard passes away? What else can change minds?
Planck searched for laws that hold everywhere and for everyone. Is that what science is for?

Werner Heisenberg was a German physicist who, at just 23, worked out a new way to describe atoms. Two years later he found one of the most famous rules in science: the uncertainty principle.

Here is the idea. To see where something is, you have to bounce light off it. For a baseball that is no problem. But an electron is so tiny that the light itself gives it a kick. The more exactly you find where it is, the less you can know about how fast it is moving, and the other way around. It is like a seesaw: push one end down and the other goes up.
Heisenberg came to think this is not just a problem with our tools. It is how nature is. Tiny things like electrons don’t have an exact place and an exact speed at the same moment.

blocks.cap: Slide to pin down the position more tightly (top). Watch the spread of possible speeds (bottom) grow.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

The blurry photo game. Ask someone to roll a ball across the floor while you take a photo. With a very fast shutter, the ball looks sharp: you know where it is, but the photo can’t show which way or how fast it was going. With a slow shutter, the ball becomes a streak: you can see its motion, but not exactly where it was. This is only a picture of the idea (for a ball, both can be known well), but it shows the kind of trade-off Heisenberg found for atoms.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Werner Heisenberg (1901–1976) studied with Arnold Sommerfeld in Munich and worked with Max Born in Göttingen and Niels Bohr in Copenhagen. In June 1925, on the island of Helgoland where he had gone to recover from hay fever, he found the first form of quantum mechanics (matrix mechanics). In 1927 he stated the uncertainty principle. He received the Nobel Prize for 1932.

During the Second World War he was a leading scientist in Germany’s nuclear research program. What he intended, and why the program never came close to a bomb, has been debated by historians ever since. After the war he helped rebuild German science.

Physics and Philosophy: The Revolution in Modern Science (1958) grew from his Gifford Lectures at the University of St Andrews, Scotland, in the winter of 1955–56. It tells the history of quantum theory, sets out the Copenhagen interpretation, and compares it with Greek philosophy, Descartes, Kant and modern ideas about language.
This book was first published in 1958, so it is still under copyright, and this rung quotes none of it. Everything here is our own summary.

In quantum mechanics a particle is described by a wave. A wave squeezed into a small region of space must be built of many wavelengths, and a particle’s wavelength fixes its momentum. So a narrow spread in position $\Delta x$ forces a wide spread in momentum $\Delta p$:

$\Delta x \, \Delta p \ \ge\ \dfrac{\hbar}{2}$, where $\hbar = h/2\pi \approx 1.055 \times 10^{-34}$ J·s. Momentum is mass times velocity, so for a particle of mass $m$, $\Delta v \ge \hbar / (2 m \Delta x)$.

blocks.name: gb-uncertainty
blocks.cap: A wave packet (top) and the spread of momenta it contains (bottom). Their widths trade off so that Δx · Δp stays at ħ/2.

blocks.html: Heisenberg first explained it with a thought experiment, a microscope for seeing an electron. To see it sharply you need light of short wavelength, but short-wavelength light carries a big, unpredictable kick, so the better you see where the electron is, the more you disturb its motion. Bohr pointed out that the microscope story is only part of it: the limit comes from the wave description itself, not just from clumsy measuring. Heisenberg accepted this.

blocks.title: An electron in an atom
blocks.q: An electron (mass $9.11 \times 10^{-31}$ kg) is confined to a region about the size of an atom, $\Delta x = 1 \times 10^{-10}$ m. What is the least spread in its velocity?
blocks.a: About 580 km/s: huge. An electron in an atom can’t sit still.

blocks.title: A baseball
blocks.q: A baseball (0.145 kg) is located to within 1 micrometer ($10^{-6}$ m). What is the least spread in its velocity?
blocks.a: About $4 \times 10^{-28}$ m/s: far too small ever to notice. That is why everyday objects seem to have exact places and speeds.

items: The Copenhagen interpretation. We must describe experiments in the concepts of classical physics (position, momentum, wave, particle), though they apply to atoms only in limited, complementary ways. The wave function gives probabilities; the act of observation turns a range of possibilities into one fact.
Potentiality. Heisenberg suggests that the quantum wave is like Aristotle’s potentia: a tendency toward events, something between an idea and a fact.

Greek roots. He finds Heraclitus, who made fire (change) the basic stuff of the world, close to modern physics, where energy turns into particles and back. And he thinks the smallest particles are less like Democritus’ tiny solid atoms than like the mathematical forms of Plato’s Timaeus.
Language. Ordinary words were made for everyday things; when we use them about atoms we must know their limits.

blocks.html: Thinking the uncertainty principle means scientists are careless, or that “anything goes.” It is an exact, tested law, and it lets physicists make very precise predictions, for example of atomic spectra and of how transistors work.

The uncertainty principle has passed every test and is part of every physics course. The book is widely read as a thoughtful scientist’s view of his own revolution. Its interpretation is another matter. Einstein, de Broglie, David Bohm and others proposed alternatives, which Heisenberg discusses and rejects in one chapter; later the many-worlds view and others joined the list. Physicists still disagree about what, if anything, the wave function describes, though they agree on the predictions. Historians, for their part, continue to weigh Heisenberg’s wartime role.

items: Aristotle’s Physics, earlier on this ladder, distinguished the potential from the actual; Heisenberg borrows the distinction for the quantum wave.
Plato’s Timaeus built the elements from mathematical shapes. Heisenberg thought modern particle physics was closer to Plato than to the atomists.
Lucretius and the atomists pictured hard, unchanging atoms. Heisenberg’s particles can be created and destroyed.
Bohr, two rungs back, gave the philosophy of complementarity that Heisenberg follows; Einstein remained its great critic.

C. H. Waddington was a British biologist who wondered about one of the most amazing things in nature: how does a single, tiny cell, a fertilized egg, turn into a whole body, with nerves, skin, muscles and blood, all in the right places?

Every cell in your body carries the same set of genes. So why does one cell become a nerve and another a muscle? Waddington drew a famous picture to explain it. Imagine a ball at the top of a hilly landscape, with valleys branching as they go down. The ball is a young cell. As it rolls, it must choose a valley at each fork, and at the bottom each valley ends in a different kind of cell.

blocks.name: gb-landscape
blocks.cap: Set the signals and roll a cell down the valleys. Then roll 20 at once. Make the valleys shallow and see how often cells go astray.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Build a landscape. Crumple a sheet of aluminum foil, then smooth it over a towel so you get hills and grooves. Tilt it a little and roll a marble or a dried pea from the top several times. Does it usually end up in the same groove? Press one groove deeper with your finger and try again. Waddington called deep, reliable grooves canalization.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Conrad Hal Waddington (1905–1975) studied at Cambridge, first geology and then embryology and genetics, and from 1947 to 1970 was professor of animal genetics at the University of Edinburgh. He was one of the first biologists to try to join genetics, the study of embryos and evolution into a single picture. He also wrote widely on science, art and society.

The Nature of Life (1961) is his short book for general readers. It explains what genes are, how a body develops from an egg, and how evolution works, and argues that the three questions can’t be understood apart.
This book was first published in 1961, so it is still under copyright, and this rung quotes none of it. Everything here is our own summary.

blocks.text: The question: from genes to a body

blocks.html: By 1961 DNA had been shown to carry genes (its structure was found in 1953). But genes alone don’t explain a body. Nearly every cell carries the same genes. A liver cell and a nerve cell differ because different genes are switched on in them, and that depends on the cell’s history and surroundings in the embryo. Waddington coined the word epigenetics (1942) for the study of how genes act during development to produce the body’s traits.

His most famous picture is a sloping landscape of branching valleys. A ball rolling down stands for a developing cell. The shape of the hills is set by the action of many genes pulling together, like guy ropes under a tent. At each fork, small signals from neighboring cells tip the ball one way or the other; once in a valley, it is hard to climb out.

blocks.name: gb-landscape
blocks.cap: Development as rolling downhill. The depth of the valleys is canalization: deep valleys give the same result despite small upsets.

blocks.html: Canalization: development is buffered, so that organisms come out much the same despite small differences in their genes or surroundings. The valleys are deep. Only a strong push, or a change in many genes, sends a cell into a different valley.

Waddington tested a bold idea. In the early 1950s he gave fruit-fly pupae a short heat shock. Some grew up with a gap in a small wing vein (a “crossveinless” wing). He bred only from those flies, generation after generation, and shocked each new batch. After a number of generations, some flies showed the trait without any heat shock. Selection had reshaped the landscape, so that a trait first produced by the environment became built in. He called this genetic assimilation. It works through ordinary selection on hidden genetic variation, not through inheritance of acquired traits.

blocks.title: Cells from one egg
blocks.q: A fertilized egg divides into 2 cells, then 4, then 8, and so on. If every cell divided each time, how many rounds of division would make about 35 trillion cells, roughly the number in a human body?
blocks.a: About 45 rounds. Growth is fast; the hard part is making each cell the right kind in the right place.

blocks.title: How reliable is development?
blocks.q: Suppose at each of two forks a cell follows its signal with probability 0.95. What is the chance it reaches the intended kind? What if the valleys are shallow, so the chance at each fork is only 0.7?
blocks.a: Canalization matters: small losses at each fork multiply.

blocks.html: In the book’s later chapters Waddington argues that evolution is not only genes and selection. The way genes act in development, and the way animals choose and change their surroundings by their behavior, help decide what natural selection can work on. He also discusses what makes something alive and argues that biology needs its own concepts, such as development and organization, alongside those of physics and chemistry.

Confusing Waddington with Lamarck. Waddington did not claim that traits acquired in a lifetime are passed on directly. In genetic assimilation, selection picks out flies whose genes make the trait easier to produce, until some produce it unaided.

For some decades Waddington’s ideas were somewhat at the edge of biology, which was busy with DNA and molecules. They have since come back strongly. Biologists now map the gene networks that make the valleys of his landscape, and stem-cell researchers use his picture to explain how cells can be pushed back uphill (Shinya Yamanaka’s 2006 discovery of how to turn adult cells back into stem cells earned a Nobel Prize in 2012). The word epigenetics has taken on a narrower modern meaning too, for chemical marks on DNA and its packaging that switch genes on and off. Debates continue about how much development and behavior should be added to the standard account of evolution.

Thorstein Veblen (say VEB-len) grew up on a farm in Wisconsin and Minnesota, the son of Norwegian settlers. When he became a professor, he looked at rich people's habits like a scientist watching a strange tribe.

He noticed something odd. Some people buy things not because they work better, but because they are expensive, so others can see how much money they have. A silver spoon made by hand stirs soup no better than a plain spoon from a machine, but it costs much more, and that, Veblen said, is part of why people want it. He called this conspicuous consumption: spending in a way that shows off.

blocks.name: gb-veblen-spoons
blocks.cap: Two spoons that do the same job. Tap through what each one "says."

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Spot the show-off. Look through a catalog or a store together. Find something that costs much more than a plain version that does the same job. Why might someone buy it? Is it always showing off, or can it be quality, beauty or a gift? Veblen's critics said he forgot those reasons.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Thorstein Veblen (1857–1929) was an economist and social critic who taught at Chicago, Stanford and other universities. The Theory of the Leisure Class (1899), his first book, was a sharp, ironic look at the wealthy families of America's Gilded Age, written in the cool language of a scientist describing customs. Its phrases have entered everyday speech.

Veblen traces the "leisure class" back to early societies where the strong took the honored work of war and hunting and left the daily drudgery to others. Ever since, he argues, avoiding useful work and spending lavishly have been marks of status. The key is that wealth must be seen:

head: Veblen's term
What it means (our summary)
rows: Trying to match or outdo others in visible wealth.
Showing status by visibly not needing to do useful work.
Showing status by spending on costly goods others can see.
Spending whose main point is that it is wasteful, and so impressive.
The human urge to do useful, efficient work, which Veblen thought status-seeking works against.

blocks.html: In his chapter on taste, Veblen argues that our very sense of beauty gets mixed up with cost. His example is a hand-wrought silver spoon, worth some ten to twenty dollars, which is no more useful than a machine-made one, and perhaps no more useful than an aluminum spoon costing a few cents. Much of the handmade spoon's beauty, he says, is really its expense.

blocks.name: gb-veblen-demand
blocks.cap: Slide the price. For most goods, people buy less as the price rises. For a status good, a higher price can make it more wanted, at least for a while. (An illustration, not real data.)

blocks.title: Reading a demand table
blocks.q: A shop finds that at \$50 it sells 20 handbags a week, and at \$80 it sells 26. By what percent did the quantity sold change, and does this look like an ordinary good or the "Veblen effect"?
steps: The price went up and sales went up too, the reverse of the usual law of demand.
blocks.a: Up 30%; it looks like the Veblen effect (though other causes, such as a change in fashion, would need ruling out).

blocks.html: The book made Veblen famous and gave economics and sociology lasting terms. Economists later named goods whose demand rises with price "Veblen goods," though they are rare and hard to prove in data. Studies of status, signaling and consumer behavior have built on his ideas. Critics have pointed out that Veblen relied on examples and irony rather than systematic evidence; that people buy costly things for many reasons, including quality, craftsmanship, durability and the pleasure of beauty; and that his own tone was often contemptuous of the people he studied. Defenders reply that his central point, that much spending is about how we look to others, is now widely accepted.
Thinking Veblen said everyone who buys a nice thing is showing off. He described a tendency in how status works, mainly among the very wealthy of his time.

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Adam Smith, whose Wealth of Nations is in the 18th-century rungs, wrote in his earlier Theory of Moral Sentiments that people seek wealth partly to be noticed and admired; Veblen made that the center of his theory.
Rousseau's Discourses blamed society's ills on comparison and the wish to be esteemed; compare Veblen's "invidious comparison."
Tawney's Acquisitive Society, the next rung, also criticizes wealth that is cut off from useful work.
Fitzgerald's Great Gatsby, in the literature rungs, shows lavish parties and display in the 1920s.

R. H. Tawney was an English teacher and historian. He taught working men and women in evening classes, fought as a soldier in the First World War, and afterward wrote a book asking: what is all our work and business for?

Think of a bakery. Its purpose is to make good bread for the town. The baker who gets up at four to bake is paid for doing that job. Tawney believed that money and property should go mainly with doing a useful job, which he called a function. He worried about a society where getting rich becomes the goal in itself, which he called an acquisitive society.
Many people disagreed with him, and the lesson gives their side too: they said that owning, saving and taking risks are useful jobs as well, and that free markets let people decide what is useful.

blocks.cap: Sort each income as Tawney would. Then read what his critics said.

What is it for? Pick three jobs you know (a nurse, a farmer, a store owner). For each, write what the job is for: what good it does for others. Is anyone paid without doing a job? Talk about whether that is fair, and why people disagree.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

R. H. Tawney (1880–1962) was an economic historian at the London School of Economics and a devoted teacher in the Workers' Educational Association. A Christian and a socialist, he was badly wounded at the Battle of the Somme in 1916. The Acquisitive Society (1920), written as Britain argued about how to rebuild after the war, made his name. He later wrote Religion and the Rise of Capitalism (1926) and Equality (1931).

Tawney's central idea is function: an activity that serves a social purpose. In a healthy society, he argues, rights, including property rights, are tied to functions: you hold them because of the service you perform. In what he calls an acquisitive society, rights stand on their own, and getting wealth becomes the main aim. He describes its appeal fairly, and then its danger:

Tawney does not attack all property. A farmer's land, a craftsman's tools and a family's home are bound up with work and life. What he criticizes is "passive" property that pays its owner without any service, his example being royalties paid to landowners on coal they neither found nor mined.

blocks.name: gb-tawney-sort
blocks.cap: Tawney's distinction, with the replies of his critics.

blocks.html: His proposals (our summary): treat industry more like a profession, such as medicine, with standards of service; give those who do the work, including managers and engineers, a real voice in running it; and end payments for ownership that performs no function. He expected different forms of ownership in different industries, public in some and private in others.

Tawney's book was widely read, especially in Britain's labor movement and among Christian social thinkers. Its critics raised strong objections. Economists of the free-market school, such as Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek, argued that no authority can know which activities serve society best; prices and profits, set by people's free choices, are how a society finds out. They added that income from property is not "passive": it rewards saving, risk and the work of putting capital where it is most useful, and that private property spread widely protects personal freedom against government power. Others asked who would decide what counts as a "function," and warned that giving that power to officials could be worse than the problem. Defenders of Tawney reply that he wanted moral purpose, not central planning, and that his questions about the purpose of economic life are still worth asking.
Thinking Tawney wanted to abolish all private property. He defended property tied to work and use, and argued against ownership "divorced from work."

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Aristotle's Politics distinguished household management from money-making for its own sake; Tawney revives that line.
Aquinas and medieval writers held that economic life is under moral law; Tawney admired that tradition and studied its decline.
Locke grounded property in labor; Tawney asks what happens when property no longer has any link to labor.
Adam Smith argued that self-interest in free markets, guided as if by an invisible hand, serves the common good; Tawney's critics stand nearer to Smith.
Veblen, the rung before this one, also criticized wealth cut off from useful work.

John Maynard Keynes (say KAYNZ) was a British economist. In the 1930s, during the Great Depression, millions of people who wanted to work could not find jobs. Keynes asked: why would a whole country get stuck like that?

His idea, in simple form: one person's spending is another person's income. If everyone gets scared and stops spending at once, shops sell less, so they hire fewer workers, who then have less to spend, and so on. Spending travels around a town in a chain. When the chain slows, the whole town slows.

blocks.cap: Watch \$100 of new spending travel around a town. Each person spends part of what they receive and saves the rest. (A simple model.)

blocks.html: Other economists disagreed with Keynes about what to do, and their side is in the lesson too.

🧩 Try this

The spending chain game. Give the first player 20 paper coins. Each player keeps a quarter of what they receive (rounding down) and passes the rest to the next player. Keep going until less than one coin is passed. Add up everything that was passed along. Was it more than 20? Why?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

John Maynard Keynes (1883–1946) taught economics at Cambridge, worked for the British Treasury, and became famous in 1919 with The Economic Consequences of the Peace, which warned that the harsh treaty after the First World War would harm Europe. The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money appeared in February 1936, in the depths of the Great Depression. In 1944 Keynes led the British delegation at Bretton Woods, which designed the postwar money system.
No excerpts here. The General Theory was first published in 1936 and is under copyright in the U.S. This lesson explains its ideas in our own words. It is in most libraries.

The economics Keynes learned held that markets tend to correct themselves: if workers are unemployed, wages fall until employers hire them again, and whatever people earn they either spend or save, and savings are lent out and spent on investment. A famous form of this is Say's law, often summed up as "supply creates its own demand." Yet in the 1930s unemployment stayed very high for years.

Keynes argued that total output and employment depend on aggregate demand: the total spending of households, businesses and government. If people decide to spend less and save more, and businesses, uncertain about the future, do not invest those savings, total spending falls. Then output and jobs fall, and the economy can settle at high unemployment with no automatic force to lift it out. Wages may be slow to fall, and even if they fall, workers' spending falls with them.

head: Idea
Keynes's point (our summary)
rows: People spend part of any rise in income and save the rest; the part spent is the marginal propensity to consume (MPC).
New spending becomes someone's income, part of which is spent again, so the total rise in income is larger than the first spending.
Interest is the reward for giving up holding ready money; in a slump, people may hoard cash rather than lend or invest.
Investment depends on confidence and expectations, which can swing widely.
If everyone tries to save more at once, total spending and income can fall, so total saving may not rise.

blocks.name: gb-keynes-multiplier
blocks.cap: The multiplier: spending, round by round.

blocks.title: The multiplier
blocks.q: If the marginal propensity to consume is 0.8, how much can total income rise from \$100 of new spending, in the simple model?
steps: Each round, people spend 0.8 of what they receive: \$100, then \$80, then \$64, and so on.
The sum of this series is $\frac{1}{1 - 0.8} = 5$ times the first spending.
blocks.a: Up to \$500.

blocks.html: From this Keynes drew a policy conclusion: in a deep slump, governments should support demand, for example by spending on public works, even if that means borrowing, and should keep interest rates low.

The General Theory changed economics, and for about thirty years after the Second World War many governments used Keynesian ideas to manage demand. It was always debated. Friedrich Hayek and the Austrian school argued that slumps come from earlier misdirected investment that has to be worked out, and that government spending can prolong the problem. Milton Friedman and the monetarists argued that the Great Depression was made far worse by a collapse in the money supply, and that steady growth of money matters more than government spending. In the 1970s many countries had high inflation and high unemployment at once ("stagflation"), which simple Keynesian models had not predicted. Robert Lucas and others argued that people's expectations adjust to policy, weakening its effects, and public-choice economists such as James Buchanan warned that governments find it easier to borrow than to repay. Today most economists combine parts of these views: many accept that demand matters in the short run and that markets adjust over the long run, and they disagree about how large the multiplier is and when policy should act.

Thinking Keynes wanted governments to spend more all the time. He argued for supporting demand in slumps, not for permanent deficits; in his later writings he favored balancing the government's ordinary budget over time.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations, in the 18th-century rungs, set out how markets coordinate economic life; Keynes asked why that coordination can fail for a whole economy.
Marx's Capital also saw slumps as built into capitalism, but Keynes wanted to save the market system, not replace it.
Veblen and Tawney, earlier rungs, criticized the motives of a money economy; Keynes focused on how it works as a machine.

The Economics Ladder topics on aggregate demand, the multiplier and schools of thought teach the models built from these debates; the American History topics on the Great Depression and the New Deal show the times.

Is saving always good? For a family? For a whole country?
When, if ever, should a government borrow to spend?
Why do economists who agree on the facts still disagree about policy?

James George Frazer was a Scottish scholar who spent his whole life in libraries, reading travelers' reports, old histories and letters from missionaries all over the world. He collected thousands of customs and stories, and asked why people in faraway places did such similar things.

Here is one pattern he noticed. In many places, people tried to make things happen by copying them: sprinkling water to bring rain, or jumping high so the crops would grow tall. Frazer called that the idea that "like produces like." In other places, people believed that things that once touched stay connected, so they kept a lost tooth or a lock of hair safe. He called these two ideas the laws of magic.

🧩 Try this

Lucky habits. Many people today have small lucky habits: a lucky sock, crossing fingers, not stepping on cracks. Ask your family what lucky habits they know. Which ones are about copying, and which are about touching? (Frazer would have been very interested!)

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

James George Frazer (1854–1941) was a classical scholar at Trinity College, Cambridge. The Golden Bough began as two volumes in 1890, grew to twelve by 1915, and was cut down by Frazer himself to the one-volume abridged edition of 1922, the form most people read. It compares myths, rites and customs from ancient Greece and Rome, Europe's countryside and peoples all over the world.

Near this lake south of Rome stood a sacred grove of the goddess Diana. Ancient writers said its priest, called the King of the Wood, held his office until a challenger broke a branch from a certain tree and overcame him. Frazer sets out to explain this strange rule, and the explanation becomes a tour of the world's customs.

Frazer calls the first the Law of Similarity (behind "homoeopathic" or imitative magic) and the second the Law of Contact or Contagion (behind contagious magic). Together he calls them sympathetic magic.

blocks.name: gb-frazer-sort
blocks.cap: Frazer's two laws, with examples of the kinds he describes.

blocks.html: Frazer saw a grand pattern. Magic, he argued, is a mistaken kind of science: it assumes nature follows fixed rules people can control, but has the rules wrong. When people find magic fails, they turn to religion, seeking the favor of higher powers. Later, science returns to the idea of a fixed order of nature, now with rules tested by observation.

blocks.name: gb-frazer-stages
blocks.cap: Frazer's three-stage scheme, and what later scholars said about it.

blocks.html: Along the way Frazer gathers stories of sacred kings, harvest customs, festivals of fire and the ancient myths of gods of vegetation who die and return with the seasons. The golden bough itself, he concludes, was the mistletoe.

The Golden Bough was hugely popular and shaped how educated readers thought about myth for decades. Poets and novelists borrowed from it: T. S. Eliot named it in the notes to The Waste Land. Anthropologists, though, came to reject much of it. Frazer never did fieldwork; he compared customs torn from their settings, often from unreliable reports, and his students, above all Bronisław Malinowski, insisted on living for years among the people one studies. The neat sequence from magic to religion to science is no longer accepted: all three exist side by side in many societies, and rites are not simply failed science. Wittgenstein objected that Frazer made other peoples' rituals look like stupid mistakes when they express something more. Scholars of religion have also questioned his grouping of different gods as one "dying and rising" type. Frazer hinted that Christian beliefs could be placed among his comparisons, which offended many readers then; later scholars questioned the comparisons themselves on historical grounds. The book remains a landmark in the history of anthropology, read now as much for what it shows about its own age as about the customs it describes.
Thinking Frazer visited the peoples he wrote about. He worked from books and letters in Cambridge, which is one reason later anthropologists distrusted his conclusions.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Virgil's Aeneid, on the Rome rungs, gave Frazer his title: Aeneas must pluck a golden bough before he can visit the underworld.
Herodotus also compared the customs of many peoples, and noticed how each thinks its own the best.
Lévi-Strauss, a later rung, studied myths as structures with their own logic, a very different method from Frazer's.
Eliot's Waste Land, in the literature rungs, drew on Frazer's vegetation myths.
Why do people in very different places have similar customs?
Can you understand a custom without living among the people who keep it?
Is magic a kind of mistaken science, or something else?
How should we judge an old book whose method later scholars rejected?

💬 Talk about it together

  1. What lucky or traditional habits does your family have? Where did they come from?
  2. Why might people in places far apart come up with similar customs?
  3. Frazer studied other peoples only from books. What might he have missed?
  4. Is it fair to call another culture's rituals "mistakes"? Why did Wittgenstein object?
  5. Virgil's hero needed a golden bough to enter the underworld. What other stories have a magic object that opens a door?
