Max Weber (say VAY-ber) was a German professor who studied how societies work. One question he asked: why do people obey leaders?

He found three main answers. Sometimes people obey because "it has always been done this way," like following the oldest person in a family or a king whose fathers were kings. Sometimes they follow a person because that person seems extraordinary: brave, inspiring, a hero. And sometimes they obey because of rules: the referee in a game, or a town clerk who follows the written law, is obeyed because of the job, not the person.

blocks.name: gb-weber-authority
blocks.cap: Tap an example to see which kind of authority Weber would call it. Many real cases mix more than one.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Who is in charge? List the people whose instructions you follow in a week: a parent, a coach, a crossing guard, a team captain. For each, ask Weber's question: do I follow them because of tradition, because of who they are, or because of the rules of their job?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Max Weber (1864–1920) was one of the founders of sociology, the study of society. He taught at Freiburg, Heidelberg and Munich, and is best known for The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism (1905), which argued that religious ideas helped shape modern economic life. The volume in the set is From Max Weber: Essays in Sociology, a selection translated and edited by H. H. Gerth and C. Wright Mills in 1946. Its best-known pieces are two lectures Weber gave to students in Munich: "Science as a Vocation" (1917) and "Politics as a Vocation" (1919).
No excerpts here. These English translations were first published in 1946 and are under copyright. This lesson summarizes Weber's ideas in our own words. The book is in many libraries.
Weber asks why people accept being ruled, what makes power legitimate in their eyes. He finds three pure types:

head: Type
Why people obey (our summary)
Examples
rows: Because things have always been so; the ruler holds power by custom and inheritance.
A hereditary king; a village elder; a family patriarch.
Because of a leader's extraordinary personal gifts, as followers see them.
A prophet, a war hero, the founder of a movement.
Because of rules that are set down and apply to everyone; one obeys the office, not the person.
A judge, a tax official, an elected officeholder under a constitution.

blocks.name: gb-weber-authority
blocks.cap: Weber's three types, with historical examples (our choices). Real cases are usually mixtures.

blocks.html: Charisma, Weber noted, is unstable: when the leader dies, followers must turn it into tradition or rules, which he called the "routinization" of charisma.

Weber defined the modern state by its means rather than its aims: it is the community that claims, with success, to be the only one entitled to use physical force within its territory. Politics is the struggle to share in or influence that power. He then asks what kind of person should take it up. He contrasts an ethic of conviction, doing what is right and leaving the results to fate, with an ethic of responsibility, answering for the foreseeable results of one's actions. A mature political leader, he argued, needs both, along with passion, a sense of responsibility and a sense of proportion. He compared politics to drilling patiently through thick, hard wood.

To students hoping science would tell them how to live, Weber gave a sober answer. Modern science is specialized, slow and always being surpassed. It has brought the disenchantment of the world: the belief that, in principle, everything can be explained by calculation, with no mysterious forces at work. But science cannot tell us which values to live by. Teachers, he said, should help students see facts clearly and understand the consequences of their choices, not use the lecture hall to preach their own politics.

Weber described bureaucracy, the modern form of administration, by its features: fixed areas of duty, a chain of command, written files, trained officials and impersonal rules. He thought it was the most efficient form of organization and also feared it could trap people in routine. He also argued that social standing has three separate dimensions: class (economic position), status (honor and prestige) and party (organized power), a deliberate widening of Marx's focus on economic class.

Weber is among the most cited social scientists. His types of authority, his definition of the state and his account of bureaucracy are standard in sociology and political science. Critics note that ideal types are simplifications that real cases never fit exactly; that the Protestant Ethic thesis has been disputed by historians who find capitalism earlier or elsewhere; and that his hope for a "value-free" social science is hard to achieve. His work is read today by scholars across the political spectrum.
Thinking Weber said the state should use force freely. He was defining what states do, not praising violence; his lecture is about the heavy responsibility that comes with power.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Aristotle's Politics also sorted kinds of rule, by who rules and for whose good; Weber sorts them by why people obey.
Machiavelli and Hobbes, earlier on this ladder, faced the role of force in politics; compare Weber's definition of the state.
Marx saw class as the key to history; Weber added status and party, and the power of ideas such as religion.
Tocqueville worried about soft, administrative power in democracy; compare Weber on bureaucracy.
The American History & Civics topics on the bureaucracy and the rule of law show legal-rational authority at work.
Why do people accept being governed?
Should a leader act on conviction or weigh consequences, or both?
Can science tell us what is worth living for?
Is efficient organization always good for people?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Name a person you obey because of their job, and one you follow because of who they are.
  2. Is it better for a leader to follow firm principles or to weigh the results? Can you think of a story where each mattered?
  3. Weber said teachers should not preach their politics in class. Why might he think that?
  4. What would a school run entirely by written rules be like? What would be good and bad about it?
  5. What does it mean for the world to feel "disenchanted"? Does it feel that way to you?

Johan Huizinga (say HOW-zing-ah) was a Dutch historian. He loved old paintings and old chronicles, and he wanted to know: what did it feel like to be alive six hundred years ago?

He found a world of strong contrasts. Nights were truly dark, with no streetlights. Winter was bitter cold, and summer feasts were full of color. Great lords wore splendid clothes while beggars sat in the street. And all day long, church bells rang out the hours, calling people to prayer, to work, to celebrate, or to mourn.

blocks.name: gb-huizinga-day
blocks.cap: Move through a day in a 15th-century town and hear when the bells rang. (Times shifted with the seasons; these are typical.)

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

A sound map. Sit quietly for five minutes, indoors or out, and list every sound you hear. Which of them tell you the time, or call people together? Then imagine your town six hundred years ago. What would you have heard instead?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Johan Huizinga (1872–1945) taught history at Groningen and Leiden. His masterpiece, published in Dutch in 1919, studies life, thought and art in France and the Low Countries, above all the court of the Dukes of Burgundy, in the 1300s and 1400s. F. Hopman's English version, The Waning of the Middle Ages (1924), was prepared with Huizinga's help and somewhat shortened; a full new translation appeared in 1996 as The Autumn of the Middle Ages. Huizinga later wrote Homo Ludens (1938), on play in culture. During the German occupation of the Netherlands he was held hostage, and he died in February 1945, a few months before the liberation.

Huizinga paints a world of extremes: dark and light, quiet and noise, cold and warmth, sickness and health, all felt more sharply than today. Life was public and full of ceremony; rank was shown in dress; feelings swung fast between tears and joy, cruelty and tenderness.

blocks.name: gb-huizinga-day
blocks.cap: The canonical hours of prayer, rung by church bells through the day (typical times).

blocks.html: Many people of that time, Huizinga says, felt the world was growing worse. He sees three paths they took: turning away from the world toward God; trying to reform it; or dreaming it more beautiful, living as if life were an ideal story. The great example of the third path is chivalry, the ideal of the brave, loyal, courteous knight, which nobles acted out in tournaments, orders of knighthood and splendid vows, even as real warfare was changing.

Religious thought, Huizinga argues, had become crowded with images and symbols: every object could point to a sacred meaning. The age was also full of reminders of death, such as the painted "dance of death," in which people of every rank are led away together. He handles these with care, and so do we.

The usual story treated the 1400s in the North as the start of the Renaissance. Huizinga argues the reverse: the art of Jan van Eyck and the culture of the Burgundian court were the rich, overripe end of the Middle Ages, an autumn rather than a spring.

The book is admired as one of the great works of history writing, praised for bringing a whole period to life through its feelings, ceremonies and images. Historians have also criticized it: it draws mostly on court chronicles, poems and paintings made for the elite, so it says little about peasants and townspeople or about economic life; its picture of a "childlike" age of extreme emotions is now seen as overdrawn; and the idea of the period as a decline is disputed, since the same centuries saw growth in trade, cities and learning. It remains a classic and a model of cultural history.
Thinking Huizinga called the late Middle Ages a gloomy dark age. He loved its art and found it full of splendor; his "autumn" is a season of ripeness as well as ending.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Chaucer and Dante, on the Middle Ages rungs, show the ideals and images Huizinga studies from inside.
Gibbon's Decline and Fall, in the 18th-century rungs, also studied an age as an ending; compare their views of decline.
Burckhardt, the Swiss historian, had pictured the Italian Renaissance as the birth of the modern individual; Huizinga answered from the North.
The Art Ladder topics on books of hours, the Northern Renaissance and Gothic architecture show the art he wrote about.
Can a historian know how people of the past felt?
Is an age an "autumn" or a "spring" depending on where you stand?
Why do people dream of a better world in hard times?
What do the sounds and ceremonies of a place tell us about its people?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. What sounds tell you the time of day where you live?
  2. Why might feelings have seemed sharper in a world with dark nights and cold winters?
  3. What ideals, like chivalry, do people today try to live up to?
  4. Huizinga used paintings and poems as evidence. What else would you want, to know how ordinary people lived?
  5. Is the end of something always sad? Can it also be ripe and beautiful?

Claude Lévi-Strauss (say LAY-vee STROWSS) was a French anthropologist, a scientist who studies human cultures. As a young man he traveled deep into Brazil to live with peoples there. Later he read thousands of myths from North and South America and asked: is there a hidden pattern in how people tell stories?

He thought there was. People everywhere, he said, think in pairs of opposites: day and night, hot and cold, raw and cooked, land and sky, life and death. Stories often take two opposites and find something in between that joins them, like a bridge.

blocks.name: gb-ls-pairs
blocks.cap: Tap each pair of opposites, then find the "in-between" that some myths use to join them (our simple examples).

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Opposites in stories. Think of a favorite fairy tale. Find two opposites in it (rich and poor, forest and castle, young and old). Is there a character or place that is in between, and joins them? Draw the two ends and the bridge.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Claude Lévi-Strauss (1908–2009) taught in São Paulo in the 1930s and made expeditions among peoples of the Brazilian interior, which he later described in Tristes Tropiques (1955). During the Second World War he escaped occupied France to New York, where he met the linguist Roman Jakobson. From Jakobson he took the idea that would shape his life's work: that the methods of the new science of language could be used on all of culture. Structural Anthropology (1958) collects his essays on that method.
No excerpts here. The book was first published in English in 1963 and is under copyright. This lesson describes it in our own words. Library copies are easy to find.

Structural linguistics showed that the sounds of a language mean nothing by themselves; what matters is the system of contrasts between them. In English, "pat" and "bat" are different words only because p and b contrast. Speakers use this system without being aware of it. Lévi-Strauss proposed that kinship rules, myths and customs are also systems of contrasts, working below awareness, and that the anthropologist's job is to find their structure.

His first example is family relations. He looked at four relationships: husband and wife, brother and sister, father and son, and a mother's brother and her son. In many societies, he found, these relations come in balanced pairs: where a boy's relation with his father is strict, his relation with his mother's brother is easy, and the reverse. He called this small system the atom of kinship.

Myths seem to say anything at all, yet similar myths appear across the world. Lévi-Strauss proposed breaking a myth into its smallest units of meaning, which he called mythemes, and arranging them by their relations rather than their order in the story, like the parts of an orchestra score. On this view a myth works on a contradiction a society cannot resolve, such as that between life and death, by finding a chain of mediators that softens it.

blocks.name: gb-ls-mediation
blocks.cap: His example from North American myths: how a hard opposition is softened step by step (our drawing of his scheme).

blocks.html: In his example, life and death are bridged by farming (which gives life) and war (which brings death); between those stands hunting, which takes life to sustain it. Then among animals, plant-eaters and beasts of prey are bridged by carrion-eaters such as the raven and the coyote, which eat meat but do not kill. That, he suggested, is why raven and coyote so often appear as the trickster, a go-between, in these myths.

Structuralism was one of the most influential movements in mid-20th-century thought, spreading from anthropology to literary criticism, psychology and philosophy. Lévi-Strauss became a public figure in France and lived to be a hundred. Critics have raised several objections. His structures are hard to test: a clever analyst may find opposites anywhere. His method tends to set aside history, change and the choices of individual people. Anthropologists such as Clifford Geertz preferred to interpret cultures through the meanings people themselves give them, while materialist anthropologists such as Marvin Harris argued that customs are best explained by ecology and economy. Later thinkers, the "post-structuralists," questioned whether stable structures exist at all. His studies of kinship and myth are still read as classics, and the search for patterns he began goes on in many forms.
Thinking Lévi-Strauss said all cultures are the same. He held that all human minds work with the same kind of logic, and that this produces endless different systems.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Frazer's Golden Bough, an earlier rung, compared customs as evidence of stages of thought; Lévi-Strauss compared them as structures with their own logic.
Sophocles' Oedipus, in the Greek rungs, is the myth he analyzed most famously, laying its episodes out in columns.
Rousseau, whom Lévi-Strauss called, in a 1962 lecture, the founder of the sciences of man.
Wittgenstein said meaning lies in use; Lévi-Strauss looked for meaning in hidden contrasts. Compare the two.
Do all people think in pairs of opposites?
Can a pattern exist in a culture if nobody in it knows the pattern is there?
Why do similar stories turn up in places far apart?
How could you tell whether a pattern is really in the myths or only in the mind of the analyst?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. What pairs of opposites can you find in a story you know well?
  2. Why do tricksters, like a clever fox or coyote, appear in so many stories?
  3. Can you follow rules you could not explain, like the grammar of your own language? Give an example.
  4. Lévi-Strauss's critics said a clever person can find patterns anywhere. How would you test a pattern?
  5. What would you want to learn if you could live for a year with a people very different from your own?

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Joseph Conrad was a sailor before he was a writer. He was born to Polish parents, went to sea as a teenager, and learned English as a grown man. In 1890 he took a job steering a small steamboat up the Congo River in Africa. What he saw there shocked him, and years later he turned it into a story.

In Heart of Darkness, a sailor named Marlow sits on a boat on the River Thames at sunset and tells his friends about a journey he once made. A trading company sent him up a great African river to find Mr. Kurtz, its most famous agent. The farther Marlow travels, the more he sees how greed for ivory has made the company's men cruel to the people who live there.

blocks.name: gb-conrad-river
blocks.cap: Follow Marlow's journey, stop by stop. (A sketch map, not to scale.)

blocks.html: For parents: this short novel is for older teens and adults. It describes the cruelty of colonial rule and uses the racial language of its time. The lesson below explains this without repeating it.

🧩 Try this

A story inside a story. Conrad's book is a story someone tells to friends. Try it: tell your family about a trip you took, but start with where you are sitting right now. Then ask: how does the teller change the story? What might the listeners never find out?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Joseph Conrad (1857–1924) was born Józef Teodor Konrad Korzeniowski to Polish parents in what is now Ukraine. He spent about twenty years at sea, became a British subject, and wrote his novels in his third language. In 1890 he worked for a Belgian company on the Congo River, in the colony then ruled personally by King Leopold II of Belgium. Heart of Darkness appeared as a magazine serial in 1899 and as a book in 1902.
Five friends wait for the tide on a yacht, the Nellie, on the Thames. As the sun goes down over London, Marlow begins:

He means that Britain, too, was once a wild frontier to the Romans. Then he tells how a Company in a European city (Brussels, though he never names it) hired him to captain a river steamer. Along the coast and at the Company's stations he sees forced labor, waste and cruelty, all for ivory. He hears again and again of Mr. Kurtz, a gifted agent who sends back more ivory than anyone, and he grows curious to meet him.

At the Inner Station Marlow finds that Kurtz, who left Europe full of fine words about bringing "progress," has made himself a tyrant over the people around him. Kurtz is dying. On the boat downstream he whispers his last words, "The horror! The horror!" Back in Europe, Marlow visits the woman Kurtz was engaged to and, unable to tell her the truth, tells her a kind lie.

blocks.name: gb-conrad-river
blocks.cap: Marlow's journey, from the Thames and back. Our summary.

blocks.html: We hear Marlow through an unnamed listener on the Nellie, so the whole tale is a story within a story. Marlow keeps saying that what he saw can't quite be put into words:
Conrad's "darkness" is not only a place. It is what can grow in anyone, Kurtz most of all, when greed and power meet no check. The book turns the language of a civilizing mission against itself.

blocks.text: A book that is argued over

blocks.html: In its day the book was read as an attack on the abuses in the Congo, which reformers such as E. D. Morel and Roger Casement were exposing at the same time. In 1975 the Nigerian novelist Chinua Achebe gave a famous lecture, "An Image of Africa," arguing that the book still treats Africa only as a dark backdrop for a European's crisis and denies its African people a voice. Many readers now hold both views together: the book condemns colonial greed, and it also shares some of the blind spots of its time. Its racial language is one reason it is for older readers.
Mixing up Marlow and Conrad, or Marlow and Kurtz. Marlow is the teller; Kurtz is the man he goes to find; Conrad stands behind them both.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Dante's Inferno, earlier on this ladder, is another journey downward into evil with a guide and a witness.
Homer's Odyssey gave the West its first great voyage tale; Conrad's is a voyage with no homecoming of the heart.
T. S. Eliot first chose Kurtz's last words for the head of The Waste Land (Ezra Pound talked him out of it), and later put the news of Kurtz's death at the head of his poem "The Hollow Men" (1925).
Chinua Achebe answered with his own novel of Africa, Things Fall Apart (1958), told from inside an Igbo village.
Why does Marlow lie at the end, when he says he hates lies? Was it right?
Can fine words about progress hide cruelty? How would you notice?
Can a book attack injustice and still share some of its age's prejudices?
What does Kurtz see when he says "The horror!"?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Marlow tells his story to friends on a boat. Why do you think Conrad framed it that way?
  2. What did the Company say it was doing in Africa, and what was it really doing?
  3. Why do you think Kurtz changed so much?
  4. Was Marlow's lie to Kurtz's fiancée kind, or wrong, or both?
  5. Achebe and Conrad saw the same story very differently. How can two readers disagree about one book?

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
Anton Chekhov was a Russian doctor who also wrote stories and plays. He liked to show ordinary people as they really are: a little funny, a little sad, and always hoping for something better.

In Uncle Vanya, Vanya and his niece Sonya have worked for years on a country farm. They send all the money it earns to Sonya's father, a famous professor in the city, because they think his work is important. Then the professor comes to live with them, and they discover he is not as great as they believed. At the end, Sonya says they must keep going, keep working, and be kind to others, and one day they will rest.

blocks.name: gb-vanya-estate
blocks.cap: Tap each person on the estate. Switch to see who works for whom, and who hopes for what.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Plant a tree. The country doctor in the play, Astrov, plants young trees because forests take a hundred years to grow. With a grown-up, plant a seed or a seedling, and make a label: who planted it, the date, and who might sit in its shade someday.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Anton Chekhov (1860–1904) grew up in Taganrog in southern Russia, the grandson of a serf. He trained as a doctor in Moscow and paid his way by writing comic sketches, then became one of the great masters of the short story. His four late plays, The Seagull, Uncle Vanya, Three Sisters and The Cherry Orchard, changed the theater. Uncle Vanya was published in 1897 and staged by the Moscow Art Theatre in 1899. Its subtitle is "Scenes from Country Life."

Vanya and his niece Sonya have run the family estate for twenty-five years, sending its income to Sonya's father, Professor Serebryakov, whose writings they once worshipped. Now the retired professor has come to stay with his beautiful young second wife, Yelena, and the household falls apart. Vanya decides the professor is a fraud and that he has wasted his life. Both Vanya and the country doctor, Astrov, are drawn to Yelena. Sonya quietly loves Astrov, who hardly notices her.
Astrov is one of Chekhov's most modern figures. He plants forests and makes maps showing how the district's woods are disappearing. Sonya repeats his ideas:

In Act III the professor announces a plan to sell the estate, which would leave Vanya and Sonya with nothing. Vanya explodes, and in a rage fires a pistol at him twice, missing both times. In Act IV the guests leave, Astrov drives off, and Vanya and Sonya sit down to the account books again. Sonya speaks the play's last words:
She goes on to say that they will work for others, bear their trials patiently, and after death find rest and peace with God: "I have faith, Uncle, fervent, passionate faith."

blocks.name: gb-vanya-estate
blocks.cap: The household on the estate: our summary.

blocks.html: Chekhov's drama happens under the surface. People talk about the weather, tea and the harvest while their lives are quietly breaking. Nothing much "happens," and yet everything changes for Vanya and Sonya.
Calling the play simply gloomy. Chekhov thought of his plays as partly comic, and the characters' self-pity is often funny. Sonya's ending is sad, but it is also about endurance, work and hope.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Ibsen, in the 19th-century rungs, put hidden truths on stage in a living room; Chekhov goes further, keeping the big moments almost offstage.
Tolstoy, whom Chekhov admired, asked how one should live; Chekhov asks the same question without giving a sermon.
Beckett's Waiting for Godot, at the end of this ladder, also shows people waiting and talking while time passes.
Chekhov's habit of letting a play end quietly, with no grand speech of resolution, shaped much of 20th-century drama and the modern short story.
Was Vanya's life wasted, as he says? What would make a life of quiet work worthwhile?
Is it good to admire someone so much that you work for them for years?
Why does Astrov plant forests he will never see grown?
What gives Sonya the strength to go on?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Vanya worked for years for someone he admired. What happens when we find out a hero is ordinary?
  2. Why do you think Sonya does not tell Astrov how she feels until it is too late?
  3. Astrov plants forests for people a hundred years from now. Who will enjoy something you do today?
  4. Is the ending of the play sad, hopeful, or both?
  5. Chekhov said a play should show life as it is. What everyday moment in your family would make a good scene?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
Henry James was an American writer who spent most of his life in England. He wrote long, careful sentences about what people think and feel but don't say out loud.

In The Beast in the Jungle, a man named John Marcher is sure that something huge and strange is going to happen to him someday, like a wild beast waiting to jump out of the jungle. His friend May Bartram promises to watch and wait with him. They wait for years and years. Marcher is so busy waiting for his big event that he never notices the most important thing right beside him: May's friendship and love. When he finally understands, it is too late.

blocks.name: gb-james-waiting
blocks.cap: Step through the years of Marcher's waiting.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Notice today. Marcher missed what was right in front of him. Tonight at dinner, each person names one good thing that happened today that they almost didn't notice: a kind word, a funny moment, a sunset.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Henry James (1843–1916) was born in New York, the brother of the philosopher William James, whose Principles of Psychology appears earlier on this ladder. Henry settled in England in 1876 and became a British subject in 1915. His novels, such as The Portrait of a Lady and The Ambassadors, often set Americans among Europeans. The Beast in the Jungle is a long story published in his collection The Better Sort (1903).

At a country house called Weatherend, John Marcher meets May Bartram again. She reminds him that ten years before, in Italy, he told her his secret: he has always felt that he is being kept for some rare and strange event, perhaps a terrible one, that will one day break upon him.

May agrees to wait and watch with him. Years pass in quiet visits, theater evenings and birthday gifts. Marcher thinks it would be selfish to marry while he is waiting for his fate. May grows ill. Before she dies, she tells him, gently, that the thing has already happened, and that he hasn't noticed.

Long afterward, at May's grave, Marcher sees a stranger whose face is raw with grief for someone he has lost. Suddenly Marcher understands. His fate was to be the one man who never loved, though love had been offered to him for years:

blocks.name: gb-james-waiting
blocks.cap: The years of waiting, our summary.

blocks.html: The "beast" is not an outside disaster. It is the empty life that comes from waiting for something grand instead of living, and loving, now.

James tells the whole story from inside Marcher's mind, so we see only what he sees. The reader may notice May's feelings long before Marcher does. That gap between what the hero knows and what we can guess is the story's quiet engine.
Expecting a jungle adventure. There is no jungle and no animal: the title is Marcher's own image for his fate.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: William James, Henry's brother, described the "stream of consciousness"; Henry wrote fiction that follows a mind from within, a method that Woolf and Joyce, later in this era, carried further.
Sophocles' Oedipus is another hero who learns the truth about himself too late.
Beckett's Waiting for Godot turns waiting itself into a play.
Proust, in Swann in Love, also studies a man who misreads his own heart.
Is it possible to waste a life by waiting for it to start?
Why doesn't May simply tell Marcher what she feels?
Was Marcher's fate fixed, or did he choose it, day by day?
What does it mean to really pay attention to another person?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Marcher waited his whole life for something big. Have you ever waited so hard for one thing that you missed another?
  2. Why do you think May agreed to wait with him?
  3. What is the "beast" in the end?
  4. Should May have told Marcher what she knew? Why might she have stayed quiet?
  5. How can we notice the people who care about us?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

For parents: Death in Venice is a story for adult readers. Its central theme is an older man's unhealthy obsession, and it ends in his death. Young readers can skip to the activity, and older teens may read the lesson below with a parent.

Thomas Mann was a German writer who won the Nobel Prize in 1929. This story is about a famous writer who lives by strict rules and hard work. On a holiday in Venice, the city on the water, he lets go of his rules completely, and it goes badly for him. Grown-up readers think about what happens when someone loses control of himself.

🧩 Try this

A city on the water. Venice is built on more than a hundred small islands, on wooden posts driven deep into the mud of a lagoon. People get around by boat and on foot over hundreds of bridges. Find Venice on a map of Italy. Then try building a tiny "Venice" in a tray of water with blocks or corks. What do you need so it doesn't sink?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Thomas Mann (1875–1955) grew up in Lübeck, Germany, in a merchant family whose decline he told in his first novel, Buddenbrooks (1901). He later wrote The Magic Mountain (1924), won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1929, and left Germany in 1933 after the Nazis came to power, settling in the United States. Death in Venice appeared in 1912. The English translation quoted here, by Kenneth Burke, was published in 1924.
Gustav von Aschenbach is a celebrated writer in Munich, honored for books of noble self-command. He has built his life on duty and work:
Tired and restless, he sees a strange traveler at a cemetery and feels a sudden longing to go south. He ends up in Venice:

At his beach hotel he becomes fixated on a beautiful boy from a Polish family, whom he never speaks to. Meanwhile a cholera epidemic is spreading through the city, and the authorities hide it to protect the tourist trade. Aschenbach learns the truth and could warn the family or leave, but he does neither. He loses his dignity, falls ill, and dies in a beach chair. The story treats his obsession as the collapse of a life built only on willpower.

blocks.name: gb-mann-venice
blocks.cap: The five chapters of the story: our summary, without detail.

blocks.html: Mann sets two forces against each other: the cool discipline that made Aschenbach great, and a longing for beauty and release that he has denied all his life. When the denied side breaks through, it destroys him. Mann drew on Nietzsche's contrast of the "Apollonian" (order) and the "Dionysian" (frenzy).
The plague matters. A city that hides its sickness to protect business mirrors a man who hides the truth from himself.
Reading the story as an adventure or a romance. It is a tragedy of self-deception, told with irony by a narrator who sees more than Aschenbach does.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Nietzsche, earlier on this ladder, gave Mann the contrast between order and frenzy in art and life.
Plato's Phaedrus, which Aschenbach recalls in the story, discusses how beauty can lead the soul upward or astray.
Greek tragedy showed great men brought down by a flaw they would not see; Mann writes a modern version.
The story inspired an opera by Benjamin Britten (1973).
Can discipline alone make a good life? What else does a person need?
Why does Aschenbach stay in Venice when he knows about the plague?
When do communities hide bad news, and what does it cost them?
How does a writer show a character's self-deception without saying it?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Aschenbach built his life on discipline. What good did it do him, and what did it leave out?
  2. Why do you think the city hid the sickness? Was that ever right?
  3. What should Aschenbach have done when he learned the truth?
  4. How can rest and enjoyment be healthy, and when do they go too far?
  5. Mann wrote with a narrator who sees more than the hero. Why might that help readers judge the hero?

blocks.html: A note for parents: Swann in Love is a story of adult romance and jealousy, for older readers. The lesson keeps to a general summary; young readers focus on Proust's idea of memory.

Choose a path

  • 🌱 For young readers
  • 📖 For teens and adults
  • 🔭 Going deeper

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
Marcel Proust was a French writer who wrote one enormous novel, seven volumes long, called In Search of Lost Time. It is about memory: how the past seems lost, and how it can suddenly come back.

In the most famous scene, the narrator, now a grown man, dips a little cake called a madeleine into a cup of tea. The taste suddenly brings back his whole childhood in the village of Combray: his aunt, the house, the garden, the church. He had not been able to remember it by trying, but a taste brought it all back at once.

For parents: the part of the novel in the Great Books set, Swann in Love, is a story of adult romance and jealousy, for older readers. Young readers can enjoy Proust's idea of memory here and leave the love story for later.

🧩 Try this

The memory game. Close your eyes. Someone gives you something to smell or taste: an orange, cinnamon, a pine needle, a cookie. What does it remind you of? Tell the memory. Then talk about why a smell can bring back a memory faster than trying hard to remember.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Marcel Proust (1871–1922) grew up in a wealthy Paris family and moved in the city's grand salons as a young man. Often ill with asthma, he spent his last years writing in a cork-lined room. In Search of Lost Time appeared from 1913 to 1927, the last volumes after his death. Its first volume, Swann's Way (1913), opens with one of the most famous first lines in fiction:
The narrator, Marcel, describes waking in the dark and not knowing where, or even who, he is:

Swann in Love, the middle part of Swann's Way, goes back to a time before the narrator was born. Charles Swann is a rich, cultivated man, welcome in the finest houses of Paris. He meets Odette de Crécy, who is not at all the kind of woman he usually admires, at the salon of the Verdurins, a pushy middle-class couple who rule their "little clan" of guests.

Two things turn mild interest into love. A "little phrase" in a violin sonata by the composer Vinteuil becomes, for Swann, the very music of his feeling. And he notices that Odette looks like a figure in a painting by Botticelli, which lets him admire her as he admires art. Soon he is jealous: he tracks her movements, suffers over every rumor, and is shut out of the Verdurins' circle when they favor a rival. In the end, his love simply wears out. The section closes with Swann's rueful thought that he wasted years of his life on a woman who "was not in my style."

blocks.name: gb-proust-swann
blocks.cap: What made Swann fall in love, and what fed his jealousy: our summary.

blocks.html: Proust shows love as something the lover makes up inside himself, from music, art and imagination, more than something he finds in the other person. Jealousy keeps it alive. Time, and memory, are what finally change it.
The story is a mirror for the whole novel. Swann's mistakes in love foreshadow the narrator's own, and Swann's taste in art and music points to the book's final hope: that art can recover lost time.
Thinking Proust is only about long sentences. They are long, but they follow how the mind works: one thought leading to another, a memory opening inside a memory.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Augustine, in the Confessions, earlier on this ladder, marveled at memory as a vast storehouse inside the mind; Proust explores it room by room.
Bergson, the philosopher (and a relative of Proust's by marriage), taught that lived time differs from clock time.
Woolf's To the Lighthouse, later in this era, admired Proust and followed thoughts from within.
Montaigne also made his own mind the subject of a lifetime's writing.
Do we love people for who they are, or for what we imagine them to be?
Why can a taste or a tune bring back the past better than effort can?
What does jealousy do to the person who feels it?
Can art save the past from being lost?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Has a smell, a taste or a song ever brought a memory back to you all at once?
  2. Why do you think Swann fell in love with someone he didn't even like at first?
  3. Swann loved a piece of music because it reminded him of a feeling. Is there a song that does that for you?
  4. What is the difference between remembering on purpose and remembering by surprise?
  5. Why might a writer take seven volumes to tell one life?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
James Joyce was an Irish writer. His first novel follows a boy named Stephen Dedalus as he grows up in Dublin, from a little child to a young man who decides to become a writer.

The book starts the way a small child hears the world, with a bedtime story about a "moocow" and the smells and songs of home. Then Stephen goes away to boarding school. He is small and shy, and he wonders about big questions. In his geography book he writes his name and his address, going all the way out to the universe.

blocks.name: gb-joyce-stairs
blocks.cap: Climb the five chapters of Stephen's growing up.

blocks.html: For parents: the later chapters, about Stephen as a teenager, include a long, frightening sermon about hell and his private struggles. They are for older readers; chapter 1 is a fine read-aloud with explanation.

🧩 Try this

Your address in the universe. Like Stephen, write your name, then your house or street, town, state or county, country, continent, "The World" and "The Universe," each on its own line. Then wonder, as Stephen did: what comes after the universe?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

James Joyce (1882–1941) was born in Dublin, educated by Jesuits at Clongowes Wood College, Belvedere College and University College Dublin, and left Ireland in 1904 to live in Trieste, Zurich and Paris. A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man appeared as a serial in 1914–15 and as a book in New York in 1916. It draws closely on his own youth. His later novels, Ulysses (1922) and Finnegans Wake (1939), are among the most daring of the century.
The style grows with Stephen. The novel opens in a small child's language:
At Clongowes, the small boy writes on the flyleaf of his geography book:
By the last chapter, Stephen is a university student arguing about beauty in long, precise sentences, and the book ends in pages from his own diary.

blocks.name: gb-joyce-stairs
blocks.cap: Each chapter ends in a moment of triumph that the next chapter tests. Our summary.

blocks.html: Stephen is caught between three powers that want his loyalty: his family, the Catholic Church in which he was raised, and Irish nationalism. In chapter 3 a preacher's sermon on hell terrifies him into confession and a period of intense devotion. In chapter 4 he is invited to consider the priesthood, and turns it down. Walking on the beach, he sees a girl wading in the sea and feels a burst of joy that he takes as his call to art. In chapter 5 he resolves to leave Ireland and to make his life as a writer, using, as he says, "silence, exile, and cunning."
Joyce's word for the sudden insights that end many scenes was "epiphany": a moment when an ordinary thing shows its meaning. The Portrait is built from such moments.

The name Dedalus points to Daedalus, the craftsman of Greek myth who made wings to escape from a labyrinth. Stephen hopes to fly free from the nets of family, faith and nation, but the myth also recalls Icarus, who flew too high.
Taking Stephen as Joyce's perfect hero. Joyce often smiles at Stephen's pride; the title says "a young man," and later books show him older and less sure.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Augustine's Confessions, earlier on this ladder, is the first great story of a young man's inner struggle with faith; Joyce's book is a modern counterpart that turns the other way.
Aquinas, also on this ladder, supplies Stephen's theory of beauty (wholeness, harmony and radiance), as Stephen reads him.
Ovid's Metamorphoses gave Joyce his epigraph and the myth of Daedalus.
Woolf and others, later in this era, took up the method of following a mind from within.
What do we owe our family, our faith and our country? Can we choose our own way and still honor them?
Why does Stephen think he must leave home to become an artist?
What is an "epiphany"? Have you had one?
How does a writer show a child growing up just through the way the sentences change?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Stephen writes his address out to "The Universe." What does that tell you about him?
  2. Stephen was punished unfairly at school and went to the rector to complain. Was that brave?
  3. Why do you think Stephen chose art over the priesthood?
  4. What things in your life pull on your loyalty, as family, faith and country pulled on Stephen?
  5. Is it possible to love a place and still need to leave it?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
Luigi Pirandello was an Italian playwright who loved puzzles about what is real and what is pretend.

In his most famous play, a company of actors is rehearsing on an empty stage. Suddenly six strangers walk in: a father, a mother and four children. They say they are characters from a story whose author never finished writing it. They want the actors to play their story, so they can live it at last. The actors try, but the characters keep saying, "No, that's not how it was!" By the end, no one is sure what was real.

blocks.name: gb-pirandello-stage
blocks.cap: The actors on one side, the characters on the other. Tap each one.

blocks.html: For parents: the characters' own story involves a painful family scandal, hinted at in the play but not shown, and it ends in tragedy for the two youngest. The lesson keeps it general.

🧩 Try this

Characters come alive. Make up a character: give them a name, a favorite food, and one problem. Then let someone else play your character in a short scene. Did they get it right? Did your character seem to "want" something you didn't plan?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Luigi Pirandello (1867–1936) was born in Sicily, studied in Rome and Bonn, and wrote novels, hundreds of short stories and some forty plays. Family misfortune, including his wife's long mental illness, shaped his interest in how differently people see the same events. Six Characters in Search of an Author was first staged in Rome in 1921, where the first-night audience was in an uproar. He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1934. Edward Storer's English translation appeared in 1922.
A Manager and his actors are rehearsing a play (one of Pirandello's own) on a bare stage. Six people dressed in mourning arrive. The Father explains:
The Manager's first reaction is impatience:

But the characters' story is gripping. The Father once sent the Mother away to live with another man, and she had three more children; after years of poverty, the family's paths crossed again in a painful, shameful way. The Stepdaughter wants it all shown; the Father wants to explain himself; the Son wants no part of it. When the actors try to play the scenes, the characters protest that the actors' version is false. The Father insists that characters are more real than actors:

A person changes from day to day, the Father says, but a character's moment is fixed forever. The play ends in a sudden double tragedy for the two youngest children, and the actors cannot tell whether it was real or acted. The Manager, exasperated, has lost a whole day's rehearsal.

blocks.name: gb-pirandello-stage
blocks.cap: Who's who on Pirandello's stage: our summary.

blocks.html: Pirandello turns the theater inside out. The play is about the making of a play, and it asks whether anyone, on stage or off, can show the truth of another person's life.
Plays about plays were not new (Hamlet stages one), but Pirandello made the frame itself the drama. Later "metatheater," from Brecht to Beckett, owes him a great deal.
Thinking the characters are ghosts or lunatics. In the play's own terms they are exactly what they say: characters, alive in the imagination, with no finished play to live in.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Aristotle's Poetics, earlier on this ladder, says a drama imitates an action; Pirandello asks who decides which version of the action is true.
Cervantes, in Don Quixote Part II, lets characters read and argue about their own book, an ancestor of Pirandello's game.
Brecht and Beckett, later in this era, also break the illusion of the stage in different ways.
Pirandello's other plays, such as Right You Are (If You Think So), show a town unable to agree on the truth about one family.
Can one person ever tell another person's story truly?
Is a character in a book in any sense real?
Why do the Father and the Stepdaughter remember the same events so differently?
Is who we are fixed, or do we change from day to day?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. If a character from your favorite book walked into the room, what would you ask them?
  2. Why did the characters hate the way the actors played them?
  3. Two people in a family can remember the same day very differently. Why?
  4. The Father says a character is always "somebody," but a person might be "nobody." What do you think he means?
  5. Why might audiences in 1921 have been upset by this play?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Joan of Arc was a real girl who lived in France about six hundred years ago. France was losing a long war with England. Joan, a farm girl who could not read, said that voices of saints told her to help the French prince become king. Amazingly, she persuaded the prince to let her lead his army, and she won a great victory at the city of Orléans when she was about seventeen.

George Bernard Shaw, a witty Irish playwright, wrote a play about her called Saint Joan. In his play Joan is brave, cheerful, stubborn and full of common sense. The grown-ups around her are not exactly villains; each thinks he is doing the right thing. Sadly, Joan was captured, put on trial and condemned. Years later her name was cleared, and in 1920 she was declared a saint.

blocks.name: gb-shaw-joan
blocks.cap: Follow Joan's road across France. (A sketch map.)

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Make your case. Joan had to convince a squire, a prince and an army that a teenage girl should lead them. Pick something you'd like to do and make your case to your family in one minute. What reasons work best? What makes people believe you?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

George Bernard Shaw (1856–1950) was born in Dublin, moved to London at twenty, and became a music and theater critic, a famous debater and the most popular English-language playwright of his day, with comedies of ideas such as Pygmalion. He wrote Saint Joan in 1923, three years after the Catholic Church canonized Joan, and it was first staged in New York that December. It was published in 1924 with a long preface. Shaw received the Nobel Prize in Literature for 1925.
The preface opens with Joan's whole story in one sentence:

The six scenes follow Joan from a farmyard at Vaucouleurs to the court at Chinon, the siege of Orléans, the coronation at Reims, and her trial at Rouen. In an Epilogue set in 1456, Joan appears to King Charles in a dream, the people of her story gather, and a visitor from 1920 brings news of her sainthood. Each in turn kneels to praise her, but when she offers to come back to life, they all, politely, make excuses and leave.

blocks.name: gb-shaw-joan
blocks.cap: Joan's road, and where each scene of the play happens. Our summary.

blocks.html: Shaw's boldest choice is the trial scene. He gives Joan's judges, the Bishop Cauchon and the Inquisitor, serious, even reasonable arguments. They fear that a person who trusts her own conscience over the Church's authority could bring chaos. Shaw makes the English lord Warwick a cool politician who fears what Joan's appeal to France as a nation could do to rule by nobles. So the play suggests that Joan was destroyed less by wicked men than by good institutions defending themselves.

For Shaw, Joan was an early example of two new forces in history: the individual conscience (which he loosely calls Protestant) and the nation (which he calls nationalism). He presents both her accusers and her as sincere. Historians and Catholic writers have disagreed with parts of his reading; it is a playwright's interpretation, not a history.
Treating the play as a simple story of heroes and villains. Shaw insisted there are no villains in it; the tragedy is that everyone acts in good faith.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Sophocles' Antigone also shows a young woman who obeys a higher law against the rulers of her city.
Plato's Apology, the trial of Socrates, is another story of a sincere person condemned by sincere judges.
Shakespeare, in Henry VI, Part 1, had shown Joan as a witch from the English side; Shaw answers him.
Huizinga's Waning of the Middle Ages, in this era's social science, paints the world Joan lived in.
When should a person follow her own conscience against those in authority?
Can good people do a great wrong while believing they are right?
Why do people honor heroes after they are gone, but find them hard to live with?
How much may a playwright change history to make a point?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. What made Joan so persuasive, do you think?
  2. Shaw says there are no villains in his play. Do you agree?
  3. In the Epilogue, everyone praises Joan but no one wants her back. Why?
  4. Have you ever had to stand up for what you believed when the adults or the group disagreed?
  5. How can we tell the difference between courage and stubbornness?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
Willa Cather grew up on the prairies of Nebraska, where pioneer families had built farms and towns along the new railroads. She wrote novels about those pioneers and the land.

In A Lost Lady, a boy named Niel lives in a little railroad town called Sweet Water. On a hill outside town is the house of Captain Forrester, a grand old man who helped build the railroads, and his lively, charming wife. The boys of the town love to play in the Forresters' meadow. As Niel grows up, he sees the Captain grow old and lose his money, and he sees the bold pioneer days give way to a time of people who care only about getting rich.

blocks.name: gb-cather-sweetwater
blocks.cap: Step through Niel's years in Sweet Water.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Then and now. Ask a grandparent or older neighbor what your town was like when they were young. What was there that is gone now? What is new? Draw two pictures of the same street, "then" and "now."

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Willa Cather (1873–1947) moved as a child from Virginia to Red Cloud, Nebraska, a town on the Burlington railroad. She became a magazine editor in New York and then a novelist, writing of the prairie in O Pioneers! and My Ántonia. Her novel One of Ours won the Pulitzer Prize in 1923, the year A Lost Lady appeared. She based Mrs. Forrester partly on a woman she had known in Red Cloud. The book begins:
Captain Daniel Forrester built railroads across the West. He loves his marsh and meadow as they are:

We see the Forresters mostly through Niel Herbert, who as a boy worships the Captain's gracious wife, Marian. One summer day a mean-spirited older boy, Ivy Peters, hurts a woodpecker for fun, and Niel, trying to rescue it, falls from a tree and is cared for in the Forresters' house. As Niel grows up, a bank in Denver fails, and the Captain gives up his fortune to repay its small depositors rather than let them lose their savings. He suffers strokes and declines. Niel is disillusioned to learn that Mrs. Forrester is not the perfect lady he imagined, and that after the Captain's death she turns for help to Ivy Peters, now a sharp lawyer who drains the Captain's marsh for profit. Years later Niel hears that she married again in South America and was well cared for to the end.

blocks.name: gb-cather-sweetwater
blocks.cap: Niel's Sweet Water, from boyhood to farewell: our summary.

blocks.html: The "lost lady" is both Mrs. Forrester and an age. The pioneers, Cather writes, were dreamers and builders; the generation after them were shrewd men who drained the marshes and cut up the land for gain.
Cather tells the story in short, clear scenes and leaves much unsaid. She called this the "novel démeublé," the unfurnished novel: take out the clutter, and let the reader feel what is left out.
Reading Niel as always right. He judges Mrs. Forrester harshly by an ideal she never claimed; Cather lets us see her love of life, and her courage, more fairly than he does.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Fitzgerald's Great Gatsby, two years later and later on this ladder, also has a young narrator who watches and judges a glamorous figure; Fitzgerald wrote to Cather that he feared he had echoed her.
Flaubert's Madame Bovary and Tolstoy wrote of women trapped by marriage and longing; Cather is gentler with her heroine.
Tocqueville's Democracy in America, earlier on this ladder, described the restless American drive to get ahead that the book's Ivy Peters stands for.
Frederick Jackson Turner's idea of the closing frontier (1893) is the history behind the story.
Is it fair to judge people by the ideal picture we have of them?
What is lost when wild land is "improved" for profit, and what is gained?
Why does the Captain choose to repay the depositors? What does it cost him?
What do the pioneers and the generation after them each value?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. The Captain gave up his fortune to keep a promise to ordinary people. What do you think of that?
  2. Why did Niel feel let down by Mrs. Forrester?
  3. Ivy Peters hurt a bird for fun as a boy. What does that tell us about the man he became?
  4. What does your town keep from its past? What has it lost?
  5. Can someone be both admirable and flawed?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
Franz Kafka lived in Prague and worked in an insurance office by day. At night he wrote strange stories that feel like dreams.

In The Metamorphosis, a young man named Gregor Samsa works very hard as a traveling salesman to support his parents and his sister. One morning he wakes up and finds he has turned into a giant bug! He can't talk to his family anymore. His sister brings him food at first, but as time goes on the family grows tired and afraid, and they start to forget that the bug is still Gregor. The story asks: what makes someone part of a family?

blocks.name: gb-kafka-family
blocks.cap: Pick a family member and see how they treat Gregor in each part of the story.

blocks.html: For parents: the story is sad and ends with Gregor's death. It is often read in high school; younger children may prefer to hear the summary and talk about the questions.

🧩 Try this

Kindness without words. Gregor couldn't speak, but he could still feel. Play a game: try to tell your family something important ("I'm hungry," "I'm sad," "thank you") without any words. How hard is it to be understood? How can we be kind to someone who can't tell us what they need?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Franz Kafka (1883–1924) was a German-speaking Jewish writer in Prague, then part of Austria-Hungary. He trained as a lawyer and worked for a workers' accident insurance institute, writing in his free hours. His relationship with his forceful father troubled him all his life. The Metamorphosis (Die Verwandlung) was written in 1912 and published in 1915, one of the few works he published. Before he died of tuberculosis he asked his friend Max Brod to burn his unpublished manuscripts; Brod refused, and published The Trial and The Castle.

About quotations: the first English translation of The Metamorphosis appeared after 1930, and the translations are still under copyright, so this lesson describes the story in our own words. See "Read the full text" above for where to find it.

Part I. Gregor wakes to find himself changed into an enormous insect. His first worry is that he has missed his train and will lose his job, which pays the family's debts. The chief clerk from his firm arrives to check on him. When Gregor finally opens the door, the clerk flees and his father drives him back into his room.

Part II. His sister Grete takes charge of feeding him and cleaning his room. Gregor learns to hide under the couch so as not to frighten her. The family discovers they have more savings than he knew, and they begin to work. When Grete and her mother clear out his furniture, Gregor clings to a picture on the wall; his mother faints, and his father, in a rage, pelts him with apples. One lodges in his back.

Part III. Wounded and neglected, Gregor grows weak. The family takes in three lodgers. One evening Grete plays the violin, and Gregor, moved by the music, creeps out. The lodgers see him and give notice. Grete tells her parents they must get rid of "it," since if it were really Gregor he would have gone away himself. That night Gregor dies. The relieved family take a tram ride into the spring countryside, making plans and noticing that Grete has grown into a young woman.

blocks.name: gb-kafka-family
blocks.cap: The family's changing treatment of Gregor: our summary.

blocks.html: Kafka never explains the transformation. He tells an impossible event in calm, exact, everyday prose. The horror lies less in Gregor's new body than in how quickly a family can stop seeing a person in someone who can no longer provide for them.
The word "Kafkaesque" now names situations that are absurd, nightmarish and bureaucratic, where a person is trapped by forces he cannot understand.

Looking for the one right meaning. Readers have seen illness, disability, a son's guilt toward his father, the deadening effect of work, and Kafka's own sense of being an outsider. Kafka asked that the insect never be drawn on the book's cover; the story works by staying open.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Ovid's Metamorphoses, an old book of transformations, usually turns people into animals as a punishment or a rescue by the gods; Kafka's change has no cause and no rescue.
Dostoevsky, in Notes from Underground, also has a man compare himself to an insect.
Freud, in this era's volumes, wrote of the power of fathers in a child's inner life, a theme Kafka also explored in his "Letter to His Father."
Beckett and the later "theater of the absurd" learned from Kafka's calm telling of the impossible.
Is a person loved for who they are, or for what they do for others?
Why does Gregor worry first about his job?
Is Grete cruel at the end, or worn out? Can she be both?
Why might telling a strange event in plain words make it more powerful?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. If someone in your family changed in a way no one understood, what would you do?
  2. Grete was kind to Gregor at first. Why do you think she changed?
  3. Gregor kept loving music even when he couldn't speak. What does that tell you about him?
  4. Why do you think the family felt happy at the end? Should they have?
  5. How can we remember that someone who is sick or different is still the same person inside?
A note for parents: A story of cruelty, abuse of power and violence ending in two deaths, for adult readers. The lesson describes it at a general level.

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

For parents: "The Prussian Officer" is a story of cruelty and violence, written for adults. Young readers can learn here about D. H. Lawrence and how he painted landscapes in words, and leave the story itself for later.

D. H. Lawrence was the son of a coal miner in England. He became a famous writer who loved the natural world: flowers, animals, sunlight and mountains. He could make you feel the heat of a summer road or the cool of a forest just with words.

🧩 Try this

Paint with words. Lawrence opens his story with soldiers marching on a hot day: a white road, patches of shade, green fields, and far-off mountains with snow on top. Go outside (or look out a window) and write three sentences about what you see, hear and feel. Use colors, temperatures and sounds. Read them aloud: can your family picture the place?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

David Herbert Lawrence (1885–1930) grew up in Eastwood, a mining town in Nottinghamshire, England, and became a teacher before his novel Sons and Lovers (1913) made his name. In 1912 he traveled to Germany with Frieda von Richthofen, whom he later married, and he watched German soldiers on maneuvers in Bavaria. "The Prussian Officer" gave its name to his first collection of stories, published in London in December 1914, months after the First World War began. (Lawrence had called the story "Honour and Arms"; his editor, Edward Garnett, changed the title.)
The story opens in heat and light:

A proud, cold aristocratic captain becomes fixed on his young orderly, a simple, healthy peasant soldier. The captain resents the young man's easy freedom and begins to torment him with small cruelties and then outright abuse. The orderly, bewildered, feels his own inner life crushed. On the march, as the heat bears down, the tension breaks in a sudden act of violence in a forest clearing. The orderly wanders off alone, feverish and lost, toward the mountains that had stood ahead of the soldiers all through the march, as Lawrence first showed them:
The story ends with both men dead. Lawrence leaves the reader with the image of the far, cool mountains the orderly never reached.

blocks.name: gb-lawrence-heat
blocks.cap: The story's movement, from the march to the mountains: our summary, without detail.

blocks.html: Lawrence shows what happens when one person tries to master another completely. Rank and pride let the captain bully; denied feeling turns to cruelty; and the victim's crushed life breaks out in violence that destroys them both.

Written just before the Great War, the story was read as a picture of the rigid military world of Prussia. Lawrence's real subject is the inner life of the two men: buried passion, pride, and the body's revolt.
Skimming the landscapes. Lawrence's heat, glare and distant snow carry the story's feeling: the pressure building on the road, and the longing for coolness and freedom in the mountains.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Hegel, earlier on this ladder, wrote of the struggle between master and servant, in which the master's power turns out to depend on the servant.
Melville's Billy Budd (published 1924) is another story of a cruel officer and an innocent young sailor.
Tolstoy and later war writers, such as Hemingway in this era, also show the soldier's world from the inside.
Freud, in this era's volumes, argued that buried feelings can break out in harmful ways.
What does power over another person do to the one who holds it?
Why can't the orderly tell anyone what is happening to him?
How can a writer use weather and landscape to show feelings?
What makes an institution, like an army, prevent or allow abuse?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Why do you think the captain treated the orderly so cruelly?
  2. What could someone being bullied by a person in authority do? Who could help?
  3. Lawrence uses heat and mountains to show feelings. Which feelings does each stand for?
  4. Is it ever right for an officer or a boss to have complete power over someone?
  5. How did the story's landscape make you feel?

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

T. S. Eliot was born in St. Louis, Missouri, and moved to England as a young man. After the terrible First World War, he wrote a long poem called The Waste Land about a world that felt broken, like a dry land waiting for rain.

The poem is built from many voices and pieces, like a collage: bits of old songs, Bible stories, Shakespeare, legends about knights searching for the Holy Grail, and people talking in London. It ends with the sound of thunder over a desert, as if rain might finally come.

blocks.name: gb-eliot-fragments
blocks.cap: Pick a part of the poem and see the older books it borrows from.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

A collage poem. Cut out ten interesting phrases from old magazines, newspapers or a page you print out. Arrange them on paper so they make a feeling or a little story. Glue them down and give your poem a title. That is a bit like how Eliot built The Waste Land.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Thomas Stearns Eliot (1888–1965) grew up in St. Louis, studied philosophy at Harvard, and settled in London in 1914, where he worked in a bank and later as a publisher. He became a British subject in 1927, the same year he was received into the Church of England, and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1948. The Waste Land appeared in 1922 in two magazines and then as a book in New York, with Eliot's own notes. His friend Ezra Pound cut the draft nearly in half, and Eliot dedicated the poem to him.
The poem's 433 lines are in five sections. It opens by turning spring, usually a time of joy, into a time of pain, because new life stirs up memories and longings:

The voices shift without warning: a woman remembering a childhood sledding trip, a fortune-teller with her cards, crowds of office workers crossing London Bridge like Dante's dead, a nervous couple, gossip in a pub, a sailor drowned at sea. Eliot's notes point to the legend of the Fisher King, whose wounded land stays barren until a knight asks the right question, which he took from Jessie Weston's book on the Grail stories and from Frazer's Golden Bough.

In the last section, "What the Thunder Said," travelers cross a dry, rocky land toward a chapel. Thunder speaks three words from an ancient Hindu text, the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad: Datta, Dayadhvam, Damyata, which Eliot's notes translate "Give, sympathise, control." Near the end the speaker says:

blocks.name: gb-eliot-fragments
blocks.cap: The five sections and some of the sources Eliot names in his notes: our summary.

blocks.html: The poem's method is its meaning. A culture shattered by war is shown in fragments; the old stories are still there, broken, but perhaps able to be gathered up. Whether the rain comes is left open.

The Waste Land became the landmark of modernist poetry: no single speaker, no story told in order, quotations in several languages, and sudden shifts of tone. Readers then and now have argued whether that difficulty is necessary or a barrier.
Trying to understand every reference on first reading. Read it aloud, like music, and notice the moods; the notes can come later.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Dante's Inferno, earlier on this ladder, gives Eliot his image of crowds of the living who seem already dead.
Augustine's Confessions and the Buddha's Fire Sermon meet in Part III, "The Fire Sermon": two great teachers from East and West who warn against burning desires.
Shakespeare's Tempest echoes through the poem's drowned sailor and its hopes of a sea-change.
Frazer's Golden Bough, in this era's social science, gave Eliot the old myths of a dying and reviving land.
Eliot's later Four Quartets moves from the waste land toward faith.
Can old stories and words help rebuild a broken world?
Why might spring feel "cruel" to someone who has lost a great deal?
What do "give, sympathize, control" ask of a person?
Should a great poem be easy to understand?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Why do you think Eliot called April "the cruellest month"?
  2. The poem is made of many voices. Whose voice is easiest to hear?
  3. What would "give, sympathize, control" look like in a family?
  4. How might a whole country feel after a terrible war?
  5. Do you like poems that are puzzles, or poems that are clear? Why?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
F. Scott Fitzgerald was an American writer of the 1920s, the "Jazz Age," when many people in New York got rich quickly, danced to new music and threw big parties.

In The Great Gatsby, a young man named Nick moves into a little house on Long Island, next door to a huge mansion. Its owner, the mysterious Jay Gatsby, throws enormous parties every weekend. Nick learns that Gatsby once loved a young woman named Daisy, who lives across the bay. Every night Gatsby looks across the water at a green light at the end of her dock. He has made himself rich hoping to win her back, as if he could bring back the past. It doesn't end happily.

blocks.name: gb-gatsby-map
blocks.cap: Follow Nick around Long Island and New York.

blocks.html: For parents: the novel includes drinking, an unfaithful marriage, a fatal car accident and a shooting, all told without graphic detail. It is usually read in high school.

🧩 Try this

Your green light. Gatsby's green light stood for a dream he reached toward. Draw a picture of a light far away across water, and inside it draw or write a dream of yours. Then talk about it: what is a good dream to work toward? Can a dream ever be the wrong one?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

F. Scott Fitzgerald (1896–1940) was born in St. Paul, Minnesota, went to Princeton, and served in the army in 1917–19, though he was never sent overseas. His first novel, This Side of Paradise (1920), made him famous, and he and his wife Zelda became symbols of the high-living twenties. The Great Gatsby (1925) sold modestly in his lifetime; it was only after his early death that it came to be seen as one of the great American novels.
The narrator, Nick Carraway, begins with a lesson from his father:

In the summer of 1922 Nick rents a cottage in West Egg, Long Island, beside the mansion of Jay Gatsby. Across the bay, in fashionable East Egg, live Nick's cousin Daisy and her rich, arrogant husband, Tom Buchanan. On his first night Nick sees his neighbor alone on the lawn:

Gatsby, we learn, was born James Gatz to poor farm people in North Dakota. As a young officer in 1917 he fell in love with Daisy, but he had no money, and while he was away at war she married Tom. Gatsby has since made a fortune by shady means, bought a mansion across from hers, and thrown parties in the hope she might wander in. Nick arranges a reunion. For a while Gatsby believes he can have Daisy back and erase the five years between. In a hot afternoon's quarrel at the Plaza Hotel in New York, Tom exposes Gatsby, and Daisy draws back. On the drive home, Gatsby's car, with Daisy at the wheel, strikes and kills a woman. Gatsby takes the blame, and the woman's grieving husband later shoots him. Almost no one comes to his funeral. Disgusted with the careless rich, Nick goes home to the Midwest.

blocks.name: gb-gatsby-map
blocks.cap: The places of the novel: a sketch map, not to scale. Our summary.

blocks.html: Gatsby's dream is part love and part the American hope of remaking oneself. Fitzgerald honors the hope and shows its corruption: money cannot buy back the past, and the people with the most money are often the most careless.
Nick is a witness who is also part of the story. He says he is honest and slow to judge, yet he helps arrange the reunion and keeps others' secrets. Reading closely means asking how far to trust him.
Treating the novel as a celebration of parties and wealth. The glamour is real, but the book is closer to a lament: the parties are empty, and their host dies alone.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Cather's A Lost Lady, two years earlier and on this ladder, also shows a young man watching a glamorous figure and an age passing.
Conrad's Heart of Darkness uses a witness-narrator, Marlow, telling of a mysterious man; Fitzgerald admired Conrad and learned from him.
Veblen's Theory of the Leisure Class, in this era's social science, named the "conspicuous consumption" that Gatsby's parties put on show.
Franklin's Autobiography lies behind the young Gatsby's schedule of self-improvement, which his father shows Nick after the funeral.
Can a person remake himself completely? What would be lost?
Why does Gatsby believe he can repeat the past?
Who in the novel is careless, and what does carelessness cost others?
Is Gatsby "great"? In what sense?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Nick's father told him not to judge others too quickly. Is that good advice?
  2. What did the green light mean to Gatsby?
  3. Gatsby worked hard for his dream. Was it a good dream?
  4. Why do you think so few people came to Gatsby's funeral?
  5. Can money make a person happy? What does this story say?
