About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
Virginia Woolf was an English writer who spent childhood summers at the seaside, in a house that looked out at a lighthouse. Years later she turned those memories into a novel.

In To the Lighthouse, six-year-old James Ramsay wants more than anything to sail out to the lighthouse tomorrow. His mother says yes, if the weather is fine. His father says the weather won't be fine. James is crushed. The trip doesn't happen. Ten years go by, the family changes, and at last James, now a teenager, sails to the lighthouse with his father. Meanwhile a painter friend, Lily, finally finishes the picture she began long before.

blocks.name: gb-woolf-time
blocks.cap: The book has three parts. Compare how many pages each takes with how much time it covers.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Inside a minute. Woolf spent pages on a single moment, telling what each person was thinking. Sit with your family for one minute in silence. Afterward, each person writes or says everything they noticed and thought during that minute. How different were your minutes?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Virginia Woolf (1882–1941) was the daughter of the writer Leslie Stephen. With her sister and friends she was at the center of London's "Bloomsbury group," and with her husband Leonard she ran the Hogarth Press. Her childhood summers were spent at St Ives in Cornwall, where the house looked out on a lighthouse. Her mother died when Virginia was thirteen. To the Lighthouse (1927) moves those memories to the Isle of Skye in Scotland, and the Ramsays are partly portraits of her parents.
It begins in the middle of a conversation:
A few pages later her husband stops at the window:

The Window covers one afternoon and evening. We move from mind to mind: Mrs. Ramsay knitting and worrying over everyone; Mr. Ramsay, a philosopher, anxious about whether his work will last; the painter Lily Briscoe, unsure she can paint at all; the guests at a dinner party that Mrs. Ramsay, for one evening, makes into a perfect whole. Even the view is seen through a mind:

Time Passes is short. The house stands empty for ten years while wind and damp creep in. In a few brief sentences set in square brackets, we learn that Mrs. Ramsay has died suddenly, that a daughter has died young, and that a son has been killed in the Great War. An old cleaning woman, Mrs. McNab, struggles to save the house.

The Lighthouse covers one morning ten years later. Mr. Ramsay at last sails to the lighthouse with James and his sister Cam, now teenagers who resent him; on the way, James finally earns his father's praise. On the lawn, Lily Briscoe returns to her old painting, thinks of Mrs. Ramsay, and with one final line at its center, finishes it.

blocks.name: gb-woolf-time
blocks.cap: Pages compared with time: the shape of the novel. Our summary; page shares are rough.

blocks.html: Woolf turns the usual novel inside out. A dinner takes many pages; ten years, with three deaths, take a few. What matters is not the clock but how moments live in the mind, and what can be made to last: a dinner, a painting, a memory.

The method is often called "stream of consciousness," a phrase first used by William James. Woolf's version glides from one person's thoughts to another's within a paragraph, so the reader feels a whole household thinking at once.
Waiting for a plot. Very little "happens" on the surface. The events are inner ones: a child's anger, a father's need for praise, a painter's moment of vision.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: William James, earlier on this ladder, named the "stream of consciousness" in psychology.
Bergson, in this era's philosophy, contrasted clock time with lived time, as Woolf's three parts do.
Proust, whom Woolf read with wonder, also made memory and time his subject.
Joyce's novels, which Woolf read with mixed feelings, also follow minds from within.
Woolf's essay A Room of One's Own (1929) asked why so few women had been able to write; Lily Briscoe, told that women can't paint, is a character of that question.
Why can one evening matter more than ten years?
Was Mr. Ramsay wrong to tell James the truth about the weather?
What can last when people die? A painting? A memory? A family?
How well can we ever know what someone else is thinking?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Mr. Ramsay told James the truth: the weather would be bad. Mrs. Ramsay gave him hope. Who was kinder?
  2. Which moments from your family's summers do you think you'll remember in ten years?
  3. Why do you think Woolf told three deaths in just a few lines?
  4. Lily kept working on her painting for ten years. What have you kept working on?
  5. Is it possible to know what someone else is really thinking?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

For parents: "A Rose for Emily" is a short, eerie story with a grim discovery at the end, usually read in high school. Young readers can learn here about how Faulkner tells a story out of order, and leave the story itself for later.
William Faulkner lived almost his whole life in a small town in Mississippi. He invented a whole imaginary county, with its own towns, families and history, and set most of his stories there.

In this story, the storyteller is not one person but a whole town, speaking as "we." The town tells what it remembers about a proud, lonely old woman, Miss Emily, but not in the order things happened. It jumps back and forth in time, the way people do when they gossip, and saves its biggest surprise for the end.

🧩 Try this

Tell it out of order. Think of a funny family story. Tell it starting at the end ("...and that's why there's a hole in the fence"), then jump back to the beginning, then the middle. Does starting at the end make people more curious? What does a storyteller gain by holding something back?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

William Faulkner (1897–1962) spent most of his life in Oxford, Mississippi. He created Yoknapatawpha County, with its town of Jefferson, as the setting of novels such as The Sound and the Fury (1929) and As I Lay Dying (1930), and won the Nobel Prize in Literature for 1949. "A Rose for Emily," published in the magazine The Forum in April 1930, was his first short story in a national magazine and is now one of the most read American stories.
It opens at the end of a life:

The "we" of the town then circles back through her life. Miss Emily is the last of a proud old family, kept from every suitor by her father. When he dies, she refuses for three days to admit it. Later she is seen with Homer Barron, a cheerful Northern foreman, and the town gossips. She buys poison without saying why; Homer disappears; a bad smell comes from her house, and the town's leaders, too polite to confront her, quietly sprinkle lime. She grows old alone, refusing to pay taxes or to accept the town's new ways.

After her funeral, the townspeople open a room upstairs that no one has entered in forty years, and discover the dark secret of what happened to Homer Barron. The story ends on that discovery, which the lesson leaves undescribed.

blocks.name: gb-faulkner-order
blocks.cap: Switch between the order of telling and the order of events. Our summary.

blocks.html: Miss Emily stands for the Old South after the Civil War: proud, decaying and unable to let the past go. The town, which both reveres and spies on her, shares the blame for what it chose not to see.

The scrambled order is the story's engine. Because the town tells its memories out of sequence, readers gather clues without knowing they are clues, as the townspeople did, until the ending makes them fall into place.
Reading it only as a horror story. Faulkner said the "rose" of the title is a salute to a woman who had suffered, a small gesture of sympathy for her lonely, tragic life.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Dickens's Little Dorrit, earlier on this ladder, has its own decaying house and a woman shut away from time; Dickens's Miss Havisham, in Great Expectations, is another.
Cather's A Lost Lady and Fitzgerald's Gatsby, in this era, also show a community watching one figure as an old order passes.
Greek tragedy often uses a chorus that speaks for a community; Faulkner's "we" is a kind of chorus.
Twain's Huckleberry Finn, earlier on this ladder, is the other great portrait of the South on this ladder.
Why does the town never confront Miss Emily? What does politeness cost here?
What does it mean to be unable to let the past go?
Is the town a fair narrator? What does it get wrong?
How does telling events out of order change what we feel?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. The whole town tells this story. Why do you think Faulkner chose "we" instead of one narrator?
  2. Why might people be afraid to ask a hard question?
  3. Miss Emily refused to change with the times. When is it good to keep old ways, and when not?
  4. What does the title's "rose" mean to you?
  5. Have you ever pieced together a mystery from clues you noticed only later?

blocks.html: A note for parents: A tragedy of murder, revenge and suicide within a family, for adult readers. The lesson summarizes the plot without detail.

Choose a path

  • 🌱 For young readers
  • 📖 For teens and adults
  • 🔭 Going deeper

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

For parents: Mourning Becomes Electra is a long tragedy about a family destroyed by murder and revenge, written for adults. This path introduces the idea behind it; the full lesson is for older teens and adults.
Eugene O'Neill was America's first great playwright. He loved the old Greek tragedies, and he wondered: what if one of those ancient stories happened in an American family?

So he took a famous Greek story, about a king coming home from war and the trouble in his family, and moved it to a big white house in New England just after the American Civil War. The characters wear 1860s clothes and speak like Americans, but the old story's pattern of anger and revenge plays out again.

blocks.name: gb-oneill-map
blocks.cap: Match each Greek character to O'Neill's American one.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Old story, new place. Pick a fairy tale you know well, like Cinderella or the Three Little Pigs. Retell it as if it happened in your own town this year. Who would each character be? What would change, and what would stay the same?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Eugene O'Neill (1888–1953), the son of a famous touring actor, grew up in hotels and theaters, went to sea as a young man, and began writing plays after a long illness. His plays brought serious tragedy to the American stage. He won the Pulitzer Prize four times and, in 1936, the Nobel Prize in Literature, the only American playwright so honored. Mourning Becomes Electra, a trilogy of three plays, opened in New York in 1931 and ran about six hours with a dinner break.
About quotations: the play was first published in 1931 and is still under copyright, so this lesson describes it in our own words. See "Read the full text" above for where to find it.

O'Neill followed the plan of Aeschylus' Oresteia, earlier on this ladder, scene by scene, but replaced the gods and the curse of fate with the inner forces of a modern family: jealousy, guilt and hidden longings, as the psychology of his day described them.

items: Homecoming (Agamemnon). In 1865, General Ezra Mannon returns from the Civil War. His wife Christine, who hates him and loves another man, Captain Adam Brant, poisons him. Their daughter Lavinia, devoted to her father, discovers what her mother has done.

The Hunted (The Libation Bearers). Lavinia's brother Orin comes home wounded from the war. Lavinia convinces him of their mother's guilt, and together they take revenge on Brant. Christine, in despair, takes her own life.

The Haunted (The Eumenides). Lavinia and Orin travel to the South Seas and return changed. Orin, tormented by guilt, also dies. Lavinia, the last Mannon, refuses any escape: she orders the shutters nailed closed and shuts herself inside the house with the dead, to punish herself for the rest of her life.

blocks.name: gb-oneill-map
blocks.cap: Aeschylus' characters and O'Neill's: our summary.

blocks.html: In the Oresteia, the chain of revenge is finally broken by a court and the gods' mercy. In O'Neill's version there are no gods and no court, and the chain ends only when the last Mannon locks herself away. The modern tragedy has no Athens to rescue it.

The title plays on two meanings of "becomes": mourning "suits" Electra, as black clothes might, and Electra herself "becomes" mourning, turning into grief. The Mannons' house, with its white columns like a Greek temple's front, is O'Neill's stage image of a classical tragedy in an American setting.
Thinking O'Neill simply copied Aeschylus. He kept the plot's shape but changed its meaning: fate becomes psychology, and the gods' justice becomes a family's private punishment.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Aeschylus' Oresteia is the model, act by act.
Freud, in this era's volumes, gave O'Neill the language of hidden family feelings he used instead of the gods.
Euripides' Electra and Sophocles' Electra told the same story in different ways; O'Neill's title points to all of them.
Ibsen brought tragedy into a middle-class home; O'Neill made it American.
Is revenge ever justice? What breaks a chain of revenge?
Can a family's past trap its children? How can people escape it?
What changes when a story about gods becomes a story about psychology?
Why do old myths keep being retold?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Why do you think O'Neill moved a Greek story to America after the Civil War?
  2. In the Greek version, a court ends the revenge. What could have ended it for the Mannons?
  3. Lavinia chooses to punish herself. Is that brave, or sad, or both?
  4. What stories have you seen retold in a new time or place?
  5. How do families pass down feelings, good and bad, without meaning to?
A note for parents: Big-game hunting, a troubled marriage and a fatal shooting, told plainly; for adult readers. The lesson summarizes without detail.

Choose a path

  • 🌱 For young readers
  • 📖 For teens and adults
  • 🔭 Going deeper

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
For parents: this story, about big-game hunting, a troubled marriage and a fatal shot, is for adult readers. This path introduces Hemingway's famous way of writing instead.

Ernest Hemingway was an American writer who loved the outdoors: fishing, hunting, mountains and the sea. He was famous for writing short, plain sentences. He believed a good story is like an iceberg: you see only the tip above the water, but most of it is hidden underneath. A writer can leave things out, and readers will still feel them.

blocks.name: gb-hemingway-iceberg
blocks.cap: Hemingway's iceberg: tap each layer, from what is said down to what is only felt.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Write an iceberg. Write a short scene, five sentences, about two people at breakfast after an argument. Don't say what the argument was about, and don't name any feelings. Only describe what they do and say. Then read it to your family: can they guess what is under the surface?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Ernest Hemingway (1899–1961) grew up in Oak Park, Illinois, worked as a newspaper reporter, and was badly wounded as a Red Cross ambulance driver in Italy in 1918. In Paris in the 1920s he developed his spare, clipped style; The Sun Also Rises (1926) and A Farewell to Arms (1929) made him famous. A safari in East Africa in 1933–34 gave him the setting for this story, published in 1936. He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1954.
About quotations: the story was first published in 1936 and is still under copyright, so this lesson describes it in our own words. See "Read the full text" above for where to find it.

It opens at lunch in a safari camp in East Africa. Everyone pretends nothing has happened, but something has: that morning, Francis Macomber, a wealthy American, ran in panic from a wounded, charging lion, and the professional hunter, Robert Wilson, had to kill it. Macomber's wife, Margot, makes no secret of her contempt, and her open scorn humiliates him further.

The story then goes back to tell the lion hunt in full, partly through Macomber's fear and even, for a moment, the lion's own view. The next day they hunt buffalo. In the heat of the chase, Macomber suddenly loses his fear and feels a wild happiness, as if he has become a man at last. Wilson is pleased; Margot is uneasy, because a brave husband will not be so easy to rule. When a wounded buffalo charges, Macomber stands his ground. Margot fires from the car, and her shot kills her husband.

blocks.name: gb-hemingway-iceberg
blocks.cap: What the story shows, and what it leaves under the surface: our summary.

blocks.html: Did she mean it? Hemingway never says. Wilson, cold and contemptuous, suggests that she did. Many readers take him at his word; others point out that she may have been aiming at the buffalo. The title is ironic and sincere at once: Macomber's "happy life," the life of a man without fear, lasted only minutes.
Hemingway's subject is courage: what it is, how it is lost and found, and what it costs. Wilson lives by a strict code of grace under pressure. Macomber, in the end, earns it.
His "iceberg" method, leaving the deepest feelings unsaid, makes readers do the work of understanding. The open ending is a result of that method.
Taking Wilson as the author's voice. He embodies the code Hemingway admired, but the story also shows his coldness, his own failings and his contempt for the Macombers.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Aristotle's Ethics, earlier on this ladder, defines courage as the right mean between cowardice and rashness; Macomber swings from one to the edge of the other.
Homer's Iliad shows warriors shamed by fear and restored by valor.
Conrad and Lawrence, earlier in this era, also test men in hard places far from home.
Hemingway's style shaped generations of American writers and journalists.
What is courage? Is it the absence of fear, or acting well while afraid?
Can one moment change who a person is?
Why might a writer leave the most important thing unsaid?
How should we treat someone who has failed in front of others?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Have you ever been afraid and then found your courage? What helped?
  2. Margot mocked her husband when he failed. How should we treat someone who is ashamed?
  3. Why do you think Hemingway didn't tell us whether Margot meant to fire at her husband?
  4. What do you think the title means?
  5. Is it better to say exactly what you feel, or can leaving things unsaid be powerful?

  • 🌱 For young readers

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Bertolt Brecht was a German playwright. He wanted plays to make people think, not just cry. So his plays have songs, signs that tell you what will happen next, and characters who sometimes seem to talk right to the audience.

Mother Courage and Her Children takes place long ago, during a war that lasted thirty years. Mother Courage pulls a wagon full of things to sell to soldiers: boots, bread, brandy and belts. She thinks the war is good for business, and she hopes to keep her three grown children safe and earn a living from it at the same time. But the war takes all three of them, one by one. Her brave daughter Kattrin, who cannot speak, saves a whole town by beating a drum to warn them.
For parents: the play is about war's cost to a family; all three children die, which the lesson mentions without detail. Best for teens and adults.

blocks.name: gb-brecht-wagon
blocks.cap: Follow Mother Courage's wagon through twelve years of war. (A rough sketch map.)

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Make a sign. Brecht hung signs before each scene saying what would happen, so the audience would watch how and why, not just what. Pick a fairy tale and write a sign for each part ("Scene 1: The wolf meets a girl in the woods"). Then act it with the signs. Does knowing what's coming change what you notice?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Bertolt Brecht (1898–1956) was born in Augsburg, Bavaria, and made his name in 1920s Berlin with The Threepenny Opera (1928), written with the composer Kurt Weill. A Marxist, he fled Germany when the Nazis came to power in 1933 and lived in exile in Denmark, Sweden, Finland and the United States. He wrote Mother Courage in Sweden in 1939, as the Second World War began. It was first staged in Zurich in 1941. After the war he founded the Berliner Ensemble in East Berlin, where his wife, the actress Helene Weigel, played Mother Courage.
About quotations: the play was first published after 1930 and is still under copyright, so this lesson describes it in our own words. See "Read the full text" above for where to find it.

The twelve scenes run from 1624 to 1636, in the middle of the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648), which began as a religious conflict between Catholic and Protestant states and grew into a European struggle for power that devastated the German lands. Anna Fierling, called Mother Courage, follows the armies of both sides with her canteen wagon. She has three children by different fathers: Eilif, bold; Swiss Cheese, honest; and Kattrin, kind, who cannot speak.

Each child is undone by a virtue the war turns into a danger. Eilif's daring wins praise in war, but when he does the same thing during a brief peace he is executed. Swiss Cheese's honesty leads him to hide his regiment's cash box, and he is shot while his mother haggles over the bribe that could have saved him. Kattrin's compassion makes her climb a roof and drum to warn a sleeping town of a surprise attack; she saves the town and is killed. At the end Courage, alone, harnesses herself to her wagon and follows the army again.

blocks.name: gb-brecht-wagon
blocks.cap: The wagon's road, scene by scene: our summary.

blocks.html: Brecht called his method "epic theater." Signs, songs and a deliberately un-magical stage keep the audience at a thinking distance (his "estrangement" or "alienation" effect), so that they judge Courage rather than simply pity her. He wanted them to see that she lives off the war that destroys her family, and never learns.

Audiences often wept for Courage anyway, and admired her toughness. Brecht revised the play to make her less sympathetic. Whether she is a victim, a villain or both is still argued; the play's power may come from that tension.

Calling the play a story of heroism, as the name "Courage" suggests. She got the nickname, the play says, for driving her wagon through a bombardment to sell bread before it went moldy: courage for the sake of business.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Grimmelshausen's 17th-century novels of the Thirty Years' War, including one about a camp follower named Courasche, gave Brecht his heroine's name and world.
Euripides' Trojan Women, on this ladder's Greek rungs, also shows war through the women it leaves behind.
Aristotle's Poetics said tragedy works through pity and fear; Brecht set out to replace that with critical thinking.
Tolstoy's War and Peace and Thucydides, earlier on this ladder, are other great portraits of war's cost.
Can a person profit from a war without sharing its blame?
Why do the children's virtues, bravery, honesty and kindness, put them in danger?
Should a play make us feel, or make us think? Can it do both?
Why does Courage never seem to learn?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Mother Courage loved her children and also loved her business. When did those two loves clash?
  2. Kattrin couldn't speak, but she saved a town. What gave her the courage?
  3. Why do you think Brecht put up signs telling the audience what would happen?
  4. Is "Mother Courage" a good name for her? Why or why not?
  5. What does war do to ordinary families, in this play and in history you know?

blocks.html: A note for parents: Some animals are killed or sold to slaughter, told simply and without detail. A family-friendly fable with a serious political meaning.

Choose a path

  • 🌱 For young readers
  • 📖 For teens and adults
  • 🔭 Going deeper

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
George Orwell was an English writer who cared about fairness, truth and plain words. Animal Farm looks like a children's fable, but it is really a story about how a fight for freedom can go wrong.

On Manor Farm, the animals are tired of working hard for a careless farmer who keeps everything for himself. They rise up, chase him away, and run the farm together. They paint rules on the barn wall, the most important being that all animals are equal. At first things go well. But the clever pigs slowly take charge. They move into the farmhouse, change the rules a little at a time, and use fierce dogs to scare anyone who complains. In the end, the other animals can't tell the pigs from the people they drove out.

blocks.name: gb-orwell-barn
blocks.cap: The rules on the barn wall, early and later. Watch what changes. (Our own wording.)

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Rules for a fair game. As a family, write five rules for a game or for chores that everyone agrees are fair. Post them. A week later, read them together: did anyone "bend" a rule? Talk about why it matters that rules stay the same for everyone, and that everyone can read them.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

George Orwell was the pen name of Eric Arthur Blair (1903–1950), born in India, educated at Eton, and a colonial policeman in Burma before he became a writer. He described poverty in England and France, and fought for the Republican side in the Spanish Civil War, where he saw a faction backed by the Soviet Union turn on its own allies. A lifelong democratic socialist, he came to oppose the Soviet system under Stalin. Animal Farm, finished in 1944, was turned down by several publishers, partly because Britain and the Soviet Union were wartime allies; it appeared in August 1945. His last novel was Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949).
About quotations: Animal Farm was first published in 1945 and is still under copyright, so this lesson describes it in our own words, including the rules in the visual.

Old Major, a respected boar, tells the animals of his dream of a world without human masters. After his death, the animals rebel, drive out the drunken farmer Mr. Jones, rename the place Animal Farm and paint their rules on the barn. Two young pigs lead: Snowball, an inventive speaker who plans a windmill, and Napoleon, quiet and scheming, who secretly raises a litter of puppies. When the dogs are grown, Napoleon uses them to chase Snowball off the farm and blames him for every later misfortune. A pig called Squealer, a gifted talker, explains away each new privilege the pigs take, and the rules on the wall are quietly altered. The loyal cart-horse Boxer works himself to exhaustion trusting the leaders, and when he collapses the pigs sell him to a slaughterer while telling the others he died in a hospital. At the end, the pigs walk on two legs, wear clothes and entertain the neighboring farmers, and the animals outside the window can no longer tell pig from man.

blocks.name: gb-orwell-barn
blocks.cap: How the rules changed: our own paraphrase of each.

blocks.html: Orwell said plainly that the book is an allegory of the Russian Revolution of 1917 and what followed. Most readers match the characters this way:

head: In the fable
In history (as Orwell meant it)
rows: the Tsar and the old regime
blocks.cap: A common reading; Orwell kept some details loose so the story would apply more widely.

blocks.html: Orwell's warning reaches beyond one country. Power without checks corrupts those who hold it; a free people needs memory, honest records and plain language, because whoever controls the words can rewrite the rules.

Orwell did not argue that the farm should go back to Mr. Jones. The fable's target is the betrayal of a revolution's ideals by a new ruling group. Readers of many political views have claimed it; its lesson about language and power is shared widely.
Reading it as only an animal story, or only as history. It is both: a fable simple enough for children and a precise political satire.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Aesop's fables used animals to teach lessons, and Swift's Gulliver's Travels, earlier on this ladder, used imaginary lands for satire.
Plato's Republic asked who should rule and how rulers can be kept from serving themselves.
Marx and Engels, earlier on this ladder, wrote the ideas Old Major's dream echoes; Orwell attacks what was done in their name, not the wish for fairness.
Thucydides described how, in civil strife, words change their meanings; Orwell's Squealer shows the same.
Why do the other animals let the pigs change the rules?
What makes power safe or dangerous in the hands of a few?
Why does Orwell care so much about written rules and plain words?
What could the animals have done to keep their farm fair?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Why did the animals rebel in the first place?
  2. How did the pigs change the rules without the other animals noticing?
  3. Boxer always trusted the leaders. Is trust always good? When should we ask questions?
  4. Why is it important that everyone can read and remember the rules?
  5. Is there a time someone changed the rules in a game you played? How did it feel?

  • 🌱 For young readers
  • 📖 For teens and adults
  • 🔭 Going deeper

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
Samuel Beckett was an Irish writer who lived in Paris and wrote in both French and English. His most famous play is very strange and very simple.

In Waiting for Godot, two old friends, Vladimir and Estragon, wait beside a bare tree on a country road for someone called Godot. They don't really know who he is or why they're waiting. To pass the time they chat, argue, tell jokes, swap hats and play games. A boy comes to say Godot won't come today, but surely tomorrow. The next day they wait again. Godot never comes. The play is funny and sad at the same time, and people still argue about what it means.

blocks.name: gb-beckett-tree
blocks.cap: Compare Act I and Act II. What changes? What stays the same?

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

The waiting game. Waiting can feel very long. Next time your family is waiting (in a car, in line, at the doctor's), invent a game to pass the time, as Vladimir and Estragon do. Afterward talk about it: what made the time go faster? Who or what were you really waiting for?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Samuel Beckett (1906–1989) was born near Dublin, studied French and Italian at Trinity College, and as a young man assisted James Joyce in Paris. During the Second World War he worked for the French Resistance and was honored for it afterward. He then began writing in French. En attendant Godot was published in 1952 and first staged in Paris in January 1953; Beckett's own English version followed in 1954. He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1969.
About quotations: the play was first published in the 1950s and is still under copyright, so this lesson describes it in our own words. See "Read the full text" above for where to find it.

Act I. On a country road with a single bare tree, Estragon struggles with his boot and Vladimir worries about the two thieves crucified beside Christ, since only one of the four Gospels says that one of them was saved. They are waiting for Godot. A pompous traveler, Pozzo, arrives driving his servant Lucky on a rope; ordered to "think," Lucky delivers a long, broken torrent of learned-sounding words. A boy brings word that Mr. Godot will not come this evening but surely tomorrow. Night falls. They agree to leave, and do not move.

Act II is the next evening. The tree has a few leaves. The friends wait again, though Estragon remembers little of the day before. Pozzo returns blind and Lucky has gone mute; Pozzo, asked when this happened, rejects the very question. The boy brings the same message and does not recognize them. Again they agree to go, and again they stay.

blocks.name: gb-beckett-tree
blocks.cap: The same evening, almost: what repeats between the two acts. Our summary.

blocks.html: The play makes waiting itself the drama. Its pattern of near-repetition suggests a life in which people hope, pass the time and keep each other company while the meaning they wait for does not arrive, or has not yet.

Beckett refused to explain Godot. Some readers see God (the name suggests it, though Beckett denied a simple meaning), some see hope, death, or the human need for purpose. Critics grouped the play with the "Theatre of the Absurd," yet many audiences find it warm: two friends who stay together however bleak the road.
Calling it a play where nothing happens. Things do happen: quarrels, kindnesses, a cruelty, a reversal of fortune. What never happens is the one thing they wait for.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Pascal's Pensées, earlier on this ladder, described people filling time with diversions so as not to face their condition; Vladimir and Estragon are masters of diversion.
Chekhov, at the start of this era, wrote of people waiting and talking while their lives slip away.
Kafka, also in this era, told absurd situations in calm, plain words.

Augustine: Beckett was fond of a saying about the two thieves that is often credited to him (scholars have not found it in his writings): do not despair, one thief was saved; do not presume, one was lost.
What are you waiting for? How do you spend the waiting?
Why do Vladimir and Estragon stay together?
Is the play hopeful, despairing or both?
Why might a writer refuse to say what his play means?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Who do you think Godot is? Why might Beckett never tell us?
  2. Why do Vladimir and Estragon keep waiting, even when Godot never comes?
  3. What is the best way to spend time while you wait for something?
  4. The friends quarrel but always make up. What keeps a friendship going?
  5. Pozzo changes completely between the acts. What does that suggest about life?
